arguments.title: The interest ban prevents direct holders from bargaining for a share of their money's earnings.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 The interest ban prevents direct holders from bargaining for a share of their money's earnings.

  • Because The bill bars issuers from paying interest just for holding tokens: “No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin.” [3].
  • Because In direct issuer-to-user arrangements, the interest that users do not receive is “instead retained (likely as profit) by the issuer.” [30].
  • So Users supply the money and bear its uninsured risk, yet the law blocks them from bargaining for interest solely for holding it. This preference for firms over their direct customers gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule as unfair.
arguments.con_html:
Response Barring one way to bargain over payment services does not by itself make issuers' reserve income an unjust transfer from their direct customers.

  • Because A payment stablecoin promises a fixed repayment: its issuer “is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value” [3]. That promise differs from a share of the issuer's investment earnings.
  • Because Providing that service has costs. The argument's source explains that issuers face “higher operating costs as they face more stringent capital, liquidity, and risk management standards” [37]. Total income from reserves is therefore not the same as profit taken without providing a service.
  • So The argument has not explained why funding a payment service from reserve income is unjust unless customers can also bargain for interest. A restriction on that contract term does not by itself establish the unfair preference for firms that the argument claims.

arguments.title: Drawing funds away from community banks threatens opportunities in poor and rural communities.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 9 Drawing funds away from community banks threatens opportunities in poor and rural communities.

  • Because This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01. It also needs that use to reduce funding for local lending. See C11.
  • Because Issuers cannot replace those banks' loans directly, because they must hold their assets as reserves.
  • Because The resulting lending loss would be “especially acute in rural and low-income areas” [29]; “stablecoins have no community lending obligations.” [29].
  • So Shifting funding away from community banks threatens a source of home, farm, and small-business loans in those places. Protecting people's chances to build a livelihood gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this expansion.
arguments.con_html:

original.title: Drawing funds away from community banks threatens opportunities in poor and rural communities.
original.pro_html:
Point 9 Drawing funds away from community banks threatens opportunities in poor and rural communities.

  • Because The lending analysis warns that deposits “could flow out of insured depository institutions and into payment stablecoins.” [29].
  • Because Issuers cannot replace those banks' loans directly: “they must invest virtually all their assets in designated short-term financial instruments held as reserves.” [42].
  • Because The resulting lending loss would be “especially acute in rural and low-income areas” [29]; “stablecoins have no community lending obligations.” [29].
  • So Shifting funding away from community banks threatens a source of home, farm, and small-business loans in those places. Protecting people's chances to build a livelihood gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this expansion.
original.con_html:
Response The community-lending forecast relies on a mistaken reading of exposed deposits and skips how reserve purchases affect bank funding.

  • Because Its rural-lending warning rests on “a one-third decline in deposit levels” [29]. Yet CRS describes the underlying transactional-deposit pool as a “$6.6 trillion market” [30] identified as potentially at risk, not a forecast that the whole pool will leave.
  • Because The original Treasury advisory presentation labels its scenarios “Hypothetical Design Components That Could Influence Market Behaviour” [31]. A pool of deposits that could switch is not a predicted outflow.
  • Because Buying Treasury backing can return the money to banks through the seller. In that case, the Council of Economic Advisers explains that total deposits are “unchanged—they have simply moved from one institution to another.” [32]
  • So Stablecoin balances do not measure deposits lost to the banking system. A claim about poor and rural borrowers also needs to establish which local banks lose usable funding. The cited forecast does not supply that link merely because issuers cannot make loans themselves.

arguments.title: A run can carry private payment risks into the wider economy and public finances.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 10 A run can carry private payment risks into the wider economy and public finances.

  • Because This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01.
  • Because The bill permits bank deposits as backing, so a rush to cash out tokens can pull funds from banks. See C09. Breaking the buck means falling below the promised dollar value.
  • Because Forced sales of backing assets can spread the stress: “These dynamics could create fire-sale patterns and turn a stablecoin run into stress on the banking system.” [43]. A fire sale is a hurried sale to raise cash.
  • Because A major issuer's collapse can reach people who never used stablecoins. See C10.
  • Because Pressure for a public rescue follows the same crisis: “Regulators would feel compelled to step in to prevent the collapse of the payment system.” [44]. If taxpayers fund a rescue, “even those who never engaged with crypto could bear the cost.” [6].
  • So Expanding these links exposes uninvolved workers, retirees, borrowers, and taxpayers to private firms' risks. [NAME] has reason to protect vulnerable people from the spillover and resist making strangers pay for it.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.

arguments.title: Commercial platforms gain another way to pressure people who depend on them for income.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 11 Commercial platforms gain another way to pressure people who depend on them for income.

  • Because The bill does not bar commercial issuers whose shares are not publicly traded. The bill does not create the combination of commerce and payments. But by removing regulatory uncertainty, the bill makes this route more usable. See C21.
  • Because A platform can use its existing business to make other payment products costly to switch to. See C22. Public Citizen gives the example of a retailer that “might disfavor a subcontractor if it failed to use the aggregator's stablecoin.” [2].
  • Because The bill's rule against forcing customers to buy another product may not reach this pressure from an issuer's affiliate. That rule is “significantly narrower than the statutory prohibition on tying applicable to banks, which applies to both the bank and its affiliates.” [45]
  • Note The bill limits this point. For public companies mainly outside finance, committee approval needs a finding that “the public company and the affiliates of the public company will comply with the tying prohibitions under paragraph (8)” [3]. So this criticism applies mainly outside that covered public-company route.
  • So Expanding this business model exposes small sellers and workers to payment terms they cannot readily refuse without risking income. Equal opportunity gives [NAME] a reason to resist making this power easier to use.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.

arguments.title: Wider dollar-token use threatens financial stability in vulnerable foreign economies.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 14 Wider dollar-token use threatens financial stability in vulnerable foreign economies.

  • Because This argument needs added use of dollar stablecoins. See C01.
  • Because Making dollar stablecoins more attractive can cause “greater substitution away from local foreign currencies.” [37]. This means people move away from their own country's money.
  • Because This makes money easier to move out quickly: “users can hold dollar proxies at home that can be instantly exchanged for real dollars offshore.” [7]. The risk is greater in “already volatile markets facing high inflation and sharp currency swings.” [7].
  • Because Wider substitution can also “undermine the monetary policy sovereignty of foreign countries.” [37]. Monetary policy sovereignty means a country's ability to manage its own money and economic conditions.
  • So Promoting dollar tokens exposes people in weaker economies to faster financial outflows and weaker tools for stabilizing their economies. [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people everywhere gives a reason to oppose imposing those risks on strangers abroad.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.

arguments.title: The public helps pay to oversee firms' new payment business.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 16 The public helps pay to oversee firms' new payment business.

  • Because The bill creates new costs for the Federal Reserve to oversee stablecoins. CBO explains who bears them: “Costs incurred by the Federal Reserve reduce remittances to the Treasury” [47]. Remittances here are the income the Fed sends to the government. CBO is the Congressional Budget Office.
  • Because CBO estimates that these administrative costs would reduce federal “revenues by $73 million over the 2025-2035 period.” [47].
  • So The public supplies part of the cost of running this private payment system, including people who never use it. Fair treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose placing those costs on the public instead of the firms earning the income.
arguments.con_html:
Response Public payment for oversight is not, by itself, an unfair subsidy for firms' payment operations.

  • Because CBO says the expense funds “examinations, risk monitoring, enforcement, and certifying state regulators.” [47] This estimate measures the public cost of supervision over eleven fiscal years.
  • Because Section 6 directs examinations at risks to “the stability of the financial system of the United States” [3]. So the spending buys protection for people outside the issuer-customer relationship.
  • So Nonusers help fund oversight from which nonusers also benefit. The argument supplies no reason why sharing the cost of this public protection treats them unjustly. The fact that firms could instead be charged does not establish that conclusion.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO reports that OCC and NCUA collect fees offsetting part of their costs, for net direct spending of $47 million versus $77 million gross. CBO also reports that the Federal Reserve's payments to the Treasury (remittances) have largely been suspended, which affects the timing of the $73 million revenue effect. CBO is the Congressional Budget Office. OCC is the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, a federal bank regulator. NCUA is the National Credit Union Administration. Sources: [47].

arguments.title: The licensing system would require officials to hear applicants who challenge their decisions.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The licensing system would require officials to hear applicants who challenge their decisions.

  • Because Different kinds of provider could qualify: “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [4]
  • Because Federal regulators could reject a substantially complete application only on safety grounds: “the activities of the applicant would be unsafe or unsound based on the factors described in subsection (c)” [3].
  • Because Applicants who appeal in time would have a right to present their case: “the applicant may appear, personally or through counsel, to submit written materials or provide oral testimony and oral argument” [3].
  • Because Listening to people who contest a decision puts tolerance into practice: disagreement does not erase their chance to explain themselves.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to support a system that judges applicants by safety and hears their reasons when they disagree with a refusal.
arguments.con_html:
Response Hearing a dispute about an issuer's fitness does not show listening to people across the differences named by this value.

  • Because Section 5 ties refusal to safety. Its factors include “financial condition and resources” [3] and “The competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders” [3].
  • Because The hearing is “to appeal the denial” [3]. It lets the applicant present evidence and arguments about that decision.
  • Because The range of eligible applicants concerns types of business. That range, and a dispute over meeting safety rules, do not show differences in the people involved, their backgrounds, or their beliefs.
  • So The argument shows a way to challenge a licensing decision. It does not show that this process puts listening to and accepting different people into practice. Disagreement about an application cannot supply that missing link by itself.

arguments.title: The bill would add protection to a payment route outside the companies and banks that can shut out unpopular voices.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill would add protection to a payment route outside the companies and banks that can shut out unpopular voices.

  • Because EFF reports a lawsuit alleging “targeting payments associated with Islam or Arab nationalities or ethnicity” [5] and “numerous examples of sex worker advocates facing account closures” [5]. EFF is the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital-rights group.
  • Because Stablecoins can move on networks open to users without a payment company's approval to join. CRS describes these networks as “decentralized, public, permissionless” [6]. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress.
  • Because Federal regulators could not reject an issuer simply for using such a network: “The issuance of a payment stablecoin on an open, public, or decentralized network shall not be a valid ground for denial of an application received under subsection (a).” [3]
  • Because Section 3's new issuance and sales limits exempt “the direct transfer of digital assets between 2 individuals acting on their own behalf and for their own lawful purposes, without the involvement of an intermediary” [3].
  • Because Section 3 also exempts payments through wallets people control themselves: “any transaction by means of a software or hardware wallet that facilitates an individual's own custody of digital assets” [3].
  • Because This route has served people outside an authoritarian state's banks. Circle's USDC aid to Venezuelan health workers was designed “to bypass the controls imposed by Maduro over the domestic financial system” [7]. USDC is the stablecoin issued by Circle.
  • Because Circle cites Amnesty International's reports of “healthcare workers being arrested for speaking out about unsafe working practices since the pandemic began” [7].
  • So The bill would add reserve duties (C04) and bankruptcy priority (C05) to regulated tokens while preserving open networks, lawful direct payments and wallets people control themselves. That protects funds sent through an alternative to ordinary payment gatekeepers.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to protect the means they use to speak, organize and support one another.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to favor protections for a payment route that supports lawful voices and ties beyond the approval of ordinary payment companies or authoritarian banks.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument does not show why protecting funds on an alternative payment route amounts to support for accepting unpopular voices.

  • Because Section 11 concerns “any insolvency proceeding of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under Federal or State law” [3]. This addresses an issuer's failure to repay, a different risk from refusing a user's lawful speech or group ties.
  • Because The direct-transfer and personal-wallet exceptions begin “This section shall not apply to” [3]. They limit section 3's new restrictions. The open-network rule likewise bars one particular reason for refusing an issuer's application.
  • Because The EFF passages above describe the refusals that motivate the argument's tolerance claim.
  • Because The Venezuelan source identifies a financial barrier: “typical bank receipts are subject to rigged forex rates” [7]. It does not identify the arrested workers as aid recipients or show that recipients had been refused payments for their views.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement does not mean favoring every safeguard for a tool they could use. The argument needs to connect this protection of money to supporting people across their differences.
  • So The examples describe payment exclusion and a way to deliver aid beyond currency controls. They do not show that the new financial protection supports the speaking, organizing, or acceptance of unpopular voices. Reports of arrests among healthcare workers cannot establish that claim for the aid recipients.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: Permitted issuers must be able to comply with lawful orders. The law firm Steptoe says freezing can reach tokens in non-custodial wallets (wallets a person controls without a company holding the coins). It says issuers will likely need some centralized control such as blacklisting. Sources: [8].

arguments.title: The bill would protect payment choices that fit migrants' and displaced people's different lives.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill would protect payment choices that fit migrants' and displaced people's different lives.

  • Because International money transfers “matter greatly for immigrant communities sending money to families abroad” [9].
  • Because MoneyGram's 2022 service used “Circle's USD Coin (USDC)” [10] and let wallet users move between cash and digital currency “all without requiring a bank account or credit card” [10]. USDC is the stablecoin issued by Circle.
  • Because UNHCR's USDC aid pilot put funds in phone wallets, “allowing people to travel within the country or cross borders without the need to carry cash” [11]. UNHCR is the United Nations refugee agency.
  • Because UNHCR explains why different payment options matter: “It’s also essential to provide people with a range of options for receiving aid, as one size does not fit all.” [11]
  • Because The bill would require issuers to “disclose in plain language all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming the payment stablecoins” [3].
  • Because Users would get advance warning of issuer fee changes: “such fees can only be changed upon not less than 7 days' prior notice to consumers” [3].
  • So Reserve duties (C04) and bankruptcy priority (C05) would protect regulated tokens used in these payments, while clear issuer fees would help users choose how to pay. These protections support ways of helping relatives and receiving aid that fit life across borders or without a bank account.
  • Because Accepting people whose lives differ includes making room for their cross-border family ties and their own choices about receiving help.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to favor protections that accommodate those choices and circumstances.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument treats protecting people's money and payment choices as accepting different people without defending that step.

  • Because The aid pilot serves practical needs: UNHCR says the funds help people “cover basic needs like rent of accommodation, food, medical care and heating during the winter” [11]. These passages show why the payment tools are useful.
  • Because The bill's fee rule gives information rights about buying and redeeming tokens.
  • Because The bankruptcy rule protects “the claim of a person holding payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [3]. The basis for this right is holding the token, whatever the holder's background or payment purpose.
  • Because Accepting people across differences is distinct from making any useful service safer for them. Identifying migrants or displaced people as users does not make every financial benefit to those users an expression of tolerance.
  • So The argument connects the bill to protection of money and information about issuer fees. It leaves the next step unsupported: why those changes express acceptance of cross-border family ties or different lives. The examples' usefulness does not show that value connection.

arguments.title: The bill would give users control over commercial uses of payment data that reveal their beliefs and group ties.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill would give users control over commercial uses of payment data that reveal their beliefs and group ties.

  • Because Linking identities to stablecoin payments can reveal “donations, memberships, habits, beliefs, and associations” [12].
  • Because Data brokers sort people by sensitive differences, including “their ethnicity or religion, their political affiliation, or their expected levels of spending” [13].
  • Because The Brennan Center identifies risks of “discrimination in housing, employment, and credit decisions” [13] from this commercial data market.
  • Because For covered public companies mainly outside finance, section 4(a)(12) restricts commercial uses of private personal information from stablecoin transactions without the consumer's consent. The restricted uses are targeted advertising or content, sale, and sharing with non-affiliates. See C20.
  • So Users could refuse these covered issuers permission to turn their private payment records into advertising profiles or pass them to commercial outsiders. This restricts a route through which beliefs and group ties become information used to sort and exclude people.
  • Because Tolerance gives [NAME] a reason to protect people's ability to keep different beliefs and associations without those differences becoming grounds for unfair treatment.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to favor these limits on commercial exposure of people's differences.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: The Brennan Center describes data brokers drawing on many sources, including public records, app developers, internet service providers (ISPs) and others. It does not mention stablecoin data. The consent condition covers targeting, personalizing or ranking advertising or other content, sale, and sharing with non-affiliates. It does not list a covered firm's own decisions about whom to serve, sharing within its corporate group, or government access. Coin Center's stated threats include government surveillance. Sources: [13], [3], [12].

arguments.title: More detailed customer checks increase the risk of rejecting religious and ethnic communities as suspect groups.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 More detailed customer checks increase the risk of rejecting religious and ethnic communities as suspect groups.

  • Because Section 4 requires closer customer checks. See C17. Steptoe identifies a change for some issuers in these know-your-customer (KYC) checks: “Therefore, these more granular KYC obligations will be an important change for some issuers.” [8] Steptoe is a law firm.
  • Because Checking customers can make their accounts unprofitable. Treasury's bank interviews found that checking nonprofit accounts “requires many resources and is often not profitable.” [14] Treasury's nonprofit consultations found that “diligence sometimes leads to closing accounts.” [14]
  • Because Avoiding penalties adds another incentive to reject customers. A 2024 congressional letter explains: “Banks are incentivized to close accounts in order to avoid enforcement” [15].
  • Because The same letter identifies who is exposed: “Financial institutions may consider Muslim and Arab, Middle Eastern, and South Asian Americans “high risk,” potentially erroneously, when sending payments or remittances abroad or donating to charities or religious institutions.” [15]
  • So Adding more detailed checks to stablecoin issuance strengthens a known incentive to reject customers whose ordinary religious giving or family payments abroad appear risky.
  • Because Accepting people across religious and cultural differences gives [NAME] a reason to resist treating those differences as grounds for blanket rejection.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose extending this risk of group-based exclusion to more stablecoin issuers and their customers.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: FinCEN's 2019 guidance required money services businesses (MSBs) to have anti-money-laundering (AML) programs, including verifying customer identification and risk-based controls. A bank-agency statement says there is no requirement for unique additional diligence for charities or nonprofits as a class. S.1582 directs tailored rules. Bank rules for customer identification programs (CIP) also allow checks that do not use documents (non-documentary procedures). FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. Sources: [16], [17], [18], [3].

arguments.title: Added identity checks raise the risk of excluding people whose documents or life histories do not fit an issuer's usual process.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Added identity checks raise the risk of excluding people whose documents or life histories do not fit an issuer's usual process.

  • Because Section 4 requires issuers to identify and verify account holders. See C17. This adds formal rules for some issuers operating as money-transfer firms. Steptoe explains their current freedom over customer checks: “MSBs are not subject to CIP or CDD rules, meaning they have additional flexibility with respect to how they KYC users.” [8] MSBs are money-services businesses, including money-transfer firms. CIP, CDD and KYC refer to identity and customer-risk checks. Steptoe is a law firm.
  • Because Treasury's January 2025 working draft, based on stakeholder roundtables, calls lack of suitable identification “a primary barrier many communities face in accessing the financial system.” [19]
  • Because The draft records different sources of that barrier: “Refugees and asylees may arrive in the United States without adequate identification documents.” [19] It also reports that “Tribal IDs used by Indigenous communities may not be recognized by financial institutions as a valid form of identification.” [19]
  • Because Name and gender changes create another mismatch: “Transgender and nonbinary people face a patchwork of state policies that make it challenging to update gender markers on IDs or to make legal name changes.” [19] People leaving prison also reported “loss or confiscation of identification documents during incarceration.” [19]
  • Because Outcomes depend on how the rules and issuers handle these cases. The same draft describes institutions that “use alternative IDs or non-documentary verification methods” [19], and Steptoe says “It remains to be seen whether PPSIs will be subject to CIP/CDD requirements that match existing rules for other BSA-regulated financial institutions” [8]. PPSIs are permitted issuers. BSA is the Bank Secrecy Act, the main U.S. law against money laundering.
  • So The bill extends more detailed verification duties to issuers serving people whom existing financial checks already struggle to recognize. Where issuers do not adopt such alternatives, that raises the risk of rejection from direct accounts for people with these backgrounds and identities.
  • Because Accepting people across different backgrounds and identities gives [NAME] a reason to resist excluding them when their documents differ or are hard to replace.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose extending this barrier to participation.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.

A bank-agency statement says there is no requirement for unique additional diligence for charities or nonprofits as a class. S.1582 directs tailored rules. Bank rules for customer identification programs (CIP) also allow checks that do not use documents (non-documentary procedures). FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. Sources: [16], [17], [18], [3].

arguments.title: Wider monitoring puts private ties to unpopular groups at greater risk of exposure, deterring participation.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Wider monitoring puts private ties to unpopular groups at greater risk of exposure, deterring participation.

  • Because Section 9(d) requires new guidance and rules for how issuers monitor transfers on blockchains, which are shared digital records of transfers. This could cover more transfers than issuers' current duties. See C19. Issuers must also identify their account holders. See C17.
  • Because Tracking can reach transfers between people who hold their own tokens: “stablecoins can be tracked across a blockchain as they move between holders, even when the transfers happen between wallets that are unhosted by intermediaries.” [20]
  • So Combining identified issuer accounts with wider tracing makes donations, dues and other payments easier to link to people beyond their dealings with the issuer. To the extent the rules require that monitoring, the bill creates an added route for exposing their group ties.
  • Because Exposure of such ties can deter association. In NAACP v. Alabama, the Supreme Court recorded that exposure of members' identities had brought “economic reprisal, loss of employment, threat of physical coercion, and other manifestations of public hostility.” [21]
  • Because Government collection itself adds risk. In its 2021 decision on donor records, Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, the Court said deterrence can occur even with “no disclosure to the general public.” [22] The Court explained that “each governmental demand for disclosure brings with it an additional risk of chill.” [22]
  • Because [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives [NAME] a reason to protect the private support and contact that let unpopular groups speak and be heard.
  • So By opening more transfers to monitoring, the bill increases the risk of deterring the support and contact that let different groups be heard and understood. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.con_html:
Response FinCEN's later proposal does not support the added monitoring on which this reason depends. The proposal and Section 9's unwritten rules are in C19. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency.

  • So The proposal is not final and Section 9's standards remain to be written, so the outcome is open. on this evidence, the argument's step from the bill to issuers monitoring transfers beyond their own dealings is unsupported. The disclosure cases explain why exposure matters, but cannot establish that the bill increases it.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Tether announced in 2024 that it would monitor secondary markets with Chainalysis tools, and confirmed adoption in May 2025. Research under Section 9 must consider the amount and sensitivity of information and privacy risks. FinCEN's guidance or rules are due within 3 years. The cited Cato commentary discusses earlier bill drafts. The two cited Supreme Court cases concern government demands for membership or donor records. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. original.title: Wider monitoring puts private ties to unpopular groups at greater risk of exposure, deterring participation.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Wider monitoring puts private ties to unpopular groups at greater risk of exposure, deterring participation.

  • Because Section 9(d) requires new guidance and rules covering “Standards for payment stablecoin issuers' systems and practices to monitor transactions on blockchains” [3]. Blockchains are shared digital records of transfers.
  • Because This opens a wider field for monitoring than issuers' current duties. Steptoe explains: “At present, stablecoin issuers are responsible for AML compliance with respect to primary market transactions to which they are a party, but are not expected to monitor all transactions across the entirety of the blockchain.” [8] Here, AML means checks against money laundering, and primary transactions are purchases or sales involving the issuer itself.
  • Because The final reach depends on rulemaking. Steptoe reads the text as one that “strongly suggests that FinCEN's rules or guidance will expect PPSIs to monitor and intervene in transactions in both the primary and, to at least some degree, secondary markets.” [8]
  • Because Tracking can reach transfers between people who hold their own tokens: “stablecoins can be tracked across a blockchain as they move between holders, even when the transfers happen between wallets that are unhosted by intermediaries.” [20]
  • So Combining identified issuer accounts with wider tracing makes donations, dues and other payments easier to link to people beyond their dealings with the issuer. To the extent the rules require that monitoring, the bill creates an added route for exposing their group ties.
  • Because Exposure of such ties can deter association. In NAACP v. Alabama, the Supreme Court recorded that exposure of members' identities had brought “economic reprisal, loss of employment, threat of physical coercion, and other manifestations of public hostility.” [21]
  • Because Government collection itself adds risk. In its 2021 decision on donor records, Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, the Court said deterrence can occur even with “no disclosure to the general public.” [22] It explained that “each governmental demand for disclosure brings with it an additional risk of chill.” [22]
  • Because [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives [NAME] a reason to protect the private support and contact that let unpopular groups speak and be heard.
  • So By opening more transfers to monitoring, the bill increases the risk of deterring the support and contact that let different groups be heard and understood. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.con_html:
Response FinCEN's later proposal does not support the added monitoring on which this reason depends.

  • Because In April 2026, FinCEN proposed rules for issuers and stated: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [23]. It also stated: “FinCEN is also not proposing to require PPSIs to file SARs on secondary market transactions” [23]. Secondary-market activity is activity not directly involving the issuer.
  • Because Section 9's separate rules must be “based on the results of the research and risk assessments required under this section” [3]. That research must consider “Privacy risks associated with the information that is collected or reviewed.” [3]
  • So The proposal is not final and Section 9's standards remain to be written, so the outcome is open. On this record, the PRO's step from the bill to issuers monitoring transfers beyond their own dealings is unsupported. The disclosure cases explain why exposure matters, but cannot establish that the bill increases it.

Evidence note: Tether announced Chainalysis monitoring of secondary markets in 2024 and confirmed adoption in May 2025. Section 9 research must consider the amount and sensitivity of information and privacy risks, and FinCEN's guidance or rules are due within 3 years. The cited Cato commentary discusses earlier bill drafts. The two Supreme Court cases concern government demands for membership or donor records. Sources: [24], [25], [3], [20].

arguments.title: Mandatory payment-blocking powers strengthen financial exclusion over disputed international judicial work.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Mandatory payment-blocking powers strengthen financial exclusion over disputed international judicial work.

  • Because The bill's freezing requirement adds a legal condition, including for issuers that did not build this power into their tokens. See C13.
  • Because Foreign issuers also need this capability to reach U.S. customers through digital-asset services. See C14.
  • Because Existing sanctions already targeted International Criminal Court judges over their rulings. UN News reported the UN rights chief's criticism that the sanctions “attack the judges for performing their judicial functions” [26].
  • Because The February 2025 sanctions order expressly covers foreign people found “to have directly engaged in any effort by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person without consent of that person’s country of nationality” [27]. Covered assets “are blocked and may not be transferred, paid, exported, withdrawn, or otherwise dealt in” [27].
  • Because Section 4(a)(6)(A) directs Treasury to coordinate with issuers so they can “effectively block a payment stablecoin of the foreign person” [3] when Treasury acts to block that person's property.
  • So Requiring issuers to build and use freezing powers strengthens the means to enforce existing financial penalties against people for judicial work the U.S. government rejects.
  • Note Requiring a lawful order does not resolve that conflict with tolerance. Section 4(a)(5)(vi) also requires “maintenance of an effective economic sanctions compliance program, including verification of sanctions lists, consistent with Federal law.” [3] The existing order makes the judicial work it specifies a ground for sanctions. The harm to acceptance in this argument is stronger enforcement of those penalties.
  • Note Holding tokens in one's own wallet does not remove issuer control. See C13.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to resist cutting them off from ordinary payments over disputed legal judgments, across national and political differences.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose making that financial exclusion easier to enforce.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument does not explain why accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to resist penalties for the judges' exercise of court power.

  • Because The sanctions order targets the efforts quoted above. So the cited dispute concerns the exercise of court power over others, not simply the expression of a different view.
  • Because Section 4's lawful-order duty adds a means of enforcing sanctions. That duty supplies no premise (stated reason) about why this particular use conflicts with tolerance.
  • Because Tolerance supports accepting people and hearing their views. The argument needs an added premise that cutting off ordinary payments for this exercise of court power rejects the judges for their differences. Describing the judicial work as disputed does not establish that premise.
  • So The example moves from a disagreement about court power to a claim about rejecting different people without supporting that move. Making the sanctions easier to enforce cannot fill this gap. Calling the sanctions lawful cannot fill this gap either.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: Permitted issuers must be able to comply with lawful orders. The law firm Steptoe says freezing can reach tokens in non-custodial wallets (wallets a person controls without a company holding the coins). It says issuers will likely need some centralized control such as blacklisting. Sources: [8].

arguments.title: Disrupting payments for fentanyl ingredients helps prevent fatal poisoning.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Disrupting payments for fentanyl ingredients helps prevent fatal poisoning.

  • Because Drug traffickers use stablecoins to buy ingredients and equipment: “Mexico-based TCOs are increasingly purchasing fentanyl precursor chemicals and manufacturing equipment from PRC-based suppliers in virtual currency, including bitcoin, ether, monero, and tether, among others.” [4] TCOs are transnational criminal organizations. PRC means the People's Republic of China.
  • Because The bill requires issuers to monitor and report suspicious transactions. See C27.
  • Because The bill also adds yearly declarations that issuers have put crime-control programs in place: “on an annual basis thereafter” and “a certification that the issuer has implemented anti-money laundering and economic sanctions compliance programs” [3].
  • Because Such reporting helps investigators stop the suppliers. See C18.
  • Because The bill also makes obeying federal blocking orders a legal duty, for permitted issuers (C13) and for foreign issuers on U.S. services (C14). This is separate from finding the payments.
  • Because The danger reaches Americans seeking medicine. The Drug Enforcement Administration reports fake pills sold to “unsuspecting customers in the United States who believe they are purchasing real pharmaceutical drugs” [5].
  • Because These pills can cause fatal poisoning. Treasury's financial crime agency, FinCEN, reports deaths where “victims were unaware that other illicit drugs or counterfeit prescription medications they used contained lethal doses of fentanyl.” [4]
  • So Required reporting, yearly accountability, and enforceable blocking duties strengthen investigators' means to interrupt ingredient purchases and the production they support. Cutting this supply of poisonous drugs serves [NAME]'s interest in protecting health and avoiding danger.
arguments.con_html:
Response The fentanyl evidence does not connect the added issuer oversight to newly detected ingredient purchases.

  • Because Suppliers hide purchases behind front companies to “create the façade of a legitimate transaction and to obfuscate the source of the illicit diversion.” [4]
  • Because The yearly statement confirms a crime-control program. It supplies no information about a particular buyer or purchase.
  • Because An issuer can see a transfer yet lack the facts needed to recognize a crime. FinCEN's proposal on this is in C18. Secondary-market transactions are those not directly involving the issuer.
  • So This response does not answer the point about blocking purchases once they are identified. The missing step is identifying concealed purchases: the argument has not shown how reporting and yearly accountability supply that information.

arguments.title: Blocking terrorist funds helps protect people in the United States from violence.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Blocking terrorist funds helps protect people in the United States from violence.

  • Because ISIS uses “stablecoins like Tether (USDT) to raise and move funds” [17]. USDT is the stablecoin issued by Tether.
  • Because ISIS's money supports both violence and the promotion of violence. The coalition against ISIS financing seeks to deprive it of “resources to commit atrocities and spread its extremist ideology.” [18]
  • Because This promotion threatens people at home. FinCEN reports that ISIS urges “attacks in the United States and Western countries” [17]. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency.
  • Because This route runs through ISIS's wider funding and promotion, not through direct payment for most attacks at home. The same FinCEN advisory says “HVE activities tend to be funded through legal means, like personal savings and the sale of personal assets.” [17] HVE means homegrown violent extremist.
  • Because Seizing stablecoins has already disrupted terrorist financing. In a case involving USDT intended for Hamas, the FBI reported: “By successfully disrupting access to these funds, we have weakened their ability to function,” [10]. Here, “their” means Hamas.
  • Because The bill makes foreign issuers' access through U.S. providers depend on blocking capability and compliance. See C14. Permitted issuers have a similar duty. See C13.
  • So The bill adds pressure to carry out freezes against terrorist funds. Denying these resources restricts support for violence and the promotion of attacks on Americans. That advances [NAME]'s personal safety at home.
arguments.con_html:
Response The terrorism evidence does not show that added U.S. trading pressure would cut funding for U.S. attacks or the propaganda that encourages them.

  • Because For the costs of domestic attacks, the source says homegrown violent extremists' activities tend to be funded through legal means (quoted above). That evidence does not connect their attack budgets to the overseas stablecoin fundraising cited.

original.title: Blocking terrorist funds helps protect people in the United States from violence.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Blocking terrorist funds helps protect people in the United States from violence.

  • Because ISIS uses “stablecoins like Tether (USDT) to raise and move funds” [17].
  • Because Its money supports both violence and its promotion. The coalition against ISIS financing seeks to deprive it of “resources to commit atrocities and spread its extremist ideology.” [18]
  • Because This promotion threatens people at home. FinCEN reports that ISIS urges “attacks in the United States and Western countries” [17].
  • Because This route runs through ISIS's wider funding and promotion, not through direct payment for most attacks at home. arguments.title: Disrupting investment scams helps protect mental health.
arguments.pro_html:

arguments.title: Moving everyday money into uninsured stablecoins would put funds needed for medical care at risk of loss or delay.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Moving everyday money into uninsured stablecoins would put funds needed for medical care at risk of loss or delay.

  • Because This argument needs some everyday household money to move into stablecoins. See C02.
  • Because Stablecoins issued under this framework “are not federally insured.” [1]
  • Because Backing a $1 token with reserves does not guarantee it can be resold for $1 where ordinary customers trade. Researchers identify the bill's “omission of any reference to maintaining par-value exchange in the secondary market (where most stablecoin users actually transact)” [23]. The secondary market is where people trade with each other, not with the issuer.
  • Because If an issuer fails, money can be frozen by a bankruptcy pause on exchanging tokens for money. See C08.
  • Because Available money matters for ordinary Americans' care. The Federal Reserve reports: “Twenty-eight percent of adults went without some form of medical care in 2024 because they could not afford it” [24].
  • So Wider use would expose more household payment funds to losses or freezes when people need money for medicine and treatment.
  • So Protecting access to care gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose this shift.
  • Note A claim on reserve assets in bankruptcy does not make money spendable while redemptions are frozen.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: The researchers cited by the argument state the Act substantially improves reserve quality and disclosure. The bill also directs rules on operational and information technology (IT) risk. Sources: [23], [3].

Evidence note: Brookings says that if holders are not paid interest, they have incentives to keep their holdings small. It also says faster payments let a given volume of stablecoins support more payments. Federal Reserve Governor Waller said in February 2025 that use of stablecoins by ordinary customers (retail use) was very limited. The governor said a significant retail impact would probably take years. The governor also said merchants could have an incentive to accept stablecoins if the coins reduce fees or attract customers. Brookings is a policy research group. Sources: [22], [25].

Evidence note: Federal Reserve Governor Waller describes limited use of stablecoins by ordinary customers (retail use) and says a significant retail impact would probably take years. Resales below the promised value (below par) and bankruptcy stays (court pauses on collecting money) were possible before this bill. These facts limit how large the effect would be and how soon it would come, and they show what was already possible before the bill. Sources: [25], [23], [26].

arguments.title: The bill strengthens the state’s tools for finding and cutting off funds for terrorists, cartels, and other security threats.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill strengthens the state’s tools for finding and cutting off funds for terrorists, cartels, and other security threats.

  • Because Stablecoins already serve these threats: “Evidence points to increased use for terrorist financing and money laundering.” [3]
  • Because Permitted issuers must check their account holders and report suspicious transactions: “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [4]. The reporting duty is in C27, and whether it helps identify payments is in C18.
  • Because Issuers must certify programs aimed at preventing “facilitating money laundering for cartels and organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations” [4]. Failure to submit the certification lets regulators “revoke the approval of the payment stablecoin issuer under this section.” [4]
  • Because The bill bars officers and directors convicted of felonies involving “cybercrime, money laundering, financing of terrorism, or financial fraud” [4]. Federal licensing also weighs the “competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders” [4].
  • Because The bill makes the ability and willingness to obey federal blocking orders a condition of issuance. See C13.
  • Because Treasury can act against foreign issuers that defy those orders, after notice. See C14.
  • Because The foreign-issuer registration review checks “whether the foreign payment stablecoin issuer presents illicit finance risks to the United States.” [4] Registered issuers must “consent to United States jurisdiction relating to the enforcement of this Act.” [4]
  • Because That foreign-issuer route excludes countries under sweeping U.S. sanctions or designated as major money-laundering risks: the country must be “not subject to comprehensive economic sanctions by the United States or in a jurisdiction that the Secretary of the Treasury has determined to be a jurisdiction of primary money laundering concern.” [4]
  • Because Treasury must research better detection methods, and its financial-crime agency must issue guidance and rules on monitoring blockchain transfers. See C19. Some services can hide who sends or receives money.
  • So Licensing checks, reporting, blocking technology, and access to U.S. trading platforms give the state ways to trace and interrupt threat financing. Better detection rules extend those defenses as methods change. That strengthens the country's ability to protect its citizens.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument does not establish added ability to find threat-linked funds soon enough to interrupt them.

  • Because The bill requires “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, high-value transactions, and appropriate enhanced due diligence” [4]. The tracing problem extends to later transfers. See C18.
  • Because Finding funds soon enough is a separate problem from having authority to freeze them: “current practices to block and freeze accounts may be too slow and too late to prevent illicit transactions” [5]. Section 9 requires research and later rules on detection. It calls for evaluating “Improvements in the ability of financial institutions to detect illicit activity involving digital assets.” [4]
  • Because FinCEN's April 2026 proposal keeps secondary-market duties for blocking and lawful orders, but would not require anti-money-laundering (AML) monitoring in the secondary market. See C18. The proposal is not final and is separate from Section 9. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency.
  • So This response does not answer the freezing duty, management screening, and foreign-issuer conditions. The response challenges the argument's inference that licensing and reporting rules improve the timely detection of threat-linked transfers after issuance.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: The April 2026 proposed rule from FinCEN and OFAC would apply duties in the secondary market (trades between other people, not with the issuer) to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. The proposal does not require issuers, as part of a program against money laundering and the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT), to monitor secondary-market activity. It also does not require them to file suspicious activity reports (SARs) on secondary-market transactions. The proposal asks for public comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. OFAC is the Office of Foreign Assets Control, which enforces U.S. sanctions. Sources: [6].

Evidence note: FinCEN's 2019 guidance treats administrators and exchangers as money transmitters with anti-money-laundering (AML) duties. Tether reported assisting a $23 million freeze in March 2025 on transfers linked to Garantex, a sanctioned exchange. Issuers' smart contracts (software that runs on the blockchain) process on-chain transfers. Treasury's March 2026 report says analytics tools can detect suspicious patterns. FinCEN's April 2026 proposal keeps secondary-market duties for blocking and lawful orders. It does not keep them for monitoring under an anti-money-laundering program or for suspicious activity reports (SARs). FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. Tether is a dollar-linked stablecoin and the company that issues it. Sources: [7], [8], [9], [10], [6].

arguments.title: The bill limits weak reserves and poor oversight that can turn mass withdrawals into a wider financial crisis.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill limits weak reserves and poor oversight that can turn mass withdrawals into a wider financial crisis.

  • Because Risky reserves expose payment money to a run—a rush to withdraw: “Private money backed by risky assets with inadequate capital would be vulnerable to destabilizing runs and lose its ability to function as a medium of exchange.” [3]
  • Because Forced sales can spread the damage: an issuer in crisis “might be forced to sell off its treasuries in panic, resulting in broader damage and loss of confidence to the financial system.” [11]
  • Because The bill requires full backing with cash or other assets readily sold or withdrawn. See C04.
  • Because The bill limits the use of backing assets for other purposes: “Reserves required under paragraph (1)(A) may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, either directly or indirectly” [4]. To rehypothecate means to reuse an asset as security for a loan. The listed exceptions cover specified reserve transactions, custody, and raising cash for redemptions.
  • Because Regulators must set “reserve asset diversification, including deposit concentration at banking institutions, and interest rate risk management standards” [4]. These address exposure to one bank and losses from changes in interest rates.
  • Because Reserve reports make the backing open to checks: issuers must “publish the monthly composition of the issuer's reserves on the website of the issuer” [4], and reports must be “examined by a registered public accounting firm.” [4]
  • Because Federal examinations assess risks to “the stability of the financial system of the United States” [4]. For issuers under federal enforcement, regulators can order them to “take affirmative action to correct the conditions resulting from any such violation or practice.” [4]
  • Because State regimes face federal certification against national requirements: the approval test is that the regime “meets or exceeds the standards and requirements described in subsection (a)” [4]. In unusual and urgent circumstances, federal authorities can “take an enforcement action against a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer or an institution-affiliated party of such issuer for violations of this Act during such unusual and exigent circumstances.” [4]
  • Because Foreign issuers using the bill's U.S. access route must face comparable regulation, including reserve rules: Treasury must find a regime “comparable to the regulatory and supervisory regime established under this Act, including, in particular, the requirements under section 4(a).” [4] Registration review also considers “whether the foreign payment stablecoin presents a risk to the financial stability of the United States” [4].
  • So Full backing, limits on reserve risks and use, and enforceable oversight address the conditions that cause runs and forced sales. Reducing those routes to a financial crisis protects the stable U.S. economy [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument leaves out how a shortage of cash links the reserves the bill permits to the panic selling the argument says the bill reduces.

  • Because The bill allows reserves held as bank deposits and cash borrowed against Treasury securities: “funds held as demand deposits” [4]; “money received under repurchase agreements, with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer acting as a seller of securities” [4]. A repurchase agreement is short-term borrowing against securities.
  • Because A promise to repay with these assets differs from cash available during stress. The argument's source explains that “uninsured deposits are risky and illiquid” [12], “raising the possibility that stablecoins backed by these assets will not offer a stable value and will be prone to runs” [12], unless those risks are reduced by “capital, liquidity, and risk management standards” [12]. The source also says these deposits create “direct two-way interconnections between the risk of banks and the risk of stablecoins.” [12]
  • Because Borrowing to meet withdrawals also creates a feedback problem: “While repo transactions are generally low risk, the provisions would allow stablecoin issuers to borrow, creating leverage. In periods when redemptions were increasing, this could prompt even more redemptions.” [5] Leverage means using borrowed money.
  • Because The bill directs regulators to set capital, liquidity, and deposit-concentration rules. Their substance matters: “Without appropriate standards to reduce runs and limit interconnections, stablecoins could create the type of fire sale dynamics from prime money market mutual funds (MMFs) during the Global Financial Crisis.” [12] A fire sale is a hurried sale of assets to raise cash.
  • So This response does not answer the backing duty, limits on reuse, and public reports. The response challenges the further claim that these rules address the conditions that cause runs: they do not show how cash stays available when deposits freeze or borrowing fuels further withdrawals. The required standards also remain to be written.

arguments.title: The bill protects payment funds when an issuer or a firm safeguarding assets fails.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill protects payment funds when an issuer or a firm safeguarding assets fails.

  • Because Covered custodians—firms safeguarding stablecoin reserves, coins used as collateral, or keys used to issue coins—must protect customer property from their own creditors and generally keep it separate. See C07.
  • Because In an issuer's failure, coin holders have first claims on required reserves. See C05.
  • Because If reserves fall short, holders' unpaid claims also get priority on the issuer's other assets to cover missing required reserves. See C06.
  • Because The issuer can ask the court to act. If the court finds reserves available for payments to similarly placed holders, it must try to approve distributions promptly: “the court shall use best efforts to enter a final order to begin distributions under this paragraph not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [4]
  • Because These protections serve access to payment money after failure: “Reserve assets of a stablecoin should be segregated and prioritized in bankruptcy, so that holders can still access their payment stablecoins if a stablecoin issuer were to fail.” [3]
  • So Protecting payment assets and giving holders a route to recover them limits the disruption a failed firm causes to households, businesses, and commerce. That protects national economic stability.
arguments.con_html:

  • Because Holders' claims would outrank “general administrative claims relating to the estate representative preserving the bankruptcy estate” [SES 13]. Lawyers warn: “The subordination of administrative claims to the shortfall claims may increase the likelihood that the estate will become administratively insolvent or that a reorganization of the debtor issuer will not be feasible.” [SES 13] This means the estate could have too little money to pay for the bankruptcy process or to keep the firm running.
  • Because Excluding reserves from the issuer's bankruptcy estate does not release them for payments. The bill expressly freezes “the redemption of payment stablecoins” [4]. The bill's target is a best-efforts order to begin distributions “not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [4] This is neither a deadline measured from failure nor a deadline for completing payouts.
  • Because The custody rule also has a cash exception for bank deposits held as reserves. See C07. So the general segregation rule does not shield that cash from the bank's own failure.
  • So The argument moves from stronger legal claims to better access to payment cash without resolving the obstacle to funding recovery, the cash-deposit exception, or the statutory pause. The argument has not shown that the bill's priority rules deliver the less disruptive recovery it claims.

original.title: It protects payment funds when an issuer or a firm safeguarding assets fails.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects payment funds when an issuer or a firm safeguarding assets fails.

  • Because Covered custodians—firms safeguarding stablecoin reserves, coins used as collateral, or keys used to issue coins—must protect customer property from their own creditors: “take such steps as are appropriate to protect the payment stablecoins, private keys, cash, and other property of a customer from the claims of creditors of the person.” [4] The bill’s general rule is that the property “shall be segregated from and not be commingled with the assets of the person.” [4]
  • Because In an issuer’s failure, coin holders have first claims on required reserves. Their claims rank “over the claims of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and any other holder of claims against the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [4].
  • Because If reserves fall short, holders’ unpaid claims also get priority on the issuer’s other assets to cover missing required reserves: “shall have first priority over any other claim” [4].
  • Because On the issuer’s request, if the court finds reserves available for payments to similarly placed holders, it must try to approve distributions promptly: “the court shall use best efforts to enter a final order to begin distributions under this paragraph not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [4]
  • Because These protections serve access to payment money after failure: “Reserve assets of a stablecoin should be segregated and prioritized in bankruptcy, so that holders can still access their payment stablecoins if a stablecoin issuer were to fail.” [3]
  • So Protecting payment assets and giving holders a route to recover them limits the disruption a failed firm causes to households, businesses, and commerce. That protects national economic stability.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO's route from creditor priority to less payment disruption skips a funding obstacle created by that same priority.

  • Because When required reserves are missing, section 11 puts holders' claims ahead of the expenses of running the bankruptcy. Bankruptcy lawyers explain that these claims would outrank “general administrative claims relating to the estate representative preserving the bankruptcy estate” [13]. Their warning concerns the repayment process itself: “The subordination of administrative claims to the shortfall claims may increase the likelihood that the estate will become administratively insolvent or that a reorganization of the debtor issuer will not be feasible.” [13] This means too little money to pay for the process or keep the firm operating.
  • Because Excluding reserves from the issuer's bankruptcy estate does not release them for payments. The bill expressly freezes “the redemption of payment stablecoins” [4]. Its target is a best-efforts order to begin distributions “not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [4] This is neither a deadline measured from failure nor a deadline for completing payouts.
  • Because The custody rule also has a cash exception. Bank deposits held as reserves “shall not be subject to any requirement relating to the separation of such cash from the property of the applicable depository institution” [4]. The general segregation rule therefore does not shield that cash from the bank's own failure.
  • So The PRO moves from stronger legal claims to better access to payment cash without resolving the obstacle to funding recovery, the cash-deposit exception, or the statutory pause. It has not shown that its priority rules deliver the less disruptive recovery it claims.

arguments.title: The bill requires defenses against technical failures and cyberattacks on payments.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill requires defenses against technical failures and cyberattacks on payments.

  • Because Stablecoins “could undermine the safety of payments if their operations are not robust to a range of operational and cyber threats.” [3]
  • Because Regulators must establish “appropriate operational, compliance, and information technology risk management principles-based requirements and standards” [4].
  • So Requiring issuers to manage these risks strengthens defenses against failures and attacks that interrupt payments. Reliable payments help keep U.S. commerce working under threat.
arguments.con_html:
Response A general duty to set issuer standards does not establish an added defense against failures of the shared networks that carry payments.

  • Because That instruction to set standards does not specify a new recovery method or how an issuer would restore a failed shared blockchain—the network recording its payments.
  • Because Analysis identifies the missing mechanism, asking whether coins could move to another blockchain after an outage: “Mechanisms to protect users in these situations exist in traditional payments, and work is ongoing to develop them for stablecoins based on permissionless blockchains.” [5] Such blockchains let people join without an operator's approval.
  • So This response does not answer the protection from issuer-level standards. The response challenges whether the claim reaches outages on shared networks. These standards are not shown to improve such outages.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: The FTC's Safeguards rules cover firms that send money by wire (wire transferors). New York licensees had duties to recover from cyberattacks. FTC is the Federal Trade Commission. Sources: [14], [15].

arguments.title: The bill limits the spread of stablecoin trouble into banking and ordinary commerce.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 The bill limits the spread of stablecoin trouble into banking and ordinary commerce.

  • Because Public companies mainly outside finance, and companies they wholly or mostly own, need unanimous approval from the bill's federal review committee before issuing stablecoins. The finding must include that issuance “will not pose a material risk to the safety and soundness of the United States banking system, the financial stability of the United States, or the Deposit Insurance Fund” [4].
  • Because This review targets the spread of financial trouble: “This provision aims to separate damage to the financial side of a large company from spreading to its non-financial functions.” [11]
  • Because The bill also narrows the issuer's business: “Issuers’ activities are restricted to offering and redeeming stablecoins and ancillary activities.” [12] Ancillary activities are supporting work, such as managing reserves and safeguarding assets.
  • So A safety gate for these commercial groups, together with limits on issuer activities, restricts routes through which payment troubles spread across the economy. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a stable country.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: Brookings says the GENIUS Act does not strictly protect the separation of banking and commerce. The activity limit applies to the issuer, and the committee test applies to public companies. Brookings is a policy research group. Sources: [12], [4].

arguments.title: The bill limits corporate barriers that can put payments under concentrated private control.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 The bill limits corporate barriers that can put payments under concentrated private control.

  • Because Such barriers threaten economic stability. Brookings warns about firms that use private data or raise the costs of switching to other payment products. See C22. Brookings is a policy research group.
  • Because The bill bars issuers from forcing customers to buy another paid product, or to avoid a competitor: an issuer “may not provide services to a customer on the condition that the customer obtain an additional paid product or service from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, or any of its subsidiaries, or agree to not obtain an additional product or service from a competitor.” [4]
  • Because The bill also directs regulators to assess, and lets them set, standards to “promote compatibility and interoperability” [4], so payment systems can work with each other.
  • So The ban protects customers' access to competing services, while the standards power addresses barriers between payment systems. Keeping money and commerce from being locked inside one company's services protects economic and monetary stability.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument treats access to competing products as evidence that users can move their payment money between competing networks.

  • Because The argument's source identifies a distinct cause of concentration and the risk from higher switching costs. See C22. Neither problem requires a forced sale of another product.
  • Because The bill bars requiring an “additional paid product or service” [4]. These sales conditions differ from the cost and technical ability to move money out of a network.
  • Because Section 12 says regulators “shall assess and, if necessary, may” [4] prescribe standards for systems to work together. Section 12 supplies a power to set standards, not a requirement that issuers accept transfers across their networks.
  • So The argument has not connected its sales ban and standards power to lower switching barriers. Permission to buy a competing service does not establish that payment balances can move there. The argument's conclusion about preventing money and commerce from being locked inside a platform skips that step.

arguments.title: The bill removes issuer-paid interest as an incentive to move money out of banks.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 The bill removes issuer-paid interest as an incentive to move money out of banks.

  • Because The bill forbids both permitted and foreign issuers to pay interest or yield solely for holding or using their coins, and such interest could otherwise draw money away from bank deposits. See C12.
  • So Removing this incentive protects bank funding for lending and a channel through which the central bank steadies the economy. Both support the national stability [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that much stablecoin use by ordinary customers (retail use) occurs through exchanges (trading platforms). CRS says GENIUS does not explicitly prevent exchanges from paying rewards on coins they hold, and that many exchanges do pay them. CRS also says Circle, the issuer of the USDC stablecoin, pays part of its reserve interest to the exchange Coinbase. CRS also says the issuer is prohibited from paying interest when it deals directly with a customer. CRS says the restriction would presumably apply to self-custody (a person holding coins without a company), and that the word 'holder' is undefined. Coinbase attributes part of its USDC balance growth to its rewards program. AAF says issuers can effectively circumvent the ban through exchanges or third parties. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. AAF is the American Action Forum, a policy research group. Sources: [16], [17], [18].

arguments.title: The bill supports U.S. capacity to develop and govern strategic payment technology at home.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 8 The bill supports U.S. capacity to develop and govern strategic payment technology at home.

  • Because A clear domestic framework supports development: “These measures lay out a missing legal framework for stablecoins” [19]; “These are reasonable guardrails that should encourage continued growth in this space.” [19]
  • Because Losing expertise abroad threatens that capacity: “Industry brain drain is a real risk to our leadership in technology and financial services” [19].
  • Because Payment technology affects state power: “As financial systems determine geopolitical leverage, sanctions enforcement, data sovereignty, and the global role of the U.S. dollar, competitiveness in this area is essential.” [20]
  • So A workable U.S. route for firms and expertise strengthens the country's capacity to build and oversee technology central to its financial power. That supports a state able to defend its citizens.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.

It also cancelled its rule that banks first needed a supervisor's nonobjection (approval). The bill also has a route for foreign issuers. arguments.title: The bill strengthens dollar-based payments against rival systems designed to escape U.S. financial controls.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 9 The bill strengthens dollar-based payments against rival systems designed to escape U.S. financial controls.

  • Because The bill supports wider use of digital dollars. See C01.
  • Because Rivals are building alternatives: “U.S. competitors are pushing alternative payment systems that are designed to weaken the dollar’s influence and U.S. centrality within the international financial system.” [23]
  • Because That shift affects the state's ability to apply financial pressure: “Russia, the BRICS bloc, and sanctioned states like Iran and Venezuela are also exploring digital assets to skirt U.S. financial controls.” [23] BRICS is a group of large emerging economies.
  • So Expanding regulated dollar payments helps keep international finance within U.S. reach. Preserving that influence strengthens the state's ability to use financial restrictions against security threats.
arguments.con_html:
Response More dollar-denominated payments do not by themselves put the channels carrying those payments within U.S. enforcement reach.

  • Because Dollar use and avoidance of U.S. controls already coexisted. The argument's source reports “98 percent of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar” [23] and explains that “Stablecoins can bypass traditional financial monitoring points via peer-to-peer or decentralized finance transactions” [23]. These are direct transfers or transactions through software rather than a conventional financial firm.
  • Because That enforcement problem includes finding funds, not just ordering a freeze. Before the bill, the Justice Department alleged that Garantex changed wallet addresses daily “to make it difficult for U.S.-based cryptocurrency exchanges to identify and block transactions with Garantex accounts.” [24]
  • Because The bill's section 3 restrictions on issuance and sales exclude “any transaction by means of a software or hardware wallet that facilitates an individual's own custody of digital assets.” [4] The bill's separate freezing powers still depend on locating the funds to be frozen.
  • So The argument has not shown that growth in regulated dollar tokens replaces rival payment channels with transactions the United States can newly detect and stop. Currency choice alone does not establish that added sanctions power.

arguments.title: The bill supports demand that lowers the government’s short-term borrowing costs.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 10 The bill supports demand that lowers the government’s short-term borrowing costs.

  • Because The bill is expected to increase stablecoin use. See C01. The bill allows “short-dated Treasury bills” [25] among required reserves.
  • Because That growth creates a source of demand for government debt: “The widespread adoption of well-regulated dollar-backed stablecoins would also drive increased demand for U.S. debt” [26].
  • Because A study published by the Bank for International Settlements finds: “Inflows into stablecoins reduce three-month US Treasury bill yields” [27]. Yields are the interest rates on this government debt.
  • So Supporting this demand helps the state borrow at lower short-term rates. Money saved on interest is available to defend citizens and meet national emergencies, giving [NAME] a security-based reason to favor the framework.
arguments.con_html:
Response The price study does not establish that this bill creates additional public resources for defense and emergencies.

  • Because Reserve purchases are not the same as extra demand across all buyers. Analysis explains that “other forms of payments media, such as cash, demand deposits, and MMMFs may shrink, reducing the demand for Treasury bills.” [5] These are cash, bank balances, and money market mutual funds that already support Treasury demand.
  • Because Lower borrowing rates are also not the same as more public money. Replacing currency shifts earnings to private issuers: “For stablecoins, the issuers get the seigniorage, whereas for currency, the seigniorage accrues to the U.S. Treasury.” [5] Seigniorage is the income from issuing money and investing its backing. The analysis concludes that “the net impact on debt service costs is likely to be negligible” [5].
  • So The argument has not established extra federal resources after counting the shift in demand and in public earnings. A measured fall in short-term yields does not fill that gap in its security-funding claim.

The analysis concludes that “the net impact on debt service costs is likely to be negligible” [5].
