arguments.title: The added debt puts more pressure on funding for defense and emergencies.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The added debt puts more pressure on funding for defense and emergencies.

  • Because The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates the bill would add about $80.6 billion to deficits over 2026–2035; its table reports “80,582” in millions of dollars [2]. A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue. Deficits mean more federal borrowing.
  • Because More debt makes the government more exposed to interest costs. Debt-service costs are payments on debt: “the larger debt is, the more an increase in interest rates raises debt-service costs.” [24]
  • Because CBO connects debt to limits on national protection: “Lawmakers might feel constrained from using federal tax and spending policies to respond to unforeseen events or for other purposes, such as to promote economic activity or strengthen national defense.” [24]
  • Because CBO also warns of harm to the U.S. role abroad if lawmakers become “reluctant to increase spending to prepare for or respond to an international crisis” [24].
  • So The bill adds debt and interest demands that put defense and crisis response under greater budget pressure. Preserving the state's ability to prepare for threats and defend citizens gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added pressure.

original.title: The added borrowing increases exposure to a financial crisis that would threaten national stability.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 The added borrowing increases exposure to a financial crisis that would threaten national stability.

  • Because An August 2025 budget update from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget included the July budget law and new tariffs. It projected debt growing faster than national output: “Debt held by the public will rise from about 100 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ($30 trillion) today to 120 percent of GDP ($53 trillion) by 2035.” [25]
  • Because CBO explains the risk of that path: “The likelihood of a fiscal crisis would increase if federal debt continued to grow faster than GDP, because mounting debt could erode investors’ confidence in the U.S. government’s fiscal position.” [24]
  • Because A loss of confidence would raise interest rates and lower the value of existing government bonds. CBO says losses to banks and other investors “could be large enough to cause some financial institutions to fail.” [24]
  • Because The damage could spread as banks lend less: “such a crisis could spread globally as liquidity declined and financial institutions reduced their lending, leading to an economic contraction.” [24]
  • So The bill adds to the debt burden behind this crisis risk. Protecting the country against financial breakdown and economic disruption gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added exposure.

arguments.title: The added debt threatens financial tools the United States uses to protect its interests.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The added debt threatens financial tools the United States uses to protect its interests.

  • Because The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates the bill would add about $80.6 billion to deficits over 2026–2035; its table reports “80,582” in millions of dollars [2]. A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue. Deficits mean more federal borrowing.
  • Because Growing debt creates risks beyond a sudden crisis. Treasury securities are US government bonds. CBO identifies “a gradual decline in the value of Treasury securities and other domestic assets, heightened expectations of inflation, and a loss of confidence in the U.S. dollar as the dominant international reserve currency.” [24] This includes the dollar's role as the main currency other countries hold in reserve.
  • Because CBO explains the funding consequence: “Such developments would make it more difficult to finance public and private activity.” [24]
  • Because The national security strategy calls U.S. financial markets “pillars of American influence that afford policymakers significant leverage and tools to advance America’s national security priorities.” [27]
  • So Adding debt adds risks to stable funding and financial influence that support U.S. security. [NAME]'s concern for a strong, secure country gives a reason to oppose those risks.

arguments.title: The larger subsidies put more public money within reach of organized fraud.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 The larger subsidies put more public money within reach of organized fraud.

  • Because The enhanced credits expand fully paid coverage for eligible low-income households: “The reduction in applicable percentages allows households with incomes between 100% and 150% of FPL to receive full subsidies, reducing consumers' premium contributions to zero dollars.” [28] FPL means the federal poverty level.
  • Because CMS, the agency running the federal Marketplace, links this feature to abuse: “the widespread availability of $0 premium plans created the incentive and opportunity for fraudulent and improper enrollments at scale” [29].
  • Because Gaps in checks of people's income remained in the rules for 2026. CMS explained that a planned check was paused: “Income DMIs will not be opened for applicants when the Marketplace attempts to verify an applicant’s attested projected annual household income with the IRS, but the IRS returns no tax data.” [30] A DMI (data matching issue) asks a person for more information when records do not match. The IRS is the US tax agency. That means missing tax records would not trigger this extra income check.
  • Because A November 2025 conviction shows an actual loss from organized enrollment fraud. The Justice Department reported a scheme seeking “over $233 million in fraudulent ACA plan subsidies for which the federal government paid at least $180 million.” [31] ACA means the Affordable Care Act.
  • So Restoring larger subsidies expands the money and incentives exposed to a proven fraud mechanism. A strong state must keep public resources from financing crime. [NAME] therefore has a reason to oppose this added exposure.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument carries an older fraud warning into 2026 without separating larger credits from a monthly signup route that had ended.

  • Because The agency running the federal insurance Marketplace (CMS) links abuse to repeated signups: “By fully subsidizing the premium for these plans, individuals could be enrolled into these plans once every month through a special enrollment period (SEP) by predatory agents and brokers without the individual's knowledge.” [29]
  • Because Before the vote, CMS listed “Removal of Monthly Special Enrollment Period (SEP)” [30] among the rules already in force. This was the signup route for people with income at or below 150 percent of the federal poverty level.
  • Because The 2025 law also bars tax credits for special signups based on income alone from 2026. Congress's research service describes the bar. The HHS Secretary leads the US health department. The bar covers “an SEP on the basis of expected household income” [32] that is “not connected to a change in circumstances specified by the HHS Secretary.” [32] It “applies to plan years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [32] HHS is the federal health department.
  • Because H.R.1834 extends the credit rules. Its credit changes concern “Extension of Rules To Increase Premium Assistance Amounts” [1] and “Extension of Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [1].
  • So Extending the credit amounts does not reopen that route. A past theft and larger lawful payments do not establish extra money reaching criminals under those rules. This response does not answer the argument’s point that an income check was paused for 2026.

arguments.title: Expanding fully paid plans makes unauthorized enrollment harder to notice and exposes citizens to disrupted care.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 Expanding fully paid plans makes unauthorized enrollment harder to notice and exposes citizens to disrupted care.

  • Because CMS, the agency running the federal Marketplace, explains how fully paid plans hide unauthorized signups: “Because these enrollees do not receive a monthly premium bill requiring action on their part, they may not be aware they are enrolled.” [29]
  • Because A planned $5 charge on automatic renewal had been paused before the January vote. CMS stated: “Qualifying consumers will continue to be automatically re-enrolled with no premium responsibility following application of Advance Payments of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC).” [30]
  • Because The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's audit agency, reported how many unauthorized signups and switches were reported: CMS received “approximately 275,000 complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35]
  • Because GAO explains that these practices can cause “loss of access to medical providers and medications” [35]. The November 2025 conviction also established harm (Medicaid is public insurance for people with low incomes): “some of these consumers experienced serious disruptions in their medical care and often lost their prior insurance coverage under Medicaid or other programs.” [31]
  • So By expanding plans that hide unauthorized enrollment, the bill increases exposure to organized abuse that can interrupt care. Protecting citizens from that threat through a reliable national insurance system gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.con_html:
Response The complaint history does not establish added hidden enrollment or disrupted care from this extension under the consent controls already in place.

  • Because CMS changed controls for existing coverage on the federal Marketplace (FFM): “Beginning July 19, 2024, CMS began blocking agents and brokers from making changes to a consumer’s FFM enrollment unless the agent or broker is already associated with the consumer’s enrollment.” [36]
  • Because CMS provides a way for a new broker to act with the consumer's involvement: “the consumer must conduct a three-way call with the Marketplace Call Center” [36].
  • Because Congress's audit agency, GAO, combines “complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35] That period includes months before these controls began.
  • So The control acts before an unassociated broker can switch existing coverage. It does not depend on a premium bill exposing the switch afterward. The complaint total mixes initial enrollments and switches across different safeguards. It does not establish added harmful switches from this extension under the rules in force on January 8. This response concerns switches of existing coverage. It does not address new unauthorized enrollments.

  • Because A planned $5 charge on automatic renewal had been paused before the January vote. CMS stated: “Qualifying consumers will continue to be automatically re-enrolled with no premium responsibility following application of Advance Payments of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC).” [30]
  • Because GAO documented the scale of reported unauthorized signups and switches: CMS received “approximately 275,000 complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35]
  • Because GAO explains that these practices can cause “loss of access to medical providers and medications” [35]. The November 2025 conviction also established harm: “some of these consumers experienced serious disruptions in their medical care and often lost their prior insurance coverage under Medicaid or other programs.” [31]
  • So By expanding plans that hide unauthorized enrollment, the bill increases exposure to organized abuse that can interrupt care. Protecting citizens from that threat through a reliable national insurance system gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.con_html:
Response The complaint history does not establish added hidden enrollment or disrupted care from this extension under the consent controls already in place.

  • Because CMS changed controls for existing coverage on the federal Marketplace: “Beginning July 19, 2024, CMS began blocking agents and brokers from making changes to a consumer’s FFM enrollment unless the agent or broker is already associated with the consumer’s enrollment.” [36]
  • Because CMS provides a way for a new broker to act with the consumer's involvement: “the consumer must conduct a three-way call with the Marketplace Call Center” [36].
  • Because Congress's audit agency, GAO, combines “complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35] That period includes months before these controls began.
  • So The control acts before an unassociated broker can switch existing coverage; it does not depend on a premium bill exposing the switch afterward. The complaint total mixes initial enrollments and switches across different safeguards. It does not establish added harmful switches from this extension under the rules in force on January 8. This response concerns switches of existing coverage; it does not address new unauthorized enrollments.
original.notes_html:
Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

Evidence note: KFF analysis finds that almost all (98%) adults who qualified for a free silver plan with enhanced credits would still qualify for a free bronze plan without them. CMS estimates that about 200,000 consumers had a desired plan changed without consent in 2025, after the July 2024 control. CMS says it worked with issuers to restore those selections. Sources: [33], [34].

arguments.title: The bill reduces a loss of insurance help that marriage can trigger at the income cutoff.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill reduces a loss of insurance help that marriage can trigger at the income cutoff.

  • Because The income cutoff can penalize two people who qualify separately but cross the married cutoff when their incomes combine. The Heritage Foundation explains that “the FPL for a couple is less than twice that for a single person” [12]. FPL means the poverty line used to set the cutoff.
  • Because The bill extends the “Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [2].
  • So For otherwise eligible couples whose insurance costs qualify for help above that limit, marrying no longer causes all aid to disappear merely because their combined income crosses it.
  • Because The comparison must also count what the couple would receive unmarried. Consider two childless adults, each with $46,950 in annual income counted for the credit: 300% of the “$15,650” [13] one-person amount. Married, their $93,900 is 443% of the “$21,150” [13] two-person amount, above the cutoff. Assume their plans stay the same, with benchmark premiums (the prices used to set the credit) totaling $20,000 a year. Under ordinary 2026 credits, the table reads “At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” [14], so they pay about $9,352 unmarried and the full $20,000 married: a $10,648 cost of marrying. Under the restored schedule, “300 | 0.0600” [15] means about $5,634 unmarried, and “400 or more | 0.0850” [15] means about $7,982 married: a $2,348 cost. For this couple the bill lowers the cost of marrying by about $8,300.
  • Because Evangelical teaching opposes “creating economic disincentives to marriage.” [4]
  • So Reducing this financial obstacle for such couples supports the traditional practice of marriage.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that premium credits can produce both marriage penalties and bonuses. Under the bill, the cost of marrying falls for some couples crossing the income cutoff (one supporting argument's example: about $8,300 lower) and rises for some couples below it (one opposing argument's example: about $1,729 higher). Both examples rest on stated assumptions. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. Sources: [16], [14], [15].

arguments.title: The bill supports church giving and paid ministry, helping congregations continue worship and teaching.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 The bill supports church giving and paid ministry, helping congregations continue worship and teaching.

  • Because Small churches use ACA coverage for staff: “Among the most affected are small congregations that usually can’t afford group plans and instead provide salary stipends to staff members for use in the ACA Marketplace” [19]. ACA means the Affordable Care Act.
  • Because A Christian fund that helps clergy (religious leaders) said its planned emergency aid depended on the larger credits: “If Congress renews the subsidies at the 2025 levels, the program will not move forward.” [20]
  • So Restoring those credits eases the strain on pastoral families and churches that help pay their insurance costs.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession, a statement of belief, makes regular giving a religious duty: “According to the Scriptures, Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.” [3]
  • Because Higher insurance bills also leave less money for giving. Tithing means giving part of one's income to a church. A pastor reported: “Riverside Church is projecting 20% attendance growth but flat giving for 2026 as more dollars go to health insurance instead of tithing” [19].
  • So Lower bills leave members more room to continue customary giving and support their congregation.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession says Sunday observance should include “exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.” [3]
  • So Easing these pressures on church budgets helps sustain the clergy, worship, and teaching through which congregations practice and pass on their faith.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: The clergy relief fund's program is a one-time $2,500 stipend for up to 1,000 clergy. The Riverside Church figure is one congregation's forecast of 20% attendance growth with flat giving for 2026. Sources: [20], [19].

arguments.title: The bill increases the financial pressure to accept a personal payment for abortion coverage.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill increases the financial pressure to accept a personal payment for abortion coverage.

  • Because Plans covering abortions beyond the federal exceptions for rape, incest or danger to life must collect an abortion-coverage payment of “at least $1 per enrollee per month” [28] and keep these payments apart: “deposit these separate payments into segregated accounts” [28].
  • Because Where state law requires Marketplace plans to cover abortion, buying one includes that payment. KFF, a health research group, describes the mandate as covering “individual plans (including Marketplace plans)” [25].
  • Because Christian health-sharing ministries state the religious concern as getting care “without being forced to fund procedures or drugs that violate their conscience.” [29]
  • So Where every Marketplace option includes this charge, refusing it means giving up Marketplace aid. The bill increases the aid a believer must give up. Preserving the practice of refusing payments that violate religious teaching gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that pressure.

Response A state coverage mandate alone does not establish that an objecting buyer has no subsidized plan without elective abortion coverage.

  • Because Washington law says, “No individual or organization with a religious or moral tenet opposed to a specific service may be required to purchase coverage for that service or services if they object to doing so for reason of conscience or religion.” [30]
  • Because A 2023 survey of Marketplace plans identifies an actual exception: “Oregon, one of the states requiring that abortion be covered, has granted an exemption to plans sponsored by religious health systems.” [31]

arguments.title: The bill increases the financial cost of marriage for some couples buying Marketplace insurance.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 9 The bill increases the financial cost of marriage for some couples buying Marketplace insurance.

  • Because Marriage combines the couple’s incomes for the credit. A joint return is one tax form for both spouses. The law requires that “the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year.” [44]
  • Because For 2026 coverage in the 48 contiguous states, the poverty-line amounts used for credits are “$15,650” [13] for one person and “$21,150” [13] for two. Two married adults therefore face a lower poverty-line amount than two separate one-person tax households.
  • Because The ordinary 2026 premium-share table reads: “At least 250% but less than 300% 8.44% 9.96% At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” [14]. Thus the share is 8.44% at 250% of poverty and 9.96% at 369%.
  • Because The bill restores the enhanced schedule. Its table from the US tax agency (IRS) gives “250 | 0.0400” [15] and “369 | 0.0773” [15]: shares of 4% and 7.73%. To find the income percentage, IRS instructions say to “drop any numbers after the decimal point.” [15]
  • So Consider two childless adults, each with $39,125 in annual income counted for the credit. Compare being unmarried throughout 2026 with being married throughout 2026. They are otherwise eligible all year. Assume their plans and full premiums stay the same, with premiums high enough to receive credits. Separately, each is at 250% of poverty; married, their $78,250 is counted at 369%. Under ordinary 2026 credits, their combined annual premium share rises from about $6,604 to $7,794 when married—a $1,190 cost. Under the restored schedule, it rises from $3,130 to about $6,049—a $2,919 cost. The bill adds about $1,729 to this couple’s annual cost of being married rather than unmarried.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession calls marriage “the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime” [45] and “the framework for intimate companionship, the channel of sexual expression according to biblical standards” [45].
  • So Maintaining this marriage tradition gives [NAME] a reason to oppose increasing the money such couples lose by marrying.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that premium credits can produce both marriage penalties and bonuses. Under the bill, the cost of marrying falls for some couples crossing the income cutoff (one supporting argument's example: about $8,300 lower) and rises for some couples below it (one opposing argument's example: about $1,729 higher). Both examples rest on stated assumptions. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. Sources: [16], [14], [15].

arguments.title: The bill protects female athletes’ access to team projects that remove pollution and reduce waste.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill protects female athletes’ access to team projects that remove pollution and reduce waste.

  • Because The bill allows males to practice with a female team only if “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1]. A roster spot is a place on a team.
  • Because Being on a team can give people an organized way to remove pollution. Fordham University rower Caitlin Boyle reported: “In the cleanup, 50 of my teammates on Fordham Rowing assisted me with picking up trash along the shores and streets of City Island in bags and then disposing of the waste properly.” [4]
  • Because These projects can also teach people. Boyle wrote: “Additionally, I held a presentation for the team educating them on basic environmental knowledge and the importance of proper waste management.” [4]
  • Because Teammates can help start larger efforts. University of Wisconsin rower Grace Latz said: “I started all of this because my teammates were taking similar classes to me and shared the same values, so it made it easier.” [5]
  • Because The recycling group Latz helped start, called REthink, later reached other parts of the university: “Since then, REthink has expanded beyond the UW athletic department to work with the UW campus, the hospital, the Wisconsin unions, dining services and UW housing.” [5]
  • So Protecting female athletes’ places on teams that do this work also protects their access to cleanups, environmental teaching and larger recycling projects. [NAME] wants to defend nature, and keeping these ways of doing so gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Boyle organized her City Island cleanup in partnership with the New York Department of Sanitation. REthink grew to about 60 members and worked with campus units beyond athletics. Sources: [4], [5].

arguments.title: The bill protects female rowers’ time on the water, where seeing environmental harm can lead to care and action.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill protects female rowers’ time on the water, where seeing environmental harm can lead to care and action.

  • Because The bill’s condition for male practice also protects a female athlete’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • Because Rowing, a sport of racing boats with oars, lets athletes see the waters they use. University of Wisconsin rower Alexandra Bogner said: “I’ve rowed on both Lake Mendota and Lake Monona and have been able to see the ecological challenges that they face” [7].

  • So Protecting female rowers from losing practice time keeps open a path from seeing pollution to removing litter and studying ways to reduce waste. That serves [NAME]’s wish to care for nature and protect it from pollution.

arguments.title: The bill protects female athletes’ access to scholarship money that supports environmental study.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill protects female athletes’ access to scholarship money that supports environmental study.

  • Because The bill allows males to train or practice with a female team only if no female loses a “scholarship” [1]. A scholarship is money that helps pay for college.
  • Because Money for athletes can support students doing environmental work. The University of Notre Dame described rower Anna Kottkamp as “an environmental science major” [8] who “went on to earn a full athletic scholarship.” [8]
  • Because Kottkamp was “an undergraduate research assistant for Jennifer Tank” [8], studying “the impact of cover crops on agricultural streams.” [8] Cover crops are plants grown between main farm crops.
  • Because Tank’s research tests ways to protect water from pollution: “Her research combines the wide-scale planting of cover crops in winter with innovative drainage strategies that can reduce fertilizer runoff to streams and rivers.” [9]
  • So Protecting athletic scholarships for female students doing this work protects money for learning how to prevent water pollution. Supporting that way to protect nature gives [NAME] a further reason to favor the bill.

  • Because Women’s school teams compete in natural places. At a cleanup of the Malden River with the Tufts University women’s rowing team, an athletics coordinator explained that “our rowing athletes train and compete on it almost every day.” [12]
  • Because On January 14, 2025, rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, could allow transgender women onto women’s teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2] Transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women.
  • Because Outdoor activities can strengthen concern for the environment. A study followed teenagers at a 15-day outdoor camp. Affective beliefs are feelings about the environment.   • Because College sailing gives a real example. Harvard University describes one sailor’s wish to protect the environment: “It's that time in the water with her teammates that has driven Hogan-Lopez to learn more about the environment and how to protect it.” [14]
  • So The ban would remove women’s outdoor competition from the choices open to transgender students who were otherwise eligible. It would end competition’s time in nature and shared experiences as a way for them to build that care.
  • Note The exception that lets students “train or practice” [1] does not give back access to competition.
  • So [NAME]’s concern for nature gives [NAME] a reason to keep this way of developing care for it, and therefore to oppose the bill.

arguments.title: The bill restricts positions leading environmental work inside women’s teams.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill restricts positions leading environmental work inside women’s teams.

  • Because Yale University places environmental leaders inside individual teams: “each participating varsity and club team has a sustainability captain. That person leads the efforts within their team and tailors the certification program to the schedule and structure of their team.” [16] A varsity team is a school’s top team.
  • Because These positions include a “sustainability captain of the varsity women’s swimming and diving team” [16]. That captain described practical care for nature: “We volunteered together at a New Haven Land Trust garden last year and performed manual labor to prepare for spring planting.” [16]
  • Because On January 14, 2025, rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, could allow transgender women onto such teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2]
  • Because Team service also removes pollution and leads people to sign up for more conservation work. At the Tufts University cleanup, “Participants collected 33 bags of trash, which included 16 bags of sorted single use plastic bottles (over 1500 bottles)!” [17] and “many students signed up to continue to be involved with the Friends of the Malden River.” [17]
  • So A position leading a women’s team’s environmental work is an opportunity tied to being on that team. It is also a way to bring teammates into practical care for nature.
  • Because The bill expressly covers “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.
  • Note The bill's exception lets students “train or practice” [1]. It does not protect a separate environmental leadership position inside a women’s program.
  • So The bill would restrict access to these positions for otherwise eligible students it excludes from women’s programs. That ends a way for those students to organize practical care for nature.
  • So [NAME] values taking part in defending nature. Keeping these chances to lead environmental work open gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose the bill.

arguments.title: The bill protects women’s fair chance to earn sports wins and recognition.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill protects women’s fair chance to earn sports wins and recognition.

  • Because Male puberty builds strength. Testosterone is a hormone, and a review of research explains that “increases in testosterone due to puberty promote muscular strength” [5].
  • Because The review looked at 24 studies of transgender women who were not athletes. Here, transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women. After 12 to 36 months of hormone treatment, the review said: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5] Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.
  • Because Strength matters in speed and power events: “In sports demanding speed and power, muscular strength and the ability to generate high rates of force are recognised as key determinant in athletic success.” [5]
  • So In events that depend on strength, the bill would keep strength advantages retained from male puberty out of the female category. Giving women a real chance to earn sports rewards serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunity and just treatment.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence does not settle whether transgender women who train and compete keep the speed and power advantage this fairness argument needs.

  • Because The review says the effects on people who train are not known. GAHT means hormone treatment that matches gender identity: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [5]
  • Because The review does not say whether the compared groups trained the same amount: “The levels of physical activity of the transwomen compared with cisgender women in the studies were not reported.” [5]
  • Because A 2024 study measured athletes at one point in time and found mixed results. Compared with cisgender women athletes, transgender women athletes had “higher absolute handgrip strength” [6] but “lower relative jump height” [6]. Relative jump height takes body weight into account.
  • So Strength kept by people who are not athletes does not show an advantage among trained athletes in a speed or power event. The one athlete study points in both directions. Its authors write: “Sports-specific studies are necessary to inform policy-making.” [6] This response does not show that no advantage exists. It also does not address places without hormone limits.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. CRS reports that some states and school districts allowed participation with no particular requirements or restrictions. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. NCAA is the main college sports organization. Sources: [4], [7].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. The statistical ranges for those comparisons include zero (no difference), and certainty is rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are averages for body composition and fitness. The text in this project's evidence collection reports no result by sport for absolute mass, speed, collisions or injuries. Only the abstract and correction notice are in this collection, so the review's full methods were not verified. The review came after the comparison date but before the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

arguments.title: The bill protects girls’ places in sports and their chances to gain education, health and leadership benefits.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill protects girls’ places in sports and their chances to gain education, health and leadership benefits.

  • Because Former college swimmer Paula Scanlan told a House committee that places were actually lost: “I know women who have lost roster spots and spots on the podium.” [10] A roster spot is a place on a team. A podium spot is a top finish in a race.
  • Because The bill allows male training or practice only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where places or sports money are limited, the competition ban and the practice condition protect female athletes from losing them to male participants. For a girl who needs sports money to attend college, protecting that money keeps open a way into education.
  • Because Girls in positive sports programs report better mental health. A 2024 study found: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because A 2024 survey of U.S. adults who had played girls’ or women’s sports found reported gains in leadership skills: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So Keeping a girl’s place in a good program keeps her chance to gain these benefits. Protecting these ways into education, well-being and adult leadership serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities in life.
arguments.con_html:
Response Protecting a place does not by itself show that opportunity has become more equal. This reason depends on the fairness claim in Point 1.

  • Because The bill’s practice exception requires that “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where a place is limited, the bill decides which student holds it. That shows who keeps the benefit. It does not show that this division of places is fairer.
  • Because The mental-health finding is about access to a good program: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because The leadership finding is about benefits people connect to playing: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So These benefits go to whoever holds the place. They do not answer who has a fair claim to it. This reason adds to [NAME]’s equal-opportunity concern only as far as the fairness claim in Point 1 holds. This response does not dispute that some female athletes would keep places and their benefits under the bill.

paths.necessity_reason: The education and health-benefit route does not require a retained physiological advantage. The local response can challenge its equal-opportunity interpretation without automatically blocking that separate benefit.

arguments.title: The bill protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and from games lost over safety concerns.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and from games lost over safety concerns.

  • Because World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, links risk in that sport to “the size, force- and power-producing advantages conferred by testosterone during puberty and adolescence, and the resultant player welfare risks this creates” [13].
  • Because World Rugby's review explains the danger to a smaller player: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.” [13]
  • Because World Rugby’s review of 12 months of lowering testosterone, a hormone, concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.” [13]
  • So In school contact competition such as rugby, excluding male competitors who have gone through male puberty removes this source of size and force mismatch. That protects athletes who are less able to withstand those forces.
  • Because Safety concerns have also cost whole teams games. After Payton McNabb was injured playing volleyball in 2022, her school board voted “to forfeit the remaining varsity and junior varsity volleyball games against Highlands School” [14], which the report describes as “attended by the transgender player.” [14] To forfeit means to give up a game. The report says: “The board cited safety concerns for players.” [14] That player’s status is not confirmed: “It is not possible to verify this athlete was trans.” [15]
  • So Where covered competition would otherwise include male competitors, the bill also removes that reason for a school to pull out its girls’ team. Protecting athletes from added collision risks and removing that ground for giving up games serves [NAME]’s concern for the weak and vulnerable, including girls [NAME] does not know.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: World Rugby's October 2020 summary states that there were no direct studies on trans women rugby players. Its collision estimate models typical male mass against typical female mass. The review cited by the argument says hormone-naive transgender women (those who have not taken hormone treatment) may not on average have the same athletic attributes as cisgender men. Sources: [16], [13], [5].

Evidence note: The McNabb injury occurred on September 1, 2022. North Carolina's state ban took effect August 16, 2023 and applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [14], [17].

Evidence note: Snopes, a fact-checking website, states in March 2025 that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender. It also states that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. Snopes also reports three more things. The school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence. The board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players, while several coaches spoke for continuing. North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, and their sports are unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [15], [2], [18].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. The statistical ranges for those comparisons include zero (no difference), and certainty is rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are averages for body composition and fitness. The text in this project's evidence collection reports no result by sport for absolute mass, speed, collisions or injuries. Only the abstract and correction notice are in this collection, so the review's full methods were not verified. The review came after the comparison date but before the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

original.title: It protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and the lost games that safety concerns can cause.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and the lost games that safety concerns can cause.

  • Because World Rugby links contact-sport risk to “the size, force- and power-producing advantages conferred by testosterone during puberty and adolescence, and the resultant player welfare risks this creates” [13].
  • Because Its review explains the danger to a smaller player: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.” [13]
  • Because World Rugby's review of 12 months of testosterone suppression concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.” [13]
  • So In school contact competition such as rugby, excluding male competitors who have gone through male puberty removes this source of size and force mismatch. That protects athletes who are less able to withstand those forces.
  • Because Safety concerns have also cost whole teams games. After Payton McNabb's 2022 volleyball injury, her school board voted “to forfeit the remaining varsity and junior varsity volleyball games against Highlands School” [14], which the report describes as “attended by the transgender player.” [14] The report states: “The board cited safety concerns for players.” [14] That player's status is unconfirmed: “It is not possible to verify this athlete was trans.” [15]
  • So Where covered competition would otherwise include male competitors, the bill also removes that reason for a school to withdraw its girls' team. Protecting athletes from added collision risks and removing that ground for forfeits serves [NAME]'s concern for the weak and vulnerable, including girls [NAME] does not know.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: World Rugby's October 2020 summary states that there were no direct studies on trans women rugby players. Its collision estimate models typical male mass against typical female mass. The review cited by the PRO says hormone-naive transgender women may not on average have the same athletic attributes as cisgender men. Sources: [16], [13], [5].

Evidence note: The McNabb injury occurred on September 1, 2022. North Carolina's state ban took effect August 16, 2023 and applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [14], [17].

Evidence note: Snopes (March 2025) states that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender, and that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. It reports that the school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence, that the board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players while several coaches spoke for continuing, and that North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, with their sports unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [15], [2], [18].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

arguments.title: The bill takes away a route to learning and educational opportunities that other students keep.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill takes away a route to learning and educational opportunities that other students keep.

  • Because Sports teach useful skills: “Sports provide meaningful opportunities for kids to feel confident in themselves and learn valuable life lessons about teamwork, leadership, and communication.” [2]
  • Because Being on a team also brings educational chances. The bill itself names “scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • Because The ban reaches beyond games to “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.
  • Because The same birth-based rule also restricts nonbinary students it classifies as male. Nonbinary students do not identify only as girls or boys. The Congressional Equality Caucus, a group of members of Congress, explains: “It would also limit the ability of non-binary and intersex students to participate in these programs as well.” [20]
  • Because Girls born with variations in sex traits, called intersex variations, also face uncertain eligibility. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [2]. They describe the result: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [2]
  • So Blocking team competition and the activities tied to it takes away chances to learn and advance. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities includes transgender, nonbinary and intersex students, which gives a reason to oppose these barriers.
  • Note Permission for “males to train or practice” [1] gives back neither eligibility to compete nor equal access to team places and benefits. Even practice is conditional: it is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1], among other protected opportunities.
arguments.con_html:
Response For students who have gone through male puberty, listing the benefits of a lost team place does not show that the eligibility rule denies equal opportunity.

  • Because Fair opportunity can require limits on who enters a sports category. In the Clark case, a court upheld keeping boys off a girls’ volleyball team because “due to average physiological differences, males would displace females to a substantial extent if they were allowed to compete for positions on the volleyball team.” [21] The reason was a real difference affecting fair competition, not just that separate teams exist.
  • Because Having been eligible under a testosterone limit does not show equal competitive conditions. Reviewing physical traits after male puberty, researchers Hilton and Lundberg reported that “the muscular advantage enjoyed by transgender women is only minimally reduced when testosterone is suppressed.” [22]
  • So Equal opportunity requires a fair basis for eligibility, not keeping every existing route to scholarships, learning or admission. For these students, the argument must show why this boundary unfairly blocks comparable students. Naming benefits and affected identities does not supply that step.
  • Note This response depends on the disputed claim that an advantage remains. A 2026 review reports: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” [8]
  • So This response does not reach students who have not gone through male puberty, sports where no advantage has been shown, or eligible girls deterred by uncertainty about intersex variations.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. CRS reports that some states and school districts allowed participation with no particular requirements or restrictions. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. NCAA is the main college sports organization. Sources: [4], [7].

arguments.title: The bill replaces individual protection against unfair treatment with automatic exclusion.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill replaces individual protection against unfair treatment with automatic exclusion.

  • Because The rule does not change by age or sport. One House member said: “this bill is a blanket ban that treats every age student in every sport the same.” [2]
  • Because On January 14, 2025, the law of the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, protected one individual girl’s participation in the states that court covers. Across the country, “Courts have reached different conclusions” [7]. In its April 2024 B.P.J. decision, that court noted that puberty-blocking treatment meant “B.P.J. has never experienced elevated levels of circulating testosterone.” [23] Testosterone is a hormone.
  • Because The court held that applying West Virginia’s ban would “treat her worse than people to whom she is similarly situated, deprive her of any meaningful athletic opportunities, and do so on the basis of sex.” [23] Similarly situated means in a comparable position.
  • So H.R.28 would make birth sex decide the question even in cases where a court had held, under the law then in force, that exclusion treated an individual girl worse than comparable students. Replacing that protection under Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, with a duty to exclude conflicts with treating everyone justly. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: The court in B.P.J.'s case found a real dispute about the facts of competitive advantage (a genuine dispute of material fact). It left her equal-protection claim for further proceedings. In September 2024 the Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court, upheld a preliminary order on equal-protection grounds in Doe v. Horne. The Supreme Court agreed to hear (granted certiorari in) B.P.J. and Hecox on July 3, 2025, after the comparison date. On June 30, 2026 the Supreme Court reversed the B.P.J. and Hecox judgments (see the note on the June 30, 2026 decision). Sources: [23], [24], [7], [25].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and sent both back to the lower courts (remanded them). It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules. It does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [26].

arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill removes support and adds stigma for students who already face serious distress and isolation.

  • Because The CDC, the federal public-health agency, did a national survey of high school students in 2023. Compared with other students, transgender students and those unsure whether they are transgender had more distress and less belonging: “Transgender and questioning students experienced a higher prevalence of violence, poor mental health, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and unstable housing, and a lower prevalence of school connectedness than their cisgender peers.” [27] Cisgender peers are students whose gender matches their sex at birth.
  • Because School sports offer health and belonging: “Sports participation is linked to increased academic achievement and fosters in students increased emotional, mental, and physical well-being and a sense of community.” [2]
  • Because Denying team membership also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights describes that exclusion as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [2] Stigma means shame or disapproval attached to a group.
  • So Taking away this source of support while adding stigma burdens students who already need protection. [NAME]’s concern for vulnerable people gives a reason to oppose that harm.

arguments.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity and bodily safety at risk.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity and bodily safety at risk.

  • Because Schools must apply the rule without a set way to check it. Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [28]
  • Because A comparable ban in Florida led to questions about a child’s private history. The Associated Press (AP) reported: “They interviewed officials at Monarch and at the daughter's middle and elementary schools, seeking to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29]
  • Because The investigation also asked teammates about her body: “When investigators interviewed the Monarch volleyball players, they said the team did not change clothes or shower together, so they were never disrobed with Norton's daughter.” [29] Disrobed means undressed.
  • Because After the investigation began, the girl left the school. AP reported: “That all ended when the investigation began and the girl left Monarch.” [29] It added: “The girl now attends school online.” [29]
  • Because Women’s rights organizations warn that checking sex may involve “forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2]. They name a further danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2].
  • So A nationwide duty to enforce birth-sex eligibility creates grounds for the same kind of intrusive questions, with risks of exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling and, as those organizations warn, abuse. Protecting children from these harms gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule.
  • Note A supporter replies: “There is no requirement for inspections” [2]. That does not answer the risk. The documented records checks and interviews already invaded privacy, and they did not need an exam requirement.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence does not establish that the bill would lead to bodily examinations or to sexual abuse resulting from them.

  • Because H.R.28 restricts participation in programs “designated for women or girls.” [1] Its text adds no requirement for bodily examinations.
  • Because AP describes questions about records and knowledge: investigators sought “to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29] That account reports no bodily examination.
  • Because Florida’s birth-sex law gives a way to decide eligibility from records: a birth certificate is accepted if its sex statement “was filed at or near the time of the student's birth.” [30]
  • So The step to bodily examinations and sexual abuse rests on an organization’s warning, not on a documented case in this evidence. This response does not answer the documented privacy harms from records checks and interviews, or the disrupted schooling that followed.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: The Florida inquiry also examined staff handling of records, and the student's mother faced discipline. NCAA policy already required annual eligibility documentation from transgender women athletes. Regulations under FERPA, a federal student-privacy law, limit officials' access to records in which they have legitimate educational interests. NCAA is the main college sports organization. Sources: [29], [19], [31].

Evidence note: Idaho's statute included a separate sex-dispute verification process, which the Ninth Circuit described as allowing gynecological exams. The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [32], [1].

original.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity, and bodily safety at risk.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity, and bodily safety at risk.

  • Because Schools must apply the rule without a set verification process. Representative Hayes notes: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [28]
  • Because A comparable Florida ban led to inquiries into a child’s private history. AP reported: “They interviewed officials at Monarch and at the daughter's middle and elementary schools, seeking to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29]
  • Because The inquiry also reached teammates’ knowledge of her body: “When investigators interviewed the Monarch volleyball players, they said the team did not change clothes or shower together, so they were never disrobed with Norton's daughter.” [29]
  • Because The inquiry was followed by the girl’s withdrawal from school. AP reported, “That all ended when the investigation began and the girl left Monarch.” [29] It added, “The girl now attends school online.” [29]
  • Because Women’s rights organizations warn that sex verification may involve “forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2]. They identify a further danger from such procedures: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2].
  • So A nationwide duty to enforce birth-sex eligibility creates grounds for the same kind of intrusive inquiries, with risks of exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling, and, as those organizations warn, abuse. Protecting children from these harms gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule.
  • Note The supporter’s reply, “There is no requirement for inspections” [2], does not answer the risk. The documented records checks and interviews already invaded privacy. An exam mandate is not needed for that harm.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s evidence does not establish that the bill would lead to bodily examinations or resulting sexual abuse.

  • Because H.R.28 restricts participation in programs “designated for women or girls.” [1] Its text adds no requirement for bodily examinations.
  • Because AP describes an inquiry into records and knowledge: investigators sought “to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29] That account reports no bodily examination.
  • Because Florida’s birth-sex law provides a records-based way to decide eligibility: a birth certificate is accepted if its sex statement “was filed at or near the time of the student's birth.” [30]
  • So The step to bodily examinations and sexual abuse rests on an organizational warning, not on a documented case in the PRO’s evidence. This response does not answer the PRO’s documented privacy harms from records checks and interviews, or the disrupted schooling that followed.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The Florida inquiry also examined staff handling of records, and the student's mother faced discipline. NCAA policy already required annual eligibility documentation from transgender women athletes. FERPA regulations limit officials' access to records in which they have legitimate educational interests. Sources: [29], [19], [31].

Evidence note: Idaho's statute included a separate sex-dispute verification process, which the Ninth Circuit described as allowing gynecological exams. The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [32], [1].

arguments.title: The bill exposes students to accusations based on appearance and to unequal burdens from enforcing the rule.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 The bill exposes students to accusations based on appearance and to unequal burdens from enforcing the rule.

  • Because Enforcing birth-sex eligibility invites suspicion of girls who do not fit stereotypes. Women’s rights organizations warn that checking practices “are especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity, other women and girls who do not conform to sexist stereotypes, and nonbinary and gender nonconforming students.” [2]
  • Because Such accusations have harmed girls who are not transgender. The same letter describes a Utah basketball player targeted for short hair and baggy clothes: “As a result, the student was subjected to harassment, bullying, and threats of violence, necessitating police protection for her and her family.” [2]
  • Because Utah’s state school board, in its own official record, confirmed harm from the public accusation, recording “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” [33]. Public accusations themselves expose children to abuse.
  • So Extending this eligibility rule nationwide exposes students to harassment for their appearance and, as those organizations warn, to unequal checking tied to race and gender stereotypes. That conflicts with treating everyone justly and protecting vulnerable children.
  • So Facing accusations, threats or humiliating checks also makes it harder to play for girls who remain eligible. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities gives a further reason to oppose this effect of enforcing the rule.

arguments.title: The bill puts educational money that serves other students at risk when schools keep inclusive teams.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 The bill puts educational money that serves other students at risk when schools keep inclusive teams.

  • Because The bill makes inclusion a new violation of Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education: “It shall be a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] to allow the participation it bars. A recipient is a school or college that receives federal money.
  • Because Existing enforcement law allows “the termination of or refusal to grant or to continue assistance under such program or activity” [36] after an “express finding on the record, after opportunity for hearing, of a failure to comply with such requirement” [36]. It also requires a finding “that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means.” [36] So money can be stopped only after a hearing, a formal finding and a failed attempt to get voluntary compliance.
  • Because That money supports education beyond the individual athlete. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), Congress’s research office, explains: “The Department of Education (ED) distributes substantial funding to elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions” [7].
  • So Schools that keep including these students would put money for the affected program at risk, which could also harm other students. [NAME]’s concern for students’ equal opportunities gives a reason to oppose making inclusion grounds for withdrawing that support.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: Section 1682, the law on enforcing Title IX, requires a hearing, an express finding and a failed attempt at voluntary compliance, and limits termination to the particular program. In 2025 a court blocked (restrained) a USDA freeze of Maine funds on procedural grounds, and the parties settled. Maine and California refused to change their policies, and the Justice Department (DOJ) sued. USDA is the US Department of Agriculture. Sources: [36], [7].

arguments.title: The bill removes a barrier to playing for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes the bill defines as male.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes a barrier to playing for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes the bill defines as male.

  • Because This kind of objection has led a team to give up a game: “A Vermont Christian high school forfeited a girls basketball game because the opposing team had a transgender player, the head of school said.” [4] To forfeit means to give up a game.
  • Because The school’s court complaint explains the religious basis of its objection: “sex is immutable.” [5] Immutable means it cannot change. The complaint says that playing that game would affirm the opposite, “in violation of its beliefs.” [5]
  • So In covered girls’ competitions, the bill removes the matchup that causes this objection. Girls with that belief can compete without giving it up.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement includes accepting girls whose religious or other beliefs differ from [NAME]’s. Keeping a way for them to play puts that acceptance into practice.
  • So [NAME] has a reason grounded in tolerance to favor removing this cost of disagreement.
  • Note There is also room to cooperate across the competition rule. The bill allows “males to train or practice with an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1] if no female loses a place, opportunity, scholarship, admission or other sports benefit. Shared training remains a way to work together across differences.
arguments.con_html:
Response Accepting girls who object to a matchup is different from accepting their rule for who else may compete.

  • Because The complaint explains the school’s religious objection to playing that game: “it would be affirming that sex is mutable, in violation of its beliefs.” [5] Mutable means able to change. That explains the objection. It does not make meeting the school’s demand an act of accepting people across differences.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement does not mean adopting their demands about others. The UNESCO declaration on tolerance, an international statement, makes this clear: “It means that one is free to adhere to one's own convictions and accepts that others adhere to theirs.” [6]
  • Because H.R.28 would make it unlawful for federally funded programs to allow “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] The same rule would apply across covered programs, whether or not anyone objects. The bill's definition rests on “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]
  • So The forfeit explains why the school wants a different rule for who may compete. It does not show why respecting these girls gives [NAME] a tolerance-based reason to impose that rule on other participants.
  • Because The training exception begins: “Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to prohibit” [1]. The exception leaves shared training possible under stated conditions. It does not require any cooperation across differences.
  • So Permission to train together does not supply the missing link between enforcing the objection and accepting people despite disagreement.

paths.necessity_reason: The route needs the exclusion rule, because that rule removes the matchup. The objection and value link are local to this argument.

arguments.title: Protecting girls’ team places keeps chances to practice understanding and acceptance.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Protecting girls’ team places keeps chances to practice understanding and acceptance.

  • Because The competition rule prevents male competitors from taking female team places. Even shared training is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1], among other protected benefits. A roster spot is a place on a team.
  • Because Girls’ teams can offer a setting for learning to work with different people. A player in a study of two high school teams with players of many ethnic backgrounds described her own learning: “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” [7]
  • So Protecting girls from this loss of places and practice keeps their access to those shared learning experiences.
  • So [NAME]’s wish for people to listen to, understand and accept others gives a reason to protect girls’ chances to practice those habits with teammates.
arguments.con_html:
Response The cited study does not establish that the team places protected by the bill give practice in accepting different people.

  • Because The change the study reports from team play is that it “made players more collectivistic in response to a values questionnaire.” [7] Collectivistic means putting the group’s goals first. The questionnaire’s example of that outlook was “I agree with Emily, learning to play as a team is more important.” [7] That measures how much a player values team goals. Accepting people with different beliefs is a different outcome. The result neither shows nor rules out such acceptance.
  • Because The player’s statement, “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” [7], appears in an account of what she learned about how groups work. In the same passage she complains about team unity and says, “I think we need team bonding.” [7]
  • So The link from a team place to practice in accepting different people rests on one player’s brief use of the word tolerance, in a passage about team unity. This response does not dispute that she names tolerance as something she learned, or that the teams included players of many ethnic backgrounds.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: The girls' basketball study reports that its workshops, a three-session intervention, did not have the intended effect of increasing understanding of a different value system. That result concerns the intervention, not team play. The change the study measured over the season was toward collectivistic responses (putting the group's goals first). It did not measure acceptance of others. The study covered two Los Angeles-area teams. Sources: [7].

arguments.title: The bill replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.

  • Because On January 14, 2025, Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, protected participation in at least some cases. In a 2024 case, “The Fourth Circuit ruled that application of the West Virginia law to the plaintiff violated Title IX, because it treated her worse than those similarly situated based on her sex and caused her harm.” [8] The Fourth Circuit is a federal appeals court. Similarly situated means in a comparable position.
  • Because Differences between individuals mattered to that ruling. The court criticized a ban that applied “regardless of whether a particular student has any genuine athletic advantages” [8]. H.R.28 would instead make birth biology and genetics decide the question for every student it classifies as male.
  • Because [NAME] values accepting people even when they disagree. That gives weight to including a classmate despite disagreement about that classmate’s gender, and to hearing the student’s situation before ruling the student out.
  • So The bill would close a path to acceptance that the law then in force protected. Hearing individual students, or choosing inclusion as a school community, could no longer change eligibility under its birth-based rule.
  • Because The restriction also reaches activities tied to team membership. The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Shared sports offer chances to know people. Researchers describe “regular social interaction; opportunities to build positive relationships with teammates and coaches” [9].
  • Because Exclusion also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that “denying transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth the chance to participate only serves to deny them an opportunity to be part of that community, further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10] Stigma means shame or disapproval attached to a group.
  • Note The limited permission for “males to train or practice” [1] does not give back eligibility to compete on girls’ and women’s teams.
  • So Required exclusion takes away shared competition and team-linked chances to build understanding, while adding to stigma against these classmates. [NAME]’s wish to accept and understand different people gives a reason to keep those chances and resist that treatment.
arguments.con_html:
Response Accepting a person does not require agreeing on team eligibility, so losing eligibility is not by itself a loss of acceptance.

  • Because Accepting people across disagreements leaves room to disagree about rules. [NAME] can listen to a student, understand the student’s situation and accept the student while reaching a different view about team eligibility. The research defining this value says it concerns “accepting and understanding those with life-styles and beliefs different from one’s own.” [11]
  • Because The bill sets a rule for sports eligibility: “For the purposes of this subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] A decision under that rule does not show how classmates regard or listen to the student.
  • So Treating eligibility itself as acceptance assumes the point in question. This response does not answer the claims that exclusion reduces contact and team-linked chances to build understanding, adds stigma, or removes a school’s choice to include.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: The cited study compared any sports team participation with none. It did not compare acceptance with and without access to girls' competition. The bill allows conditional training or practice. Sources: [9], [1].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and sent both back to the lower courts (remanded them). It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules. It does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [12].
