arguments.title: The bill gives sex-based accusations more power to threaten girls’ places on teams.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill gives sex-based accusations more power to threaten girls’ places on teams.

  • Because Schools would have to follow a rule that makes birth sex decide eligibility. The bill applies to “a recipient of Federal financial assistance who operates, sponsors, or facilitates athletic programs or activities” [1]. A recipient is a school or college that receives federal money.
  • So Where schools have included transgender girls, the bill would make a claim that a girl was born male a basis to challenge her eligibility. This gives such accusations a path to exclusion.
  • Because That path has already been used under Utah’s rules for school sports eligibility. The Associated Press (AP) reported that Utah’s athletics association “secretly investigated a female athlete — without telling her or her parents — after receiving complaints from the parents of two girls she had defeated in competition questioning whether the girl was transgender.” [13] The complaint was “among several the association had looked into in its efforts to comply with the Utah law” [13].
  • Because Public accusations can also bring harassment. In a separate 2024 case, Utah’s state school board found that a member’s post suggested “that one of the female students in the picture may not be female” [14]. The board recorded “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” [14] resulting from the post and comments.
  • Because Girls who look different face a particular risk. Women’s rights and sports groups warn that sex checks are “especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity” [10].
  • Note The House member managing the bill says: “There is no requirement for inspections” [10]. Sex challenges and public accusations do not require physical exams.
  • So The bill creates grounds for exclusion that can turn differences in bodies, appearance and gender expression into reasons for suspicion and harassment. [NAME]’s tolerance toward different people gives a reason to oppose that risk, including, as those groups warn, an added risk for girls of color.

arguments.title: The bill removes a source of serious injury risk in female contact sports.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes a source of serious injury risk in female contact sports.

  • Because Rules based on hormones allowed these matchups in U.S. college sports. Testosterone is a hormone. May 2024 rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, included women’s rugby and stated: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [4] A threshold is a limit. Transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women.
  • Because A review of studies of transgender women who were not athletes found higher strength and muscle measures than in women who were female at birth, after hormone treatment: “values remain above that observed in cisgender women, even after 36 months.” [5] Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.
  • Because World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, links size and speed differences to injury: “When two opponents in a tackle are significantly different with respects to mass or speed, these risk factors increase significantly.” [6] This passage is about risks of head and neck injury. A tackle is when one player stops another by force.
  • Because World Rugby's review of lowering testosterone concluded that “safety and fairness cannot presently be assured for women competing against transwomen in contact rugby.” [7]
  • Note That conclusion was the basis for guidance about “the international level of the game” [7]. World Rugby’s guidance does “not preclude national unions from flexibility in their application of the guidelines at the domestic/community level of the game” [7].
  • So Where hormone-based rules allowed these matchups, H.R.28 would prevent them in covered female competitions. This removes the collision danger from those matchups.
  • So Safer conditions for an ordinary way to exercise serve [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury and danger.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Snopes, a fact-checking website, states in March 2025 that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender. It also states that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. Snopes also reports three more things. The school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence. The board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players, while several coaches spoke for continuing. North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, and their sports are unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [8], [9], [10].

Evidence note: World Rugby's estimate models typical male mass against typical female mass. A 2024 athlete study recommends evaluating transgender women athletes as their own group rather than using cisgender men as proxies. The hormone review did not report activity levels of the groups compared. Sources: [6], [11], [5].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. The statistical ranges for those comparisons include zero (no difference), and certainty is rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are averages for body composition and fitness. The text in this project's evidence collection reports no result by sport for absolute mass, speed, collisions or injuries. Only the abstract and correction notice are in this collection, so the review's full methods were not verified. The review came after the comparison date but before the evidence cutoff. Sources: [12], [13].

arguments.title: The bill protects girls’ chances to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill protects girls’ chances to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.

  • Because Limited team places can mean lost participation. ABC7 News reported that Taylor Starling was moved to the junior varsity (lower) team when a transgender runner joined a seven-place varsity (top) team, “causing Starling to miss a varsity cross-country meet.” [14] After a complaint under Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, she “was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet.” [14]
  • Because The bill keeps female competition for those female at birth. It also makes male practice depend on protecting each female’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • So The bill prevents that source of exclusion from female competition and practice. Where a girl has no other team place, this keeps her chance to exercise on a team open.
  • Because The federal health department explains that sports “participation is one way for youth to get the physical activity they need to be fit and healthy.” [15]
  • Because A U.S. study compared girls with boys during Title IX’s expansion of girls’ sports. It reported that the expansion “resulted in greater physical activity and improved weight and body mass.” [16]
  • Because The CDC, the federal public-health agency, states that “regular physical activity prevents risk factors for various health conditions like heart disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes.” [17]
  • Because The CDC also reports that active young people have “stronger bones and muscles.” [17] The brain-health benefits it lists include “reduced symptoms of depression.” [17]
  • So Keeping sports opportunities open protects a way to get exercise and its physical and mental health benefits. Protecting that way serves [NAME]’s wish to protect health and avoid disease.
arguments.con_html:
Response The one team-place example given does not show lost access to healthy exercise.

  • Because Starling “was bumped down to the JV team.” [14] JV means junior varsity.
  • Because The report adds that “she was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet. ML remains on the team as well.” [14] ML is the transgender runner in this report.
  • So Starling kept access to school sports, and both runners ended up on the varsity team. Losing varsity status for one meet does not show less exercise or lost health benefits.
  • Because The health study concerns more girls joining sports: “Title IX caused a significant increase in girls’ sports participation.” [16]
  • So That research is about girls added to sports, while the example is about a girl who stayed active. The evidence given does not support the step from being moved down to exercising less. This response does not address a girl cut from a team with limited places and no other place to play.

arguments.title: The bill protects bodily privacy in female changing activities tied to team participation.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill protects bodily privacy in female changing activities tied to team participation.

  • Because The bill’s reach includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.
  • So A changing activity for women or girls that is open only because of team participation falls under the bill’s female-only rule.
  • Because Undressing with others against one’s wishes can damage a sense of security. Representative Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines: “We did not give our consent to be exploited and exposed to a 6-foot-4 fully naked man.” [9] She added: “You allowed college women to be traumatized” [9].
  • So Applying the rule to those changing activities removes that path to unwanted shared undressing. Privacy in intimate settings supports feeling personally secure, which [NAME] values.
  • So Separately, a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.
arguments.con_html:
Response The bill’s text and the quoted account do not show that shared changing is a covered activity.

  • Because The bill limits its new definition of sex to “the purposes of this subsection” [1].
  • Because The bill's definition of athletic activities “includes, but is not limited to, all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Representative Walberg quotes Gaines describing the exposure: “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” [9] A locker room is a room for changing clothes.
  • So That account does not show that access depended on team participation, or that the shared changing was itself a covered athletic activity. A room’s connection to sports does not establish the condition this legal argument needs. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.

arguments.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse and trauma.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse and trauma.

  • Because The bill sets a birth-sex rule but does not say how to check it. Representative Hayes noted that it provides “neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” [18].
  • Because Idaho passed an intrusive rule for checking sex. The Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court, described it as allowing “intrusive medical procedures to verify her sex, including gynecological exams” [19]. A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs.
  • Because The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that H.R.28 invites “invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [9] that “make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [9].
  • Because Such checks also threaten mental health. The court explained: “The psychological burden of these searches falls not only on transgender women like Lindsay but also on all women and girls who play female athletics.” [19]
  • Because Fear of checks also threatens participation. Representative Randall warned that intrusive questions and examinations would be “dissuading girls' participation in sports” [9]. Dissuading means persuading people not to do something.
  • So The new federal eligibility rule creates risks of bodily intrusion, abuse and distress in an ordinary school activity. By discouraging girls from playing, it also threatens the health benefits of exercise. Avoiding these dangers serves [NAME]’s aim to stay safe and healthy.
arguments.con_html:
Response Idaho’s separate medical-testing rule does not establish that H.R.28 would expose girls to intrusive exams.

  • Because H.R.28 defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without ordering medical inspections. The House member managing the bill described the intended method: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [9]

arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Public challenges to girls’ sex expose them to harassment and threats of violence.

  • Because The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that H.R.28 “will invite scrutiny and harassment of any other student perceived by anyone as not conforming to sex stereotypes” [9].
  • Because This kind of accusation has already put a girl in danger. After a Utah state school board member questioned a basketball player’s sex, the board found that her post “created a substantial risk of harm” [21].

  • So Making birth sex a federal condition for playing gives these accusations a new role in decisions about who can play. Threats against girls who are not transgender, and against their families, make this a safety concern in ordinary school sports. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

arguments.title: The exclusion cuts off a way to get exercise, mental health support and health checkups.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The exclusion cuts off a way to get exercise, mental health support and health checkups.

  • Because The ban reaches ordinary school sports as well as top-level competition. As Representative Bonamici explained: “this bill applies to every student of every age in every sport the same way” [9].
  • Because Federal health guidance links youth sports with “Increased physical activity levels” [15] and physical activity with “Reduced risk of cancer and diabetes” [15].
  • Because A Colorado survey linked playing on three or more sports teams, compared with none, to “reduced likelihood of depression” [23] among transgender students.
  • Because Sports also provide supportive relationships. The study cites research showing that “increased social support in adolescence, including that provided by team sports participation, protects against depression” [23].
  • Note The bill’s conditional permission “to train or practice” [1] leaves the competition ban in place.
  • Because Boys’ teams do not keep every excluded girl in sports. Transgender girls in a survey reported avoiding sports because they feared being “forced to play on a team or use a facility that does not align with their gender identity” [24].
  • Because Leaving sports also risks losing a reason to see a doctor. In a study of health care providers who treat transgender youth, one warned that patients who no longer need sports exams “may miss health issues and immunizations due to not coming in” [25].
  • So Closing access to competition removes a way to keep exercising and to have supportive relationships. For students pushed out of sports, it also puts sports-linked checkups at risk. Protecting physical and mental health gives [NAME] a reason to oppose these losses.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: The Colorado study measured the number of sports teams played and states that it cannot assess whether team participation directly reduces adverse mental-health outcomes. The missed-checkup statement is one provider's prediction, and the provider study notes that its prompt lacked precision because many bills do not ban participation outright. Sources: [23], [25].

arguments.title: Official rejection threatens mental health beyond students who lose a team place.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Official rejection threatens mental health beyond students who lose a team place.

  • Because Denying students a place in school sports marks them as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights describes this as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth” [9]. Stigma means shame or disapproval attached to a group.

  • So The law’s rejection of some students threatens the supportive school ties that protect mental health, even when no one leaves a sport. Protecting health in everyday school life gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.

arguments.title: Exclusion cuts access to sports as a way to build safer communities.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Exclusion cuts access to sports as a way to build safer communities.

  • Because Requiring transgender students to play on teams based on sex at birth drives some out of sports. A 2025 study summarizes earlier research: “policies requiring youth to play on teams with their assigned sex, dissuade youth from participating” [16]. To dissuade means to persuade people not to do something.
  • Because The loss also reaches girls born with variations in sex traits, often called intersex variations. Women’s sports organizations report: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [10] Chilled means made people afraid to take part.
  • Note The conditional practice exception allows “males to train or practice” [1]. It guarantees no place in practice and leaves the competition ban in place.
  • So Where schools now include them, the bill cuts off a way into sports for students it excludes or discourages.
  • Because Sports also provide a setting linked to less use of illegal drugs. A review of 17 studies that followed young people over time reports: “Sport participation was associated with reduced illicit drug use during adolescence.” [17] Associated means the two happen together. It does not by itself prove cause.
  • Because The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) describes organized sports as a tool for preventing violence: “Research shows that organized sport participation can reduce youth violence” [18].
  • Because School sports build community ties. The civil rights coalition explains that “School athletics are very often the centerpiece of communities across the country” [10] and that exclusion means “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10] HHS links sports with “Improved teamwork, social skills, and social responsibility” [19].
  • Because Community ties are connected with public safety. The U.S. Surgeon General, a top federal health official, links stronger community ties with “lower levels of community violence” [20].
  • So Exclusion closes a way to cooperation, community ties, less illegal drug use and, as HHS describes it, violence prevention. Keeping those forms of protection helps the United States protect its people. That serves [NAME]’s goal of a secure, stable country.
arguments.con_html:
Response The research does not establish that changed eligibility would reduce violence prevention or community safety.

  • Because HHS cites “McMahon S, Belur J. Sports-based Programmes and Reducing Youth Violence and Crime.” [18] That review states: “None of the evaluations present robust enough evidence to directly establish causal links between interventions and outcomes.” [21] It reports some correlational evidence, meaning things that happen together, not proof of cause.
  • Because A separate review of studies on youth crime concludes that “in general, sports involvement is not reliably related to more or less juvenile delinquency” [22]. Delinquency means youth crime. HHS itself says: “Coaching, program design, and funding affect these outcomes” [18].
  • So Fewer sports places cannot simply stand for lost crime prevention. The argument has not linked the affected programs to the features that provide that protection.
  • Because The Surgeon General’s discussion of lower crime concerns residents’ “willingness to act” [20] for community members.
  • So Losing a school sports tie and losing trust in a neighborhood are different outcomes, and the argument does not connect them. This response does not address the drug-use route.

Evidence note: The values paper cited in this argument states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: The mental-health study compared any team participation with none, and its authors say they could not deduce cause and effect and that depression can make participation harder. HHS introduces its mental-health and disease findings with "is associated with". The suicide figure describes existing risk among transgender and questioning students. HHS associates youth sports with reduced suicide risk and physical activity with reduced cancer and diabetes risk, and one study found lower depressive and anxiety symptoms among team athletes. CDC reports that about 26% of transgender and questioning students attempted suicide in the past year. HHS is the federal health department. CDC is the federal public-health agency. Sources: [16], [19], [23].

Evidence note: The Surgeon General's advisory reports that people in neighborhoods connected to community institutions prepare for and recover from natural hazards more quickly. That passage does not address school sports. Sources: [20].

  • So Exclusion closes a route to cooperation, community ties, less illegal drug use and, on HHS’s account, violence prevention. Preserving those forms of protection helps the United States protect its people. That serves [NAME]’s goal of a secure, stable country.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s research does not establish that changed eligibility would reduce violence prevention or community safety.

  • Because HHS cites “McMahon S, Belur J. Sports-based Programmes and Reducing Youth Violence and Crime.” [18] That review states: “None of the evaluations present robust enough evidence to directly establish causal links between interventions and outcomes.” [21] It reports some correlational evidence, not proof of cause.

arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill preserves the established practice of separate female competition.

  • Because Separate school sports have a long legal history: “Long-standing Title IX regulations permit separation of the sexes in school sports programs provided schools offer equal athletic opportunities.” [6] Title IX is the federal law against sex discrimination in education.

That removed the 2024 regulations. The older sports rule quoted above permitted separate teams. H.R.28 would add an express requirement to exclude male competitors from female sports.

arguments.title: The bill takes a decision about children’s upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill takes a decision about children’s upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.

  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention, a large Christian denomination, teaches that “parents are the primary stewards of and decision-makers for their children, rather than teachers, doctors, or the state” [18]. A steward is someone responsible for caring for something.
  • Because Catholic teaching protects work that smaller groups can do themselves. It calls it an injustice to “assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.” [19]
  • Because Sports rules are already partly a local responsibility: “Currently, schools, parents, and communities manage youth sports leagues and write rules about who can participate in different sports at different levels.” [14]
  • Because Existing reviews of individual students already consider safety and fairness. The Congressional Research Service describes Illinois’s 2024–25 rules as “requiring approval to participate based on consideration of individual circumstances” [6] and as considering whether “allowing eligibility would be inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • Because H.R.28 would remove that choice at covered schools. As Representative Norcross explained: “It inflicts blanket bans without the ability of states, local governments, schools, and parents to make reasonable exceptions.” [20]
  • So Even when parents and a willing school approve a child’s participation after an individual review, the federal rule would bar girls’ competition if it classifies that child as male. Keeping the family and local roles taught by [NAME]’s tradition gives a reason to oppose that loss of authority.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument has not shown that the particular sports exception being removed belongs to the family and local duties its religious sources protect.

  • Because The cited Baptist resolution places parents’ decisions “under the authority of God, recognizing that they will be held responsible for their choices” [18].
  • Because The Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission, a Southern Baptist agency, explains: “The duty of parental authority is not the right to teach children whatever they desire. Rather, it is normed by what is good, true, and righteous.” [21] Normed by means limited by that standard.
  • Because That same body addressed this sports decision on January 13, 2025: “Schools that allow biological males to participate in female sports programs are discriminating against biological females.” [22]
  • So In this account, approval by parents and a school does not turn that eligibility exception into an act of Christian care or rightful parental teaching. The argument cannot conclude that religious authority protects the exception just because parents and a school want it.
  • Because The Catholic principle of leaving work to smaller groups also serves duties beyond those groups. The same source says: “To ensure the common good, the government of each country has the specific duty to harmonize the different sectoral interests with the requirements of justice” [19]. Harmonize means bring together.
  • Because Illinois’s 2024–25 policy made eligibility a decision for the statewide sports association: “IHSA will make final rulings on student participation.” [23] The association's review considered whether eligibility would be “inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • So Showing that a lower body can run a review does not show that its eligibility standard meets the religious account of justice. The argument has not shown that allowing this exception is a duty the cited traditions reserve to families or local groups. Its claim of lost religious authority therefore lacks the needed link.

arguments.title: Disputes over sex eligibility can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Disputes over sex eligibility can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.

  • Because Schools would have to apply the bill’s definition of sex, but it gives no way to check disputed eligibility. Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [24]
  • Because Women’s sports organizations warn that resulting checks “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [14].
  • Because Questions about intimate matters have occurred under a comparable state ban. The National Women’s Law Center reports that a Florida investigation included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25]
  • Because Catholic teaching connects children’s privacy to moral upbringing: “Respect for privacy must be considered in close connection with decency and modesty” [26]. Modesty is keeping the body and private matters covered or private.
  • So Applying the rule in schools that now allow participation would require them to settle disputes about sex eligibility. The Florida account documents intimate questions, and the organizations also warn of invasive checks. For [NAME], keeping the particular religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy supplies the Tradition connection. General safety and dignity are separate reasons.
arguments.con_html:
Response The House member managing the bill identifies a way to use records, which limits the argument about bodily examinations.

  • Because The bill adds a violation of Title IX, the federal education law, for “a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] and defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1]. Its text sets no examination procedure. A recipient is a school or college that receives federal money.
  • Because The bill’s manager described a way to apply the bill through records: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [14]
  • Because The Florida source reports a state investigation that included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25] That describes questions, not a bodily examination.
  • So The manager’s account of using records relates to the proposed step from this rule to bodily examinations. It does not answer the documented risk of intimate questions, or show that the religious modesty concern disappears. This is a limited response to the examination part only.

arguments.title: Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of water that wildlife uses.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of water that wildlife uses.

  • Because The Department of the Interior manages many federal lands. It reported that border staff and equipment reduced damaging traffic: “By deploying personnel, equipment, and infrastructure, CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • Because The Forest Service said that people crossing the border leave trash behind: “Perhaps one of the most well known of the impacts of illegal immigration is the litter left behind” [3].
  • Because This trash can ruin water that wild animals drink: “Water sources near this contamination are often so fouled by pollution that wildlife can no longer use them.” [3]
  • So Section 201 pays for staff, and Section 103 pays for surveillance. Both support patrols like the ones Interior describes. Where added patrols reduce crossings through wild areas, they can reduce this pollution. Protecting water that wildlife uses serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
arguments.con_html:
Response These local gains do not show that S.2's added patrols would reduce this traffic instead of moving it somewhere else.

  • Because Interior reported gains in some places: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3] “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
  • So Enforcement can reduce traffic in one place and push it into wild land in another. So one step is missing: that added patrols would reduce the traffic near wildlife water, and not only move it.

arguments.title: Catching people faster protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Catching people faster protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.

  • Because Section 103 pays for towers on the southwest and northern borders only if CBP (Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency) has tested and accepted them “to deliver autonomous capabilities.” [1] “Autonomous” means the system works without constant human control.
  • Because CBP reported that people were caught faster with autonomous towers: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that “unauthorized trails and roads have been created on the Forest by illegal foot and vehicle traffic.” [3] It said that when these trails spread, this “damages and destroys cactus and other sensitive vegetation; disrupts or prohibits revegetation; disturbs wildlife, their security and travel routes; causes soil compaction and erosion” [3].
  • Because Crossing traffic also broke a fence that protected the habitat (home area) of endangered species. The fence became “ineffective in restricting livestock use” [3]. As a result, “This fence damage has allowed the destruction of endangered species habitat to continue” [3].
  • So Paying for staff and faster detection makes it easier to stop damaging traffic and fence damage. That protects plants, wildlife habitat and soil from destruction, which [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:
Response Catching someone faster does not show that there is less damage to trails, plants or fences.

  • Because The tower report describes a narrower result: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3] “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
  • So Speed of response does not measure total travel through habitat or fence damage avoided. Enforcement can also push traffic into wild areas. So this argument does not connect faster catching to less damaging traffic overall.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: Surveillance money already in law: The Congressional Research Service (CRS), the research office of Congress, says the 2025 budget law (P.L. 119-21) provides $6.17 billion for inspection and surveillance technology. Sources: [5].

arguments.title: Stopping unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful species brought in from elsewhere.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Stopping unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful species brought in from elsewhere.

  • Because In March 2025, the Department of the Interior described harm from unlawful border activity: “national parks, wildlife refuges and the species they protect are adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6]. “Invasive species” are plants or animals that come from elsewhere and harm local nature.
  • Because Border operations have reduced the activity that carries these risks: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • So Added staff and surveillance help stop this traffic. Less unlawful travel through parks and refuges can reduce one way that harmful species spread there. Reducing this spread is a way to protect nature.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument treats immigration enforcement as a way to control invasive species, but does not show how stopping people would keep species out.

  • Because Interior lists “invasive species introductions” [6] among the harms, but it does not explain how these species arrive.
  • Because Seeds can travel on people. The National Park Service explains: “Seeds can readily become lodged in our boots and stuck to our clothing.” [7]
  • So The missing step is keeping species from reaching habitat. A person caught after walking through the land may already have carried the seeds there. The list of harms and the general report of reduced border activity do not show that S.2 would reduce this spread.

Point 3 Intercepting unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful introduced species.

  • Because In March 2025, Interior described harm from unlawful border activity: “national parks, wildlife refuges and the species they protect are adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6].
  • Because Border operations have reduced the activity carrying these risks: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • So Added staffing and surveillance support interception of this traffic. Less unlawful travel through parks and refuges can reduce one route by which harmful species spread there. Reducing such introductions is a way to protect nature.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO treats immigration interception as invasive-species control without showing which introductions it would reduce.

  • Because Interior lists lands and species as “adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6], but does not identify the species or how they arrive.
  • Because Seeds can travel on people. The National Park Service explains: “Seeds can readily become lodged in our boots and stuck to our clothing.” [7]

Point 4 Preventing damaging crossings also addresses one cause of destructive wildfires.

  • Because The Forest Service documented the link: “Large numbers of warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators have caused wildfires that have destroyed valuable natural and cultural resources.” [3] “Cross-border violators” means people crossing the border illegally.
  • Because S.2 supports a way of reducing this activity that has worked in some areas. The Department of the Interior reported that border operations “have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • So Stopping people before they travel and camp in natural areas makes it easier to prevent these fires. Avoiding fires that destroy nature gives [NAME] another reason to favor S.2.
arguments.con_html:
Response The sources do not connect S.2's added arrests to fewer abandoned campfires in these forests.

  • Because The Forest Service names “warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators” [3] as a cause of wildfires.
  • Because The same testimony says that enforcement beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3] “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
  • So This argument relies on Interior's general report of reductions in some areas. But the fire evidence comes from a forest where enforcement pushed traffic into the backcountry (remote land). So added patrols may not mean fewer people camping there. One step is missing: that patrols would reduce crossings in fire-prone wild land, and not only move them.

arguments.title: Joint patrols let land officers focus on protecting natural resources.

Point 6 Joint patrols let land officers focus on protecting natural resources.

  • Because The Forest Service reported that border enforcement took its officers away from conservation: “The law enforcement efforts in response to cross-border violators and smugglers of controlled substances diverts our officers from other management and resource protection activities.” [3]
  • Because The Department of the Interior described “intelligence-supported joint patrols on Interior and USFS managed lands.” [2] (Joint patrols use officers from more than one agency. USFS is the Forest Service.) Interior reported that duties were divided: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” [2] These are violations that harm the land and its resources.
  • Because Together with the immigration staff in Section 201, Section 103 pays for “Enhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals, at the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1]

arguments.title: Patrol support helps land managers carry out planned burns that care for plants.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 Patrol support helps land managers carry out planned burns that care for plants.

  • Because The Forest Service uses fire to care for land, as well as fighting unwanted fires: “The Forest Service works to both fight wildland fires and to use prescribed fires as a tool to manage vegetative resources.” [3] Prescribed fires are planned burns.
  • Because Security is part of this work: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” [3] The same testimony says: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.” [3]
  • So Section 101 pays for duties other than immigration and customs enforcement. That supports staff who help make these work areas safe. Helping people carry out this care for plants supports the active defense of nature that [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:
Response The testimony does not separate help with fighting fires from help with planned burns.

  • Because The testimony describes clearing fire areas and guarding firefighters: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” [3] It adds: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.” [3]
  • Because The discussion covers both kinds of fire work: “during prescribed fires or fire suppression operations” [3]. Prescribed fires are planned burns. Fire suppression means fighting fires.
  • So General security help at fires does not show that Border Patrol support made planned burns possible. Without that step, the claimed support for plant care rests on a guess about which fire work agents helped with.

arguments.title: S.2 supports detention operations that risk polluting land and water.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 S.2 supports detention operations that risk polluting land and water.

  • Because Section 202 pays to run enforcement facilities through “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” [1].
  • Because The city government of Social Circle, Georgia, warns that running ICE's planned detention center would “risk sewage overflows into nearby land and water” [16]. ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
  • Because Maryland's assessment of a warehouse in Williamsport explains the same risk. Its agencies estimate sewage flow at “more than seven times the existing projected flow for the facility’s prior commercial use.” [17]
  • Because Maryland's agencies explain the risk: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” [17].
  • Because These waters support wildlife: “A number of State-listed Endangered species, Species in Need of Conservation, and other Rare species rely on the waters in the vicinity of the Warehouse property.” [17]

arguments.con_html:
Response This sewage argument leaves out limits on these warehouse plans that existed before June 9, 2026.

  • Because Social Circle had locked the water meter at the planned detention center. Its city manager described the condition: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity.” [18]
  • Because An April 15 court order stopped work at the Williamsport warehouse while the case continues: “Defendants are enjoined during the pendency of this lawsuit from construction and renovation at the warehouse located at 16220 Wright Road, Williamsport, Maryland 21795 (the “Williamsport Warehouse”) for the purposes of operating the warehouse as a detention and processing facility;” [19]
  • Because Maryland's warning concerns going beyond sewer capacity: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” [17]. Maryland also requires a fix: “Any necessary upgrades must comply with applicable State permitting requirements and be funded by DHS.” [17]

arguments.title: S.2 equips border patrols whose off-road driving damages desert wilderness.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 S.2 equips border patrols whose off-road driving damages desert wilderness.

  • Because Section 201 pays for “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1] for immigration enforcement.
  • Because At Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, an agreement between agencies allows off-road patrols in emergencies: “This agreement authorizes border enforcement agents to drive off-road in wilderness under exigent or emergency circumstances that involve threats to human health and safety.” [20] “Exigent” means urgent.
  • Because In 2012, the National Park Service reported that, since the agreement began, “monitoring data have shown that off-road-vehicle impacts have increased” [20].
  • Because The Park Service explains the physical harm from these roads and trails: “These incursions damage soils, vegetation, and wildlife habitat.” [21]
  • So Extra money for these patrols supports off-road driving that damages soil, plants and habitat. Protecting wild places gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this money.
arguments.con_html:
Response More border-patrol staff does not by itself mean more damaging off-road driving at Organ Pipe.

  • Because Section 201 pays for several uses of staff: “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1].
  • Because The agreement behind this example allows agents to patrol “on foot or on horseback” [22].
  • Because The Park Service later described more staff aimed at reducing vehicle use: “The U.S. Border Patrol Ajo Station has increased its Horse Patrol Unit (HPU) with the recent graduation of agents through the class. The Ajo Station HPU patrols at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in an effort to reduce mechanized equipment in the wilderness.” [23]
  • So Paying for staff and damaging vehicle use are separate steps. The 2012 report of more damage does not show that S.2 adds such driving or keeps it going. The horse patrols at this same site show why more staff alone does not establish that link.

arguments.title: S.2 puts forest protection and tree-planting crews at risk of removal.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 S.2 puts forest protection and tree-planting crews at risk of removal.

  • Because Sections 201 and 202 pay immigration enforcement staff “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because This work reaches forest workers. In 2025, Border Patrol arrested a firefighter whose work included “clearing fallen trees and other debris to prevent the Bear Gulch fire, a 9,000-acre blaze, from growing” [24]. He was later “quietly deported to Mexico” [24].
  • Because ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) has also removed tree-planting crews. After a 2007 raid on a company replanting burned land in Boise National Forest, “Ten of the workers were deported to Mexico and four others were released pending an immigration hearing” [25].
  • Because This work had a short planting season. A Forest Service spokesperson explained: “You have to plant in cooler times, when the ground is moist” [25].
  • Because Late replanting threatens nature. In 2025, the Forest Resources Association warned that without timely reforestation (replanting), “these lands risk erosion, habitat loss” [26].
  • So More ability to arrest and remove these workers puts time-sensitive forest care at risk. Protecting forests gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added ability.
arguments.con_html:
Response The forestry examples do not show that S.2 raises the risk that needed forest work is left without crews.

  • Because Later reporting on the 2025 case found that crews kept working: “Both of the private crews have active agreements with the Forest Service and have been assigned to new fires.” [27]
  • Because The 2007 report describes efforts to replace arrested workers: “For now, Olson said his office is working with the company to get replacement workers as soon as possible.” [25]
  • Because The forestry association's warning is about temporary work visas (H-2B visas). Its proposed solutions include: “An exemption for forestry workers from the H-2B visa cap to address the reforestation backlog.” [26] It is not a warning about arrests.
  • So Arrests alone do not show that forest work would lack crews, because crews continued to get work and replacements were sought. A warning about late planting does not show that S.2 raises the chance of those delays. So one step is missing: from the added enforcement money to more unfilled forest work.

Point 7 S.2 strengthens surveillance tools that can discourage people from defending nature.

  • Because Section 103 pays for aircraft and related equipment of Customs and Border Protection (CBP): “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” [1]

Response This argument does not connect general staff money for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) to more teaching for children and families.

  • Because Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported that in fiscal year 2024, “HSI also conducted 258 elder fraud cases” [3], producing “121 indictments, 52 convictions, and $12.6 million seized.” [3]. HSI also investigated romance scams: “HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” [3] cases that year.
  • So More capacity to investigate these scams, secure convictions and seize criminals' proceeds strengthens protection against financial exploitation. [NAME] has a reason to protect victims' resources and seek justice for them, including strangers targeted because of age or trust.
original.con_html:
Response The fraud totals do not establish more protection against scams from S.2 under HSI’s changed priorities.

  • Because The fraud results are explicitly past results: “In FY 2024, HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” [3] cases and “258 elder fraud cases” [3]. They describe an earlier distribution of investigators’ work.

arguments.title: S.2 adds resources to stop drugs that cause overdoses.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 S.2 adds resources to stop drugs that cause overdoses.

  • Because Section 103 adds $3.45 billion for inspection equipment, air and sea response, surveillance and related work: “$3,450,000,000 for the following” [1]. Its purposes include “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders” [1].
  • Because The work includes “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1]. Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs. ICE describes the danger as “the synthetic drugs that fuel overdose deaths” [3]. An overdose means taking enough of a drug to cause serious harm or death.
  • So Finding and stopping these drugs keeps seized drugs from reaching people. More resources for this work strengthen protection for people at risk of overdose, whose lives matter to [NAME].
arguments.con_html:
Response Cheap replacement weakens the step from a seized shipment to less drug use overall.

  • Because Drug-policy researchers Jonathan Caulkins and Peter Reuter explain: “But traffickers can easily replace what is seized.” [7] They say fentanyl is cheap to make and easy to move: “It is absurdly cheap for high-level traffickers to replace seizures.” [7]
  • Because A 2026 review of many studies (search through April 2025) treated some seizures as disruptions by police. The results point in different directions. Local or regional studies linked seizures to more overdoses nearby or the next year, while a study in a Florida county linked fewer seizures to more deaths. These are associations (things found together), not estimates for S.2's border resources. [8]
  • So Replacement challenges the step from seized shipments to fewer drugs reaching people and less overdose risk. It does not deny that the seized drugs themselves stay off the street. Neither the review nor cheap replacement proves that more seizures have no benefit.

arguments.con_html:

arguments.title: S.2 provides resources to protect agency workers from injury.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 13 S.2 provides resources to protect agency workers from injury.

  • Because The bill pays for staff training and equipment, including money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel” [1] and similar money for other agency staff.
  • Because A report by the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) describes protective gear as “equipment to protect them while on duty.” [17] It also describes defensive training “to mitigate and prevent assaults” [17].
  • So Resources for protective equipment and safety training support safer work. Protecting workers against known job dangers is part of treating them justly, which gives [NAME] a reason to favor this money too.
arguments.con_html:
Response The safety report's training problem comes from unclear rules, which this money does not change.

  • Because The report found unclear training rules: “ICE does not clearly define requirements for refresher training” [17]. It recommended that ICE “Mandate that law enforcement officers complete refresher” [17] training quarterly.
  • Because S.2 pays agencies to “hire, pay, train, and equip” [1] staff, but it does not set that schedule or fix the guidance.
  • So So money alone may not improve the training that the report says is missing. This response does not cover equipment. The same report says “Seventy percent of ICE personnel we interviewed believed additional equipment is needed” [17].

arguments.title: S.2 pays for holding more people who pose no public safety threat and favors custody over monitored release.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 S.2 pays for holding more people who pose no public safety threat and favors custody over monitored release.

  • Because The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, says the money would let the Department of Homeland Security continue the Trump administration's mass deportation strategy. It says this strategy has included “locking up immigrants who pose no public safety threat” [18].
  • Because Section 202(9) sets aside an arrest and custody fund of “Not less than $350,000,000” [1].
  • Because For this fund, the bill rules out spending on release or on alternatives such as check-ins, except when existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” [1]. “Parole” here means letting a person out of custody for a time.
  • So The bill adds capacity to take away people's freedom under a strategy that reaches people who pose no safety threat. It also rules out less restrictive uses of this fund. Just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose paying for that loss of freedom.
arguments.con_html:
Response The lack of a public safety threat does not by itself show that this custody is needless or unjust.

  • Because Custody can have a purpose other than preventing violence. For people already ordered removed, the Supreme Court tests detention against a period “reasonably necessary to secure removal” [20]. It names the purpose of “assuring the alien’s presence at the moment of removal” [20]. This case does not cover every kind of immigration custody.

arguments.title: S.2 pays to extend enforcement with a record of singling people out by race or background.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 S.2 pays to extend enforcement with a record of singling people out by race or background.

  • Because Section 202 pays for more federal staff and for local police to take part through “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1]. These agreements “allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions” [23].
  • Because Human Rights Watch found federal agents in Los Angeles “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [19].
  • So More staff and a wider enforcement network extend the reach of an operation with documented stops based on race. Being held because of one's background conflicts with equal opportunities and just treatment.
arguments.con_html:
Response The Los Angeles findings do not show that the added staff and local agreements would spread race-based stops under the approach reported before Congress's June 9 vote.

  • Because Human Rights Watch places those findings in the “campaign of raids and detentions throughout the summer of 2025 in Los Angeles” [19].
  • Because On May 5, CBS reported the account of Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, that “Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.” [24]
  • Because The same report says ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) had prioritized “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” [24].
  • So Evidence about the earlier operation does not show that the added money would carry race-based stops forward under this reported change. The CBS report is an official's account, and it does not discuss the local agreements. This does not show that such stops have ended.

arguments.title: S.2 keeps open detention with documented dangers to the health of children and sick people.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 S.2 keeps open detention with documented dangers to the health of children and sick people.

  • Because Section 202 pays for “facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Human Rights Watch documented conditions in Florida in 2025, including “overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” [19].
  • Because Before Congress's June 9 vote, Senator Kim described a very sick man he met in detention: “He should have been in a hospital, but, instead, he was isolated in that cramped room for 5 months.” [26]
  • Because Children also face unsafe conditions: “In Dilley, families described receiving food with worms and mold, tainted water, and inadequate education.” [25]
  • Because The new operating money lasts until September 2029, although these are “federal agencies that are typically funded through the annual appropriations process.” [27] This means Congress usually decides their money each year.
  • So The bill keeps a system with these dangers going and adds money it can use without new yearly approval. That makes refusing a future year's operating money a weaker way to demand safer conditions.
  • So Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [19] Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling. Paying for more detention without those reforms exposes people who depend on their jailers to more harm. Protecting children and sick people gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this money.

arguments.title: S.2 spreads harm through communities beyond the people arrested.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 S.2 spreads harm through communities beyond the people arrested.

  • Because Senator Smith described help needed during Minnesota's enforcement operation: “Churches and neighbors organized mutual aid and delivered prescriptions to folks who couldn't leave their own homes.” [28] She also described “food deliveries for people who were afraid to go to the grocery store.” [28]
  • Because Children suffered lasting trauma and missed school: “Kids traumatized by these tactics and still not back in school.” [28]
  • Because School harm also reaches children of U.S.-born parents. A research review reports that “negative academic impacts following immigration enforcement actions extended to U.S.-born students with U.S.-born parents.” [29]
  • Because The same review describes lasting effects, with “one study finding notable reductions in 4-year college enrollment following a large-scale worksite raid in Texas in 2018.” [29]
  • So Paying for more such operations extends a threat to getting food and medicine, and to children's well-being and schooling. Protecting vulnerable people and equal chances in life gives [NAME] a reason to oppose these wider harms to communities.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument carries the effects of particular past operations forward without accounting for the change in approach before Congress's June 9 vote.

  • Because CBS reported that Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, had been told to work on “winding down the Minneapolis operation” [24]. It also described a shift by ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) toward “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” [24].
  • So Those reports weaken the use of the Minnesota food, medicine and school harms to predict what added money would do. This does not answer the research on school harm after enforcement actions, and it does not show that such operations have ended.

arguments.title: S.2 pays for enforcement under a paused but not cancelled home-entry policy, without requiring warrants from judges.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 S.2 pays for enforcement under a paused but not cancelled home-entry policy, without requiring warrants from judges.

  • Because Representative Thompson reported that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) used earlier money to “break into homes without warrants” [2]. A warrant is official permission to enter or arrest.
  • Because S.2 adds enforcement money without the proposed requirement for warrants from judges: “It does not require officers to get judicial warrants.” [2]
  • Because In May, the DHS secretary wrote that ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) “has not rescinded the memorandum; however, I have paused the practice of entering an illegal alien’s residence who is subject to a final order of removal with an I-205” [30], “while I assess the policy.” [30] “Rescinded” means cancelled. An I-205 is ICE's removal warrant.
  • So S.2's operating money would pay for operations in which such entries could start again after the review, and it adds no rule requiring a judge's approval. Protecting people from unchecked entry into their homes is part of treating strangers justly. So this risk gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the money.
arguments.con_html:
Response The lack of a new warrant rule does not show that S.2 makes it more likely that the paused home entries start again.

arguments.title: S.2 supports cases against people who persecute others for their identity or beliefs.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 S.2 supports cases against people who persecute others for their identity or beliefs.

  • Because Section 202 pays for ICE staff across its branches, including investigators and lawyers, “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1] ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
  • Because ICE's human rights center handles immigration cases involving “individuals who have persecuted others based on race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion” [2]. To persecute means to harm or punish people because of who they are or what they believe.
  • Because Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the part of ICE that investigates crimes, also investigates crimes including “torture, genocide, recruitment and use of child soldiers” [2].
  • Because HSI's work includes “Supporting efforts to return violators to their home countries to face justice for the crimes they committed there.” [3]
  • Because Past money helped ICE's human rights center “increase staffing and, in turn, to generate more case leads.” [2]
  • So Section 102 adds resources for criminal human rights investigations; section 202 adds resources for immigration cases against persecutors.
  • So Persecution attacks the differences [NAME] values accepting. Holding persecutors responsible gives [NAME] a reason to pay for this work.
arguments.con_html:
No response specific to this point is provided.

Shared objection Reported changes in staff assignments weaken the step from a larger general budget for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) to more staff for the work in this argument.

  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned en masse to immigration enforcement” [4].

arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 S.2 adds capacity for enforcement that targets people by ethnic or national background.

  • So This argument projects the earlier campaign's methods onto added staff without addressing this later change. So more enforcement capacity alone does not establish more use of that particular way of choosing people. This is an official's account, and it does not show that such stops have ended.

arguments.title: S.2 pays for separating established immigrant neighbors from their families and communities.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 S.2 pays for separating established immigrant neighbors from their families and communities.

  • Because S.2 pays for “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1] “Removal” means deportation.
  • Because A report published before Congress's June 9 vote found: “Individuals who are not public safety threats and have deep ties to their communities have been indiscriminately targeted under this administration.” [16] It also records children experiencing “family separation as a result of a parent being detained.” [16]
  • Because The bill sets aside “Not less than $350,000,000” [1] for certain immigration arrest and custody work, including “custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens” [1].
  • Because Some adults qualify without a conviction: “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” [1]. A detainer is a government request to hold a person for immigration officers.
  • Because This arrest fund cannot pay for release or community alternatives unless existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” [1].
  • So The added deportation money and the arrest fund's preference for custody strengthen the means of separating people from community life, including parents and people without convictions.
  • So Accepting different people as neighbors gives [NAME] a reason to oppose more ability to exclude the established community members described above, who are not threats.
arguments.con_html:
Response Separation from family and having no conviction do not by themselves show rejection of people for being different.

  • Because The transport provision pays for “alien departure or removal operations.” [1] Removal is a civil process tied to immigration status, not a criminal punishment: “deportation is classified as a civil rather than a criminal sanction” [17].
  • Because The arrest fund includes an adult who, “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” [1]. These conditions concern criminal process and immigration custody. They are not tests of ethnicity, faith or opinion.
  • Because The limit on release spending applies to “funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph” [1] and keeps the exception “except as required by existing law” [1]. It does not cancel release rights or stop other money from paying for release.
  • So This argument identifies family disruption and a preference for custody. Neither one makes acceptance of a person's background or beliefs depend on that person staying. The missing value step is why enforcing these civil rules rejects difference. Having no conviction does not supply that step.

arguments.title: S.2 expands the police role that leads Latino residents to withdraw from contact and community life.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 S.2 expands the police role that leads Latino residents to withdraw from contact and community life.

  • Because S.2 pays for “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1]. These are “agreements that allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions” [18].
  • Because A 2012 survey of Latinos in four counties found that people were reluctant to contact police “specifically because they fear that police officers will inquire about the immigration status of themselves, their friends, or their family members.” [19]
  • Because The same survey found: “Many Latinos feel isolated and admit to withdrawing from their community.” [19]
  • Because Recent reporting also describes this withdrawal. In March 2025, CalMatters reported a volunteer's account that “some families have refused to leave the house for fear of apprehension by immigration enforcement agents.” [20]
  • So Expanding the immigration role of local police strengthens a reason residents give for avoiding contact. The harm reaches beyond people who are detained: fear keeps other neighbors apart.
  • So [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a reason to oppose this added barrier to everyday contact.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence does not connect the added withdrawal to the local police roles that these agreements create.

  • Because The survey is about police involvement in general, in 2012. Its measure includes the statement “I feel more isolated because local law enforcement is more involved in immigration enforcement” [19].
  • Because These agreements cover different kinds of work. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) describes its Warrant Service Officer model as allowing local officers “to execute civil immigration warrants on behalf of ERO.” [21] ERO is ICE's enforcement branch. This model concerns warrants for people already in custody, not new street questioning.
  • Because The recent article concerns federal raids and rumors, including times when “volunteers show up to a report of a raid, only to find the rumors were prank calls.” [20] It also reports: “The sheriff has previously insisted in a video message that his office does not enforce federal immigration law.” [20]
  • So The recent article describes fear in a place where the sheriff says he does not do this work. So the article does not show the effect of these agreements. This argument does not say which added police contacts would create the barrier. This response does not answer the survey's general finding about police involvement.

arguments.title: S.2 gives more legal help to the side seeking deportation while immigrants face barriers to telling their own story.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 S.2 gives more legal help to the side seeking deportation while immigrants face barriers to telling their own story.

  • Because S.2 pays for government lawyers “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” [1] A removal proceeding is the legal process that decides whether a person must leave the United States.
  • Because The American Immigration Council explains the existing imbalance: “Yet, in every immigration case, the government is represented by a trained attorney who can argue for deportation, regardless of whether the immigrant is represented.” [17]
  • Because The same report explains why detention makes it harder for an immigrant to answer: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.” [17]
  • Because A detention inspection described before Congress's June 9 vote found “no way for detainees to contact their families and lawyers.” [16]
  • So The bill directs added legal help toward the case for deportation in a system where people in custody face documented barriers to presenting their own case.
  • So [NAME]'s wish to hear and understand those people gives a reason to oppose this spending priority.
arguments.con_html:
Response Paying for government lawyers does not by itself show a choice against hearing immigrants' circumstances.

  • Because Listening to someone's circumstances does not require agreeing that the person should win a legal case.
  • Because The report places immigrants' communication barriers in detention: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.” [17] This does not describe an effect of hiring government lawyers.
  • Because The government's lawyer does not decide whose story wins. The same report explains: “If the Notice to Appear does not state a valid ground for removal, the judge must terminate the case.” [17]
  • So This argument shows that immigrants need legal help. It does not show that paying for the other side rejects their account or blocks it. The unequal spending becomes an argument about tolerance only by assuming that support for the government's case works against listening to immigrants.

arguments.title: S.2 pays for operations with a record of using force against peaceful opponents and people reporting on them.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 S.2 pays for operations with a record of using force against peaceful opponents and people reporting on them.

  • Because S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1] This is money for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement).
  • Because In October 2025, Human Rights Watch documented “excessive force against peaceful protesters, legal observers, volunteer street medics, and journalists” [22] outside a detention center in Broadview, Illinois.
  • Because Its findings rest on witnesses and video: “Witnesses and video confirm that DHS agents used tear gas and fired projectiles directly into groups of protesters, including from the detention facility roof, often without warning, and without protesters appearing to pose any risk to agents.” [22] DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.
  • So Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [14] Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling. Added operating money without those reforms supports enforcement with a documented pattern of frightening peaceful critics and people who help others hear their views.
  • So Accepting people who disagree gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added support for this intimidation.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument's prediction of more intimidation leaves out changes in the operations and command behind these confrontations.

  • Because Human Rights Watch tied the rising tension at Broadview to Operation Midway Blitz and “an increase in immigration raids and seizures throughout the Chicago area.” [22]
  • Because Before Congress's June 9 vote, CBS reported that President Trump gave Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, the job of ending the Minneapolis operation: “Earlier this year, Mr. Trump charged Homan with winding down the Minneapolis operation after the fatal shootings of U.S. citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Good by federal immigration agents sparked intense, bipartisan backlash.” [15]
  • Because CBS also reported a change in the command behind the city sweeps: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [15]
  • So This argument uses confrontations during an earlier approach to predict the added operating work, without addressing changes made before Congress's June 9 vote. So the earlier record does not show that S.2 extends that way of treating peaceful critics. This does not show that such incidents have ended.
