The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. It reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This replacement-tariff setting differs from the frozen comparison of ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [43].

Evidence note: The Cambodia and Malaysia cyber clauses appear in the agreements' digital trade articles. Cambodia's says "collaborating with the United States to address cybersecurity challenges." Malaysia's says "endeavoring to collaborate" and that this "may include" exchanging information on threats and best practices. Neither names U.S. critical infrastructure. The CISA advisory the PRO cites concerns PRC actors on U.S. networks and does not name either country. Sources: [50], [40], [51].

original.title: It helps churches keep familiar forms of worship music.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps churches keep familiar forms of worship music.

  • Because Tariffs raise the cost of imported instruments: “Now, tariffs are causing a big jump in costs for music stores.” [4]
  • Because Evangelical pastor Kevin DeYoung urges churches to retain an established practice: “But if your church already has an organ my advice is to keep using it.” [5]
  • Because He explains its purpose: “The organ fills in the cracks, provides an underneath sound, and encourages churches to sing louder and freer.” [5]
  • So When churches buy or replace covered imported instruments, the bill removes an added cost of keeping their familiar worship music. Preserving that religious practice serves [NAME]'s value of tradition.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The NPR price report says a large portion of musical instruments come from overseas. The stores it profiles sell or rent band instruments, one of them brass only, and it does not mention organs or churches. DeYoung's 2011 advice concerns a church that already has an organ. Executive Order 14257 covers all articles except listed exceptions; the annex tables are not in the packet. Sources: [4], [5], [6].

original.title: It helps families keep Christian Christmas customs.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps families keep Christian Christmas customs.

  • Because A Christmas-tree importer reported higher prices caused by tariffs: “it also had to raise prices by 10% as a result of the tariffs.” [7]
  • Because Focus on the Family describes a recurring custom that uses a Christmas tree: “A family slumber party by the Christmas tree is a tradition our kids love year after year.” [8]
  • Because It connects family celebrations to faith: “When we slow down to celebrate, we are showing our family that our faith matters—and that they matter.” [8]
  • So Removing the added tax on covered Christmas goods cuts an ongoing cost of buying or replacing what these customs use. This helps [NAME] preserve family ways of celebrating Christian faith.

catalog.retirement_reason: General household provision is the substantive benefit; the religious quotation does not establish continuation of a particular family custom or organization.

original.title: It supports inherited Christian duties of providing for a family and caring for children.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It supports inherited Christian duties of providing for a family and caring for children.

  • Because On the day of the vote, Senator Wyden described the taxes' household burden: “Americans across our country are shouldering the cost of these tariffs, which are taxes jacking up the price of groceries, electronics, clothes, strollers, and other everyday goods.” [9]
  • Because Southern Baptist teaching assigns a husband the “responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family” [10] and a wife the duty “to serve as his helper in managing the household and nurturing the next generation.” [10]
  • So Removing this added cost of household necessities helps families meet those duties. For [NAME], supporting this inherited pattern of family life is a reason grounded in tradition to favor the bill.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Kansas City Federal Reserve's September 2025 Beige Book says contacts reported suppliers reluctant to lower prices even when tariff rates fell, causing some stickiness in input costs. Sources: [11].
original.retirement_reason: General household provision is the substantive benefit; the religious quotation does not establish continuation of a particular family custom or organization.

original.title: It lowers an added cost of tools parents use to pass Christian faith to children.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It lowers an added cost of tools parents use to pass Christian faith to children.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching states the inherited duty: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [10].
  • Because A maker describes a tool for that teaching: “When you squeeze its hand, the Talking Jesus Doll speaks 10 of Jesus' phrases from the Bible – including the Lord's Prayer and John 3:16.” [12]
  • Because CBS documented the maker's exposure to the earlier, higher tariffs: “With sky-high tariffs in place, he had paused shipments from China, and had containers of goods waiting in limbo overseas.” [13]
  • So Ending the remaining reciprocal tax removes an added cost from these imported teaching aids. Helping parents carry out the religious duty of passing their faith to children directly serves [NAME]'s wish to preserve Christian beliefs across generations.
original.con_html:
Response A seller's claim that a doll teaches Bible verses does not establish that the doll helps [NAME] pass on an accepted Christian tradition.

  • Because The maker states its aim: “The objective of the doll is to make the love and lessons of Jesus tangible for young children.” [12]
  • Because The Southern Baptist teaching calls parents to teach “spiritual and moral values” [10]; it does not identify this product as a way to do so.
  • Because The fit between images of Jesus and inherited Christian teaching cannot be assumed. Defending the Westminster catechism's rule against such images, James Norris writes, “since an image of God cannot be a medium for worship it ought never to be a tool for education in the faith.” [14]
  • So The PRO supplies the maker's purpose, but no basis for placing this aid within the tradition [NAME] seeks to keep. Lower import costs for the doll do not supply that missing link between the product and following [NAME]'s religion.

original.title: It helps families continue regular church offerings and Christmas gospel outreach.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It helps families continue regular church offerings and Christmas gospel outreach.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching says “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.” [10]
  • Because An April report warned that tariff-driven price rises put giving at risk: “At the same time, donors may give less as they face rising prices and a turbulent stock market.” [15]
  • So Relieving this pressure on household budgets helps protect families' ability to keep regular offerings and fund church work.
  • Because Gift-based outreach is another established practice: “Operation Christmas Child has been collecting and delivering shoebox gifts to children worldwide for more than three decades.” [16]
  • Because Participants pack a “shoebox gift filled with fun toys, school supplies, and personal care items” [16]. These goods include a heavily imported product: “Over 80% of toys sold in the U.S. are made in China, according to The Toy Association trade group.” [13]
  • Because Franklin Graham states the religious purpose: “these simple gifts open the door for the Gospel.” [16]
  • So Removing the added tax on commercially imported toys bought for these gifts lowers a cost of continuing this outreach. Regular church offerings and this established Christmas gospel practice are the traditions at stake.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The Kansas City Federal Reserve's September 2025 Beige Book says contacts reported suppliers reluctant to lower prices even when tariff rates fell, causing some stickiness in input costs. Sources: [11].

Evidence note: The charity report is from April 2025 and names food and clothing among nonprofit costs. The Toy Association figure covers all U.S. toy sales, not shoebox items. Sources: [15], [13].

catalog.retirement_reason: Constitutional checks and a conservative organization's approval do not establish preservation or observance of an inherited cultural or religious practice.

original.title: It upholds the inherited constitutional order defended within the religious right.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It upholds the inherited constitutional order defended within the religious right.

  • Because The bill lets Congress check presidential tariff policy. Senator Murkowski called the vote “Congress reasserting our authority as a co-equal branch of government with defined powers and responsibilities.” [17]
  • Because Family Research Council treats respect for that inherited order as a conservative commitment: “The written Constitution was designed to permanently explain what the federal government was to be, what it could do, and what it could not do.” [18]
  • Because A 2017 Family Research Council brief on a judicial nominee, mainly concerned with judicial power, also names elected lawmaking and the executive's adherence to law: “The primacy of law-making by our elected representatives and the adherence to the rule of law by the executive branch form the keystone of our governmental framework.” [19]
  • So Ending this presidential emergency through Congress puts those established commitments into practice. [NAME]'s wish to maintain traditional ways of thinking gives that use of Congress's power weight in favor of the bill.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The NEA provides for a vote "to determine whether that emergency shall be terminated." The FRC brief cited by the PRO is a 2017 document supporting a judicial nominee and goes on to discuss the growth of judicial power. The Administration argues Congress delegated this authority under IEEPA. Sources: [20], [19], [21].
original.retirement_reason: Constitutional checks and a conservative organization's approval do not establish preservation or observance of an inherited cultural or religious practice.

catalog.retirement_reason: The justification is justice and honest dealing. Calling a tariff position biblical does not supply a distinct Tradition connection.

original.title: It puts an older Christian teaching about justice in trade into practice.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It puts an older Christian teaching about justice in trade into practice.

  • Because American Calvinist Frederick Nymeyer's 1956 critique applied inherited religious standards to tariffs: “Nymeyer argued that tariffs violate well-established biblical principles of justice and honesty.” [22]
  • Because Acton Institute carried that teaching forward in 2016: “Christians should reject protectionist tariffs not only because they are economically unsound, but also because of their immorality and incompatibility with Christianity.” [23]
  • Because These taxes seek to encourage home production through higher import costs. The White House says the remaining reciprocal tax is meant “to encourage domestic production” [24].
  • Because The consumer burden criticized in that tradition applies here. Senator Paul explained the taxes targeted by the resolution: “They drive up the costs for things Americans buy every day and make it harder for American businesses to thrive and create more jobs” [9].
  • So Ending these import taxes follows this strand of Christian teaching about biblical justice in trade. Honoring that teaching gives [NAME] a reason grounded in tradition to favor the bill.
original.con_html:
Response The age and Christian authorship of the arguments against import taxes do not establish them as teachings [NAME] has a reason from tradition to follow.

  • Because Christianity Today describes Nymeyer as “A protégé of libertarian economist Ludwig von Mises and a Calvinist himself” [22]. The article presents his application of biblical principles to a disputed policy.
  • Because Acton's conclusion is the author's policy judgment: “Christians should reject protectionist tariffs not only because they are economically unsound, but also because of their immorality and incompatibility with Christianity.” [23]
  • Because The American Family Association offers a different account of the religious rule: “Tariffs are not inherently good or evil. They are tools – sometimes necessary, often risky, and always consequential.” [25]
  • So The PRO must connect the particular Nymeyer–Acton reading to the religious or cultural teaching [NAME] seeks to maintain. Showing that two Christian writers made the argument decades apart does not establish that connection. Applying an old biblical principle to trade is not, by itself, evidence that the policy judgment is an inherited teaching for [NAME].
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Christianity Today presents Nymeyer as a Calvinist businessman, protégé of Mises, in a dispute with Kuyper's different view. American Family Association's The Stand says tariffs are not inherently good or evil. Sources: [22], [25].
original.retirement_reason: The justification is justice and honest dealing. Calling a tariff position biblical does not supply a distinct Tradition connection.

original.title: Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.

  • Because A U.S. study of growing imports from China during 1990–2014 found harm to men's work and pay: “On average, trade shocks differentially reduce employment and earnings of young adult males.” [27]
  • Because Those earnings losses affect family life: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27]
  • Because Marriage and the husband's provider role are religious commitments in [NAME]'s cultural tradition. The Southern Baptist faith statement says, “Marriage is the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime.” [28] Of a husband, it says, “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.” [28]
  • Because That family pattern also carries a duty to pass on the faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [28].
  • So By removing a defense against import-driven job and pay losses, the bill puts marriage and the provider role at greater risk. Keeping those religious roles and passing them on gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.con_html:
Response A price advantage for U.S. products does not establish that these taxes protect the men's jobs and pay on which the family argument depends.

  • Because The bill says the April 2 emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] The relevant comparison is keeping or ending its import taxes as of October 30, 2025.
  • Because The family study ties marriage losses to men's earnings relative to women's: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27] It studies rising Chinese import competition during 1990–2014, not the effects of these taxes.
  • Because A study of local employment under the 2018–2019 taxes reports that “import tariffs do not appear to increase employment in manufacturing” [29]. It directly tests the step from import protection to factory jobs that the marriage study does not test.
  • Because A Federal Reserve study of the 2018–2019 taxes found that “a positive effect from import protection is offset by larger negative effects from rising input costs and retaliatory tariffs.” [30]
  • Because For the 2025 taxes, the textile trade group's president warned in October: “Reciprocal tariffs on these items hurt domestic textile producers and drives offshoring, undermining U.S. manufacturing jobs” [31]. She was discussing taxes on certain imported materials and machinery unavailable at home.
  • So American Giant's U.S. production and a price advantage do not establish that this extra tax layer preserves men's jobs or pay. Without that link, the historical import losses do not establish that ending these taxes puts marriage, husbands' provider roles or passing on the faith at greater risk.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases had relative employment reductions, with a positive protection effect offset by input costs and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [29], [30].

original.title: Removing that protection also threatens the local congregations that carry inherited worship customs.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Removing that protection also threatens the local congregations that carry inherited worship customs.

  • Because A study using U.S. church data for 1990–2010 found that Chinese import shocks “led to a reduction in the number of churches” [32]. It also found they “caused an increase in the number of religious adherents” [32].
  • Because Members' means support church life. The Southern Baptist faith statement calls for regular giving: “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally” [28]. Losing income leaves less money for that duty.
  • Because Losing local work can pull younger generations away from their congregations. The account of the Ragsdale Church of Christ's closure reports, “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33].
  • Because A congregation is a place where families keep particular customs alive. Ragsdale's final gathering was “an old-time singing — the kind they used to have every fourth Sunday.” [33]
  • Because Worship there was also a family practice across generations. Member Emily Smartt “remembers being there with her parents and late husband.” [33]
  • So Ending this protection puts the jobs and income that help sustain local congregations at risk. Keeping those congregations and their shared customs alive honors [NAME]'s religious heritage, giving [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.
original.con_html:
Response The church evidence does not show that keeping these taxes protects local congregations or their inherited customs.

  • Because The cited church-study abstract examines “trade shocks to manufacturing industries stemming from Chinese imports” [32], using U.S. church data for 1990–2010. Applying its finding to this bill requires the missing step from point 1: that ending this tax layer harms the jobs or income that support congregations.
  • Because Ragsdale's preacher reported that “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33]. That example shows a reason members leave; it supplies no link between those departures and the import taxes this bill ends.
  • So Neither source establishes that ending these taxes would cut church income or drive members away. The duty to give and the value of shared worship customs do not fill that gap. The PRO has not shown that the bill threatens the congregations that carry those customs.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Ragsdale's preacher attributes the congregation's decline to location, societal changes and economics, including generational change. The Cesur et al. abstract finds fewer churches and more adherents following Chinese import shocks in 1990-2010. Sources: [33], [32].

original.title: It strengthens workers’ route to uncover pollution and enforce environmental safeguards at work.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It strengthens workers’ route to uncover pollution and enforce environmental safeguards at work.

  • Because Union contracts can give workers a regular role in environmental oversight. The 2018 U.S. Steel agreement requires “A Joint Environmental Sub-Committee of the Joint Safety and Health Committee” [4] at each location and says it “will meet regularly to discuss environmental issues affecting the Company and to make appropriate recommendations.” [4]
  • Because The company must let that group review “all non confidential environmental reports, monitoring results, analyses, materials received from the EPA and other agencies” [4].
  • Because The same contract requires the company to “comply with all applicable laws and regulations concerning the health and safety of Employees at work and the protection of the environment.” [4]
  • Because Contract duties have a complaint process: “the Union may process grievances through the grievance procedure, including arbitration” [4]. Its outcome is binding: “A decision of the Board shall be final and binding upon the Company, the Union and all Employees concerned.” [4]
  • So These terms give workers information, a voice and a way to enforce environmental duties. By making first contracts harder to block through delay, the bill strengthens this route to challenging pollution. That serves [NAME]’s wish to protect nature.
original.con_html:
Response The bill’s binding route does not clearly reach environmental oversight terms that lack a direct link to workers’ jobs.

  • Because The PRO’s enforcement route depends on specific contract language. The agreement’s complaint process concerns “a violation by the Company of this Agreement” [4]. Grievances can enforce environmental duties only where those duties are in the contract.
  • Because The PRO’s guide says employers can lawfully refuse talks about optional topics “that lack a direct job nexus.” [5] This means topics without a direct link to workers’ jobs.
  • Because The bill’s panel issues a decision “settling the dispute” [3] based on five business and employment factors, such as “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3]. None names pollution oversight, and the bill does not change which subjects employers must negotiate.
  • So For environmental oversight without a direct job link, the PRO identifies no way the bill’s deadlines or panel get past an employer’s lawful refusal. This response does not answer oversight terms tied to workers’ own safety and health, or the grievance rights a first contract can create for terms it does contain.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [6], [7].

original.title: It strengthens bargaining for protected action against work that threatens the environment.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It strengthens bargaining for protected action against work that threatens the environment.

  • Because Workers can bargain for the right to stop dangerous work: “Under the National Labor Relations Act, health and safety is a mandatory subject of collective bargaining in private sector workplaces.” [8]
  • Because A process negotiated at Delaware City Refining Company gives workers “the authority, without fear of reprimand or retaliation, to immediately STOP any work activity that presents a hazard to you, your co-workers, the environment” [8].
  • Because It protects their income: “there shall be no loss of pay, seniority, or benefits during the period of refusal” [8].
  • So A stronger first-contract process helps workers secure these protections. They let workers act before dangerous work harms nature, without losing pay for intervening. [NAME] values such action to defend the environment.
original.con_html:
Response The required duty to bargain that the PRO cites concerns safety and health; it does not establish a required route to work refusals over hazards to the environment alone.

  • Because The safety guide states the duty in those terms: “the other side must bargain in good faith over safety and health issues, including SWA.” [8] SWA means workers’ authority to stop unsafe work.
  • Because The same guide says the terms vary: “Because there is no law mandating SWA, the SWA process is specific to an employer or workplace.” [8] The environmental wording the PRO cites comes from the Delaware City process.
  • So The PRO moves from a required subject of talks to rights that also cover environmental hazards. The guide does not say environment-only coverage is a required subject. This response does not answer stop-work terms for worker hazards that would also avert environmental harm.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [6], [7].

original.title: It strengthens bargaining for workplace programs that save resources and cut climate pollution.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It strengthens bargaining for workplace programs that save resources and cut climate pollution.

  • Because U.S. employers and unions may agree on climate goals. A guide to green bargaining explains that “employers and unions are still free to bargain over them.” [5]
  • Because The guide’s international contract models include “building efficiency improvements and recycling and composting programs” [5] and “employee transit programs that promote the use of public transportation, bikes, and carpooling.” [5]
  • Because A U.S. example makes the route concrete. U.S. Steel’s contract requires joint work to “identify, analyze, and make recommendations regarding ways to conserve energy, improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions” [4].
  • Because Contracts also fund environmental work. Minneapolis janitors won a “contract that included funding for a Labor-Management Cooperation Fund for a green education initiative” [9].
  • Because Climate pollution harms nature. The IPCC finds that “Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming” [10] and that “Hundreds of local losses of species have been driven by increases in the magnitude of heat extremes” [10].
  • So By strengthening the route to a first agreement, the bill helps workers bargain for environmental programs and resources to carry them out. Saving resources and working to cut the gases that warm the planet serve [NAME]’s care for nature.
original.con_html:
Response For climate commitments treated as optional subjects, the PRO identifies no way the bill’s binding route overcomes an employer’s refusal.

  • Because The green-bargaining guide says employers and unions “are still free to bargain over them.” [5] That passage concerns climate goals treated as optional subjects; it does not require either side to accept talks about them. The guide adds that “making employers bargain over climate change may not always be possible” [5].
  • Because The Supreme Court explains the rule for topics outside wages, hours and other employment terms: “each party is free to bargain or not to bargain, and to agree or not to agree.” [11]
  • Because The bill requires a decision “settling the dispute” [3] based on five business and employment factors, including “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3]. It does not change which subjects employers must negotiate.
  • So Optional climate commitments would still depend on an employer’s voluntary agreement. This response does not answer programs that are themselves terms of employment, or the guide’s separate argument that some climate matters can be required subjects.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [6], [7].

original.title: It supports the people who protect wildlife and habitats.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It supports the people who protect wildlife and habitats.

  • Because Conservation workers face first-contract delays too. Audubon’s first agreement “was reached after more than two years of negotiations” [12].
  • Because Audubon’s agreement links its staff to nature protection: “Audubon is committed to the mission of protecting birds and the habitats needed to sustain them” [13] and “Audubon’s workforce is integral to the success of Audubon’s mission” [13].
  • Because That first contract provides practical support for their skills: “Audubon shall support career development training that enhances the skills necessary to successfully perform the employee’s job or other Audubon career positions by providing paid leave to eligible employees” [13].
  • Because Pay and benefits also support conservation staffing. Defenders of Wildlife tied its bargaining effort to “developing a top-tier benefits package to retain and attract top talent” [14]; the resulting agreement “optimizes staff compensation and establishes new benefits for all current and future staff.” [14]
  • So Giving newly organized conservation staff a binding route through stalled talks supports their efforts to secure pay, benefits and training. Supporting the staff who carry out wildlife and habitat protection serves [NAME]’s value.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Defenders of Wildlife release reports contract terms and management’s goal of retaining and attracting staff. It reports no measured change in retention or conservation capacity. The agreement was fast-tracked in the new chief executive’s first 100 days. Sources: [14].

original.title: It addresses a barrier to moving away from fossil fuels: fear that new jobs will not support workers’ families.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It addresses a barrier to moving away from fossil fuels: fear that new jobs will not support workers’ families.

  • Because Contracts put benefits in writing in electric-vehicle battery jobs. An Ultium worker explained: “now my benefits are guaranteed in writing, ensuring financial security for my family” [15].
  • Because Contracts can also support workers changing jobs: “unions can bargain for employer-sponsored training programs that give employees an opportunity to learn new skills.” [5] They can negotiate “robust severance pay and layoff benefit plans and even early retirement” [5].
  • Because Interviews with 48 union energy workers in New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania identified fear of poor pay and benefits as a barrier to backing cleaner energy. The researchers conclude: “This analysis demonstrates that there are ways to gain their support, particularly if training, family sustaining wages and benefits, and location are integrated into transitions.” [16]
  • Because The bill puts family needs into binding contract decisions. A panel must base its decision partly on “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [3].
  • So For clean-energy workplaces that newly organize, a binding route to settling wages and benefits can ease part of the financial insecurity these workers identify. Strengthening that part of the move away from fossil fuels can help build support for cutting the emissions that harm nature.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The energy-worker study interviewed 48 unionized workers, all in the Mid-Atlantic region, and its authors note this limit. The Spring Hill Ultium agreement builds on a national contract; workers there signed cards in September 2024 and ratified a local agreement by March 2025. Sources: [16], [15].

Evidence note: In the energy-worker study, workers cite lower pay and precarity in renewable jobs, and the authors say those industries risk becoming non-union and low-wage. They name training, family-sustaining wages and benefits, and location together, and note particular concern for workers whose skills are not in demand in wind and solar. The study does not measure whether first-contract terms change these workers’ expectations. The bill’s comparator factor refers to other employers in the same business. Sources: [16], [3].

original.title: It protects organizations through which workers can defend nature together.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It protects organizations through which workers can defend nature together.

  • Because First-contract delay puts new unions at risk. Representative Scott explains: “Dragging out negotiations gives corporations a long chance to break up a union.” [17]
  • Because Workers use unions to build environmental alliances. Researchers report that union members active on climate issues have “forged new alliances with other unions and environmentalists” [16].
  • Because These organizations have helped win nature protections: “the AFL-CIO helped establish the National Wilderness Preservation System; the United Auto Workers was the leading funder of the first Earth Day and more recently supported raising emissions standards for autos.” [18]
  • So For workers organizing to defend nature through their union, limiting first-contract delay helps protect a group they can use for that action. Keeping this route to environmental campaigns open serves [NAME]’s value of taking part in nature protection.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The historical environmental actions cited come from national union bodies, and the alliance passage concerns members already active on climate. The same article states that unions face a tension, particularly those whose members work in extractive industries. Sources: [18].

original.title: Workers lose a way to insist on contract terms that cut pollution and waste.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 Workers lose a way to insist on contract terms that cut pollution and waste.

  • Because Contracts can fund changes in how work is done. Minneapolis janitors won “Funding for a green cleaning initiative to reduce waste and water and energy consumption while transitioning away from toxic chemicals, with the goal of significantly lowering carbon emissions from buildings.” [19]
  • Because Winning those terms required workers to put environmental aims ahead of other benefits. Their bargainers reported: “We ultimately won, but had to compromise on the amount of funding and sacrifice other issues like additional holidays that were important to groups of the members.” [19]
  • Because Workers normally can reject a contract: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” [20]
  • Because The employer can start the bill's mediation process after 90 days of talks without the union's consent: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [3]
  • Because The panel's five required factors concern the business and workers' living costs and pay. None requires pollution cuts. They include “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.” [3]
  • So A panel can settle a first contract without pollution-cutting terms that workers would insist on before approving it. Workers cannot reject that result, and changing it during the two-year term requires the employer's written consent. Losing that control puts workers' ability to secure such funding at risk, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Minneapolis janitors bargained a renewal: their contract had expired in December. It illustrates green terms and bargaining trade-offs, not a first-contract vote the bill would bypass. Under current law an employer may implement a final offer after genuine good-faith impasse, and the bill requires maintaining current terms pending agreement. Panel factors can accommodate green work methods even though they do not require pollution cuts. Sources: [21], [22], [3].

original.title: Imposed strike limits can weaken workers' ability to take part in defending nature.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Imposed strike limits can weaken workers' ability to take part in defending nature.

  • Because Employers seek strike bans in first contracts: “One thing you can be sure of when bargaining your first contract: management will demand a contract clause barring strikes while the agreement is in effect.” [23]
  • Because Current law leaves unions free to refuse: “Nothing in the NLRA, however, requires a union to agree to a no-strike clause.” [23] The union can also resist through action: “the union may strike to keep it out of the contract.” [23]
  • Because The bill puts disputed contract terms within the panel's reach. Lawyers reviewing it describe “authority to determine all terms of the parties’ first CBA” [22]—their first union contract.
  • So A panel can impose a strike ban that workers never accepted, putting contract limits on walkouts beyond their control.
  • Because Green demands can concern workers' training and daily tasks. Local 26 sought a “training program for Green Technicians (including $0.20 differential) and expanded use of green cleaning.” [21]
  • Because Strike pressure helps workers press such demands. The janitors' bargainers explained that “the companies will simply try to ignore those demands—unless the union is willing to sacrifice and ultimately strike.” [19]
  • So An imposed strike ban can restrict walkouts used to press work-related green demands. Because [NAME] values taking part in defending nature, protecting this means of collective environmental action gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
original.con_html:
Response A strike-ban clause adds little against the green-demand strikes the PRO cites, because those strikes seek new contract terms.

  • Because The cited green strike took place after a contract expired: “The janitors’ contract ran out in December, but they agreed to go on working while negotiations progressed.” [21] The bill's arbitration rule covers “an initial collective bargaining agreement” [3], and its award binds “for a period of 2 years” [3].
  • Because Current law already limits strikes to rewrite terms fixed by an existing contract. The NLRB's guide says: “The party must continue in full force and effect, without resorting to strike or lockout, all the terms and conditions of the existing contract until 60 days after the notice to the other party was given or until the date the contract is scheduled to expire, whichever is later.” [24] This concerns changing agreed terms, not every strike during a contract.
  • So For demands to add green contract terms, the PRO has not shown what a ban clause adds beyond these existing limits. This response does not answer two things: an award itself ends the first-contract bargaining in which workers could strike for such terms, and a ban could reach walkouts not aimed at changing contract terms.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A law-firm analysis in the PRO’s packet says the bill leaves open the lawfulness of strikes and lockouts during first-contract talks, and that interest arbitration elsewhere typically rests on a mutual commitment against them. Sources: [22].

original.title: The bill gives unions that fight pollution controls a new way to secure their membership and funding.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill gives unions that fight pollution controls a new way to secure their membership and funding.

  • Because Binding first-contract arbitration can help new unions obtain contracts: “Other research has found that first-contract arbitration helped more Canadian workers sign first contracts.” [25]
  • Because Coal organizing is one use for this route. The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) says: “We are going to continue working to organize coal miners, but we must also look outside of the coal industry to grow our membership for a sustainable future” [26]. It also explains why growth matters: “To survive in the long term, we must grow our membership.” [26]
  • Because Contracts can arrange regular collection of members' dues, the payments that fund unions: “provisions that require management to automatically deduct union dues from workers’ paychecks and route them into the labor organization’s account.” [27]
  • So The bill's route to binding contracts can give unions organizing coal and other fossil-fuel workers a firmer base of members and dues income.
  • Because A larger foothold in oil and gas can strengthen the stake in defending those industries. Writing about California politics, Capital & Main reports: “When unions organize workers in the oil and gas industry, they develop a vested interest in protecting those jobs — and can form a serious barrier to environmental justice and climate policy.” [28]
  • Because These unions already turn resources into political pressure. CalMatters reports: “The building and construction trade unions also have long bankrolled California’s labor-friendly Democrats.” [29]
  • Because That pressure has helped defeat environmental limits. CalMatters reports that “Ventura County voters sided with the oil and gas industry and the building trades unions when they overturned similar restrictions the county board of supervisors had placed on local oil wells” [29].
  • Because Coal unions also fight emissions limits in court. In its 2024 challenge to carbon-emission standards for coal-fired power plants, the UMWA stated: “We therefore have no choice but to file this petition, suing the EPA and stopping this rule from ever being implemented.” [30]
  • So Helping these unions sustain members and income can strengthen organized resistance to pollution controls. That risk works against [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature from pollution and gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Canadian first-contract research is reported for workers generally, not by industry. Capital & Main attributes the California building trades’ refinery position to a 2014 state apprenticeship law and a Project Labor Agreement. UMWA’s organizing also includes West Virginia state employees, and state employers are outside the NLRA. Sources: [25], [28], [26], [24].

original.title: It gives workers with less power a way past an employer's use of delay.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It gives workers with less power a way past an employer's use of delay.

  • Because Treasury's research review explains the power gap: “employers typically have the upper hand in the relationship with their employees, even in the absence of anti-competitive practices.” [3]
  • Because Congress identifies how delay deepens that gap: “The employers can use those delays to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer.” [1]
  • Because The process above lets either side seek a binding settlement. Neither side can block the panel merely by refusing to choose its members: “if the individual or labor organization or the employer fail to do so, the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1]
  • Because Both sides have a place on the panel: “with one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [1]
  • So Workers gain a settlement route beyond persuading the stronger party to agree. Making their right to bargain usable protects people with less power and supports just treatment.
original.con_html:
Response The mediation agency’s documented service limits raise a real question about how quickly and usefully workers with little bargaining power could use the new route.

  • Because The bill depends on the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS): “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].
  • Because FMCS's April 3, 2026 budget submission says it had limited mediation to health-care groups with at least 250 represented workers and “bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction” [4].
  • Because Its proposed service form, published May 15, still says of first-contract cases: “These cases will be assigned to a mediator if they meet the current criteria/metrics for case assignment.” [5]
  • Because A supporter of the bill identifies the practical condition: “Without a robust, government-supported mediation and arbitration system, the Faster Labor Contracts Act would not be able to live up to its promise.” [6]
  • So Preventing an employer from blocking appointments does not resolve this service gap for small units seeking mediation and timely referral. This response does not show that the route is unavailable: the bill’s duty has no size limit, and the time to referral runs from the request.
original.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study covers contracts from 1987 to 1996 in campaigns where a contract was reached, and states that “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power.” Its stated prevalences include grievable safety clauses in 55 percent of private contracts, discrimination clauses in nearly three-quarters, schedule language in one-third of private contracts, vacancy posting in more than three-quarters, job training in about one-quarter, private-sector tuition at 16 percent, and some restrictions on outsourcing in about one-third of private agreements. The bill’s panel factors do not prescribe particular contract terms. Sources: [7], [1].

Brief context note: A review of Canadian first-contract arbitration states that boards and arbitrators limit awards by employer financial capacity and recognize that arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

original.title: It requires a worker election before the employer's duty to bargain ends.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It requires a worker election before the employer's duty to bargain ends.

  • Because Existing rules allow withdrawal of union recognition after a contract expires when evidence shows lost majority support and the union has not requested an election in time: “If no such petition is timely filed, the employer may rely on the disaffection evidence to affect withdrawal. That evidence—assuming it establishes actual loss of majority status—will be dispositive of the union’s lack of majority status at the time of actual withdrawal; and the withdrawal of recognition will be lawful assuming no other grounds exist to find it unlawful.” [9]
  • Because The bill requires that “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1].
  • So Workers retain collective representation until an election removes it. Requiring a vote before ending that protection gives workers a fairer process, serving [NAME]'s concern for just treatment.
original.con_html:
Response In the cases this provision changes, the PRO does not explain why continued recognition treats workers more fairly.

  • Because Unions newly approved by the federal labor board already receive a protected first year: “An employer must bargain in good faith during these first 12 months and cannot withdraw recognition of the union, even if the union allegedly loses majority support through no fault of the employer.” [10]
  • Because The PRO's source concerns withdrawal near an existing contract's expiry. It requires evidence that “establishes actual loss of majority status” [9]. It also gives the union an election route: “the incumbent union may file, within 45 days from the date of that announcement, an election petition” [9].
  • So In the situation the PRO cites, the bill’s added effect falls where a majority has shown disaffection and the union has not sought a vote. The PRO gives no reason why continued recognition until a decertification election treats those workers’ expressed wishes more fairly. This response does not dispute that an election is a fair way to confirm workers’ wishes.
original.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study covers contracts from 1987 to 1996 in campaigns where a contract was reached, and states that “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power.” Its stated prevalences include grievable safety clauses in 55 percent of private contracts, discrimination clauses in nearly three-quarters, schedule language in one-third of private contracts, vacancy posting in more than three-quarters, job training in about one-quarter, private-sector tuition at 16 percent, and some restrictions on outsourcing in about one-third of private agreements. The bill’s panel factors do not prescribe particular contract terms. Sources: [7], [1].

Brief context note: A review of Canadian first-contract arbitration states that boards and arbitrators limit awards by employer financial capacity and recognize that arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

original.title: It protects existing pay and conditions while workers seek an agreement, including after a genuine deadlock.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects existing pay and conditions while workers seek an agreement, including after a genuine deadlock.

  • Because Existing law lets an employer impose previously offered terms after good-faith talks reach a deadlock: “the employer may unilaterally change terms and conditions of employ, so long as these changes are consistent with offers that the union has rejected.” [11]
  • Because The bill instead requires employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [1].
  • So Workers gain protection against cuts while seeking a contract. This protects people whose households cannot absorb lower pay or worse hours.

original.title: It strengthens workers' route to pay that supports their families and opens life opportunities.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It strengthens workers' route to pay that supports their families and opens life opportunities.

  • Because Treasury's research review finds a wage gain from union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” [3]
  • Because The bill requires any panel decision to consider “the employees' cost of living” [1] and “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [1].
  • So The binding-contract route gives workers stronger access to wage settlements, with basic living needs expressly counted. This serves [NAME]'s concern for workers and dependents vulnerable to financial hardship.
  • Because Higher pay also supports opportunities for workers' children: “In turn, the higher pay and job security of both unionized and nonunionized middle-class workers can further spill over to their families and communities through more stable housing, more investment in education, and other channels.” [3]
  • Because Pay gains can spread beyond the union through competition for workers: “Nonunionized firms in competition with unionized workplaces may choose to raise wages, change hiring practices, or improve their workplace environment to attract workers.” [12] Treasury also reports: “The empirical evidence finds that these positive spillovers exist.” [12]
  • So The income path also reaches children's education and workers outside the union. These wider gains support [NAME]'s concern for equal life opportunities beyond [NAME]'s own circle.

The bill’s panel factors do not prescribe particular contract terms. Sources: [7], [1].

It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

The authors say unions have been somewhat unsuccessful at securing significant wage gains. It does not estimate the effect of first-contract arbitration. Sources: [13].

original.title: It makes protection during illness, caregiving and old age more reachable.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It makes protection during illness, caregiving and old age more reachable.

  • Because A U.S. study of first contracts signed in 1987–1996 found concrete benefit protections: “first contracts establish, codify, and expand health insurance, pensions, and substantial paid leave benefits.” [7]
  • Because Treasury's review cites research finding that “the higher rates of fringe benefits at newly unionized firms are the direct result of collective bargaining.” [3]
  • So Helping workers reach first contracts strengthens access to care, paid time away and retirement income. These protections serve people at vulnerable stages of life and those who depend on their care.

original.title: It helps workers secure enforceable safety rules.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It helps workers secure enforceable safety rules.

  • Because The historical first-contract study found that “55 percent of private sector contracts have grievable health and safety clauses.” [7] These let workers challenge breaches of safety rules through the contract's dispute process.
  • Because Unions bargain over safety and back workers who report hazards: “They bargain to improve safety practices, protect their members against retaliation for reporting a violation, or make complaints on members’ behalf about hazards” [3].
  • So A stronger path to a contract makes enforceable safety protections more reachable. This serves [NAME]'s concern for people exposed to harm at work.

original.title: It helps workers secure fair rules for discipline and an independent hearing when treatment is disputed.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It helps workers secure fair rules for discipline and an independent hearing when treatment is disputed.

  • Because The first-contract study found agreements requiring “discipline and discharge to be based on just cause” [7]—a good reason for punishment or dismissal.
  • Because Contract procedures bound employers to “independent third-party review of disputes between management and employees.” [7]
  • So Easier access to these contracts gives workers a stronger route to rules against arbitrary punishment and a hearing outside the employer's sole control. That directly serves [NAME]'s concern that everyone receive just treatment.

original.title: It broadens access to pay rules that reduce bias against women and racial minorities.
original.pro_html:
Point 8 It broadens access to pay rules that reduce bias against women and racial minorities.

  • Because Treasury identifies union practices that make pay less dependent on bias: “promoting wage-setting practices that are less susceptible to implicit bias.” [12]
  • Because Open pay scales particularly help workers with less individual bargaining power: “These types of practices, and others like publicly available pay schedules, benefit women and vulnerable workers who can be less likely to negotiate aggressively for pay raises.” [12]
  • Because Treasury reports evidence of results: “Empirical studies have confirmed that unions have, indeed, closed race and gender gaps within firms.” [12]
  • So Helping workers reach contracts extends access to shared pay rules that reduce unequal treatment. This supports [NAME]'s concern for fair treatment and equal opportunities regardless of race or gender.

original.pro_html:
Point 9 It opens a more usable route to enforcing protections against discrimination.

  • Because First contracts have included “anti-discrimination measures for both gender and race.” [3] Union contracts have also protected “workers with disabilities and LGBTQ+ workers.” [3]
  • Because Contract clauses add a way to enforce protection beyond bringing a legal claim. The study explains that their enforcement takes “significantly less effort, cost, and time than claims filed under state or federal law.” [7]
  • So Making these contracts more reachable gives workers facing bias a more accessible way to defend fair treatment. That serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and justice for people [NAME] does not know.

original.title: It helps workers secure schedules that make employment easier to combine with caregiving.
original.pro_html:
Point 10 It helps workers secure schedules that make employment easier to combine with caregiving.

  • Because The first-contract study records rules for “the posting of schedules” [7] and explains that scheduling clauses give workers “predictability and control over their work schedules.” [7]
  • Because Unpredictable hours impose practical costs: “on-demand scheduling can be costly to workers who incur high costs of going to work without the ability to plan ahead, perhaps due to last-minute commuting and childcare arrangements.” [3]
  • So Helping workers secure predictable hours reduces a barrier to holding a job while caring for dependents. This protects caregivers' livelihoods and their opportunities to work.

original.title: It helps workers gain clear rules for pursuing better jobs.
original.pro_html:
Point 11 It helps workers gain clear rules for pursuing better jobs.

  • Because The first-contract study found rules laying out “the process for promotions and the filling of vacancies beyond basic seniority rights.” [7]
  • Because Those contracts also provided for “the posting of vacancies.” [7]
  • So Posted openings and a stated process tell workers what opportunities exist and how to pursue them. Broadening access to these rules supports [NAME]'s concern for equal opportunities.

It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

original.title: It helps workers secure access to training.
original.pro_html:
Point 12 It helps workers secure access to training.

  • Because The first-contract study found agreements “specifying job training or in-service training” [7]. Its private-sector benefit table also records “Tuition paid” [7].
  • Because Training costs matter to equal opportunities. Treasury explains: “Income inequality often feeds back into inequality of opportunity, which impedes growth if disadvantaged people cannot access the resources necessary to acquire job skills or start businesses.” [3]
  • So Contract training and help with tuition open a route to skills for workers whose own resources limit their choices. That serves [NAME]'s concern for equal life opportunities.

Brief context note: The first-contract study covers contracts from 1987 to 1996 in campaigns where a contract was reached, and states that “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power.” Its stated prevalences include grievable safety clauses in 55 percent of private contracts, discrimination clauses in nearly three-quarters, schedule language in one-third of private contracts, vacancy posting in more than three-quarters, job training in about one-quarter, private-sector tuition at 16 percent, and some restrictions on outsourcing in about one-third of private agreements. It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

original.title: It helps workers secure limits on replacing their jobs with outside labor.
original.pro_html:
Point 13 It helps workers secure limits on replacing their jobs with outside labor.

  • Because The study found private-sector first agreements with rules “restricting the use of temporary workers, subcontracting, and supervisors doing bargaining unit work.” [7] These limit shifting represented employees' work to temporary staff, outside firms or managers.
  • So Making such limits more reachable gives workers a way to defend the jobs their households rely on. This protects people vulnerable to losing their income.
original.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study covers contracts from 1987 to 1996 in campaigns where a contract was reached, and states that “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power.” Its stated prevalences include grievable safety clauses in 55 percent of private contracts, discrimination clauses in nearly three-quarters, schedule language in one-third of private contracts, vacancy posting in more than three-quarters, job training in about one-quarter, private-sector tuition at 16 percent, and some restrictions on outsourcing in about one-third of private agreements. The bill’s panel factors do not prescribe particular contract terms. Sources: [7], [1].

It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

original.title: It offers a way to settle first-contract disputes without relying on a strike or lockout.
original.pro_html:
Point 14 It offers a way to settle first-contract disputes without relying on a strike or lockout.

  • Because Either side can request mediation, followed by a binding decision if talks fail, as set out above.
  • Because Canadian research identifies the bargaining incentive behind this approach: “Together these results suggest that FCA encourages collective bargaining by creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement.” [14] FCA means first-contract arbitration.
  • Because Stoppages threaten workers' livelihoods: “strikes, lockouts, and other labor disruptions that can be devastating for workers and much more costly to the nation’s economy.” [15]
  • Because Disrupted services also put vulnerable people at risk. Treasury cites research finding that “nurse strikes, though uncommon, lead to diminished patient outcomes” [3].
  • So The bill gives workers an alternative way to seek a first contract and both sides an incentive to settle. Reducing reliance on harmful stoppages protects workers' incomes and people who depend on their services.
original.con_html:
Response The Canadian study does not separate the effect of the settlement incentive from the different legal rules that came with it.

  • Because First-contract arbitration lets a third party set the agreement. The study notes: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop” [14]. H.R.5408 contains no matching requirement [1]; its command is that the panel “shall render a decision settling the dispute” [1].
  • Because The study says the data do not let it estimate “the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” [14] Here, incidence means how often first-contract strikes or lockouts occur.
  • So The PRO has not shown that the reduction found across those Canadian systems would follow from this bill's settlement route. This response does not answer the narrower point that arbitration gives parties an alternative to relying on a stoppage.
original.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study covers contracts from 1987 to 1996 in campaigns where a contract was reached, and states that “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power.” Its stated prevalences include grievable safety clauses in 55 percent of private contracts, discrimination clauses in nearly three-quarters, schedule language in one-third of private contracts, vacancy posting in more than three-quarters, job training in about one-quarter, private-sector tuition at 16 percent, and some restrictions on outsourcing in about one-third of private agreements. The bill’s panel factors do not prescribe particular contract terms. Sources: [7], [1].

Brief context note: A review of Canadian first-contract arbitration states that boards and arbitrators limit awards by employer financial capacity and recognize that arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

Evidence note: The Canadian first-contract study reports no statistically significant effect of arbitration on the duration of first-agreement work stoppages, alongside its reported reduction in their incidence. Sources: [14].

original.title: It binds workers to terms they cannot reject by voting.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It binds workers to terms they cannot reject by voting.

  • Because Member approval is an existing safeguard under union rules: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” [2]
  • Because The bill instead makes the panel’s vote decisive: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute” [1]. Its binding decision requires no approval vote by workers.
  • So Workers bear the consequences of their pay, hours, and workplace rules. Letting them reject terms they judge harmful gives their needs a direct check on the outcome. Removing that safeguard weakens fair treatment in decisions governing their livelihoods.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A union must represent all employees in the unit fairly and in good faith. Under the bill, the union selects one panel member and the panel must consider employees’ ability to sustain themselves and their families. Sources: [17], [1].

original.title: It pressures workers to settle before they have enough time to understand and press their needs.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It pressures workers to settle before they have enough time to understand and press their needs.

  • Because First-contract talks often involve beginners: “newly unionized employers and newly formed unions are often inexperienced in negotiations.” [2]
  • Because Preparing a first contract requires detailed review of many issues. Labor lawyers explain: “there are too many topics requiring in-depth discussion, negotiation, and drafting to reach agreement in that timeframe.” [18]
  • Because Workers currently use continued bargaining and economic pressure to seek better terms: “workers can use strikes to try to pull employers closer to their demands.” [2]
  • Because The employer can trigger the bill’s route to binding terms despite workers’ objections: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [1] More time requires agreement: “or such additional period as the parties may agree upon” [1].
  • So Workers cannot keep disputed terms open simply by withholding agreement. An employer can start the move to outside decision-makers while workers still want time to assess proposals or press their demands.
  • Because Representative Fine identifies the resulting pressure: the timetable “increases pressure on workers to settle before they have fully fought for what they deserve.” [19]
  • So Protecting workers who depend on their pay and benefits includes giving them a fair chance to understand and defend those needs. Pressure to accept less before losing direct control threatens that protection.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill does not limit the time an arbitration may take once a panel is referred. A review of Ontario cases reports that parties often settle before arbitration concludes and may resume negotiations after an application. The panel must consider the employees’ cost of living. Sources: [2], [8], [1].

original.title: It risks locking workers into safety rules that do not fit their workplace.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It risks locking workers into safety rules that do not fit their workplace.

  • Because The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors warns that arbitrators unfamiliar with a facility could impose “work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations” [20].
  • Because Matching prevention to the workplace matters for worker protection. OSHA explains: “The process described in these recommended practices can, and should, be tailored to the needs of each workplace.” [21]
  • Because The imposed contract lasts two years unless changed by “written consent of the parties.” [1]
  • So A safety rule that misses the workplace’s actual hazards can leave workers exposed to injury. Giving such a rule binding force despite workers’ objections puts the protection of people facing those hazards at risk.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The panel includes one union-selected and one employer-selected member, and its decision must be based partly on the size and type of the employer’s operations. The FMCS-published arbitrator code says an arbitrator lacking specialized knowledge must decline, withdraw or request technical help, and should comply with a party’s request to visit a work area; the code addresses voluntary arbitration and is applied to agency rosters. A 2009 review says both parties produce evidence to the arbitrator. These warnings and responses cite no record of how arbitrated rules have fit particular workplaces. Sources: [22], [23], [1].

original.title: It risks jobs and livelihoods by letting outsiders impose costs a business cannot sustain.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It risks jobs and livelihoods by letting outsiders impose costs a business cannot sustain.

  • Because A panel can commit a business to costs without its agreement. Representative Walberg warns: “Those contracts could mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain, threaten jobs, kill growth, and in some cases, shut businesses down entirely.” [19]
  • Note The bill requires decisions to consider “the employer's financial status and prospects” [1]. The risk lies in outsiders judging those finances and operations incorrectly. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe warns: “Panel arbitrators may not understand the business” [16].
  • Because A mistaken first contract can shape later ones. Steptoe explains that imposed terms “would set the standard for all future contracts because of the difficulty of unwinding the many complex provisions that go into a collective bargaining agreement.” [16]
  • So Unsustainable costs threaten workers’ jobs and small owners’ livelihoods. Losing that income harms families with little financial cushion and closes opportunities to earn a living. Concern for vulnerable people gives [NAME] a reason to resist this added risk.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO does not show why outside decision-makers add a risk of unaffordable costs when the process requires them to examine the business’s finances.

  • Because The award must be based on “the employer's financial status and prospects” [1] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.” [1]
  • Because Outside decision-makers can apply affordability limits. Slinn and Hurd report that Canadian labor boards and arbitrators have taken “a very conservative approach to first contract awards” [8], limiting them “based on the employer’s financial capacity” [8].
  • So This experience challenges the assumption that an arbitrator’s outside status adds a risk of unaffordable terms. The PRO’s reason is a lawyer’s warning that arbitrators may not understand the business; it offers no example of such an award. Its prediction about later contracts depends on the same claim of added risk in the first contract.

original.title: It puts more strain on public help that poorly funded unions depend on.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It puts more strain on public help that poorly funded unions depend on.

  • Because The bill adds mandatory mediation and panel-arrangement duties: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” [1] After failed mediation, “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].
  • Because On June 9, King and MacDonald warned: “The FMCS does not have anywhere near the personnel to meet the obligations this legislation would impose upon it.” [24] FMCS is the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service.
  • Because A June 12 state account of the damage from the 2025 cuts confirms that “the majority of the federal agency’s employees have not returned.” [25]
  • Because Small unions have fewer alternatives. The service is particularly valuable to “small business and small unions that cannot necessarily afford to hire private mediation services.” [15]
  • Because Moving a dispute to a panel does not supply a deadline for finishing it: “The Faster Labor Contracts Act limits the amount of time that can pass before binding arbitration is invoked, but it does not limit the timeline of arbitration.” [2]
  • So Adding compulsory work to a depleted service creates competition for scarce help and another source of delay. Workers whose unions cannot buy private help have fewer ways around that strain. Equal opportunity requires protecting their access to the help needed to secure pay and workplace protections.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect the new mediation and referral duties to a loss of help that poorly funded unions could obtain under current law.

  • Because The staffing report describes already restricted access. Apart from critical-industry and class-action exceptions, negotiation services were limited to employers with “a minimum of 250 employees” [25].
  • Because The bill’s first-contract duty contains no employer-size cutoff: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” [1]
  • Because Referral does not wait for completed mediation. The clock is the “30-day period beginning on the date on which the request for mediation is made” [1]. If agreement has not been reached, “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1], unless the parties agree to more time.
  • Because Deciding the contract is the panel’s task, distinct from the service’s mediation and referral work. Existing FMCS practice already uses a separate source of decision-makers: “Arbitrators are not FMCS employees.” [26]
  • So The PRO has not shown how these duties would take help away from poorer unions under the already restricted system. This response does not answer added strain on units that remain eligible for FMCS help, or the absence of a deadline at the panel stage.

original.title: It exposes binding workplace decisions to political influence over appointments.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It exposes binding workplace decisions to political influence over appointments.

  • Because The bill normally gives each side a panel choice and calls for “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” [1]. But if seats remain unfilled after the 14-day selection period, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1]
  • Because Labor-policy researcher Rachel Greszler warns that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations to hire individuals for arbitrator positions based on their political leanings.” [2]
  • So When the parties cannot fill the seats, federal choices determine who can impose their terms. Selecting arbitrators for their political views threatens workers’ access to judgments based on their circumstances and needs. Concern for just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to protect workers from that influence.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s step from the designation power to political selection rests on one advocate’s prediction.

  • Because Each side normally chooses a panel member, and the third seat remains “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” [1]. The service fills “any members not selected” [1], so the power arises when seats go unfilled.
  • Because The PRO’s support for political selection is the statement that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations” [2]. That passage gives no example or evidence about how such designations are made.
  • So The bill does place those appointments with a federal agency. The further step, that those choices would turn on political leanings, is supported only by that prediction. This response does not show that such pressure would not occur.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The FMCS-published arbitrator code lists honesty, integrity, impartiality and general competence as qualifications for arbitrators and addresses voluntary arbitration; it does not set rules for how an agency designates panel members. The packet documents a 2025 executive order directing reductions at FMCS, which concerns staffing and not arbitrator selection. Sources: [22], [27].

original.title: It puts resources for pay and collective protection at risk through compulsory proceedings and new legal fights.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It puts resources for pay and collective protection at risk through compulsory proceedings and new legal fights.

  • Because King and MacDonald warn that compulsory arbitration requires “complex and cost-heavy hearings” [24]. Steptoe identifies another expense: “Courts will be asked to interpret the new statute and define the limits of the arbitrators’ authority.” [16]
  • Because The lawyers identify a direct risk to workers’ income: “This approach will direct employer resources to litigation and potentially decrease the amount of wages and benefits an employer can provide to employees.” [24]
  • Because Imposing terms by law also gives opponents a basis to challenge union funding. King and MacDonald argue: “The government will be involved whenever an arbitral-created contract requires fair-share fees. All of those contracts will be open to attack in our courts.” [24] These are fees for representing workers who do not join the union.
  • Because Those fees support help for members and nonmembers. Labor-law scholar Ann Hodges explains that a fee clause “permits the union to charge a fee for representation to those who do not want to join the union and pay full union dues.” [17] Yet “the union must represent all the employees in the unit fairly and in good faith.” [17]
  • Because Workplace access faces a separate legal attack. King and MacDonald argue that “any time this bill imposed a contract with union access rights, it would take property and violate the Fifth Amendment.” [24] Their claim is that requiring employers to admit union representatives takes a property right without paying for it.
  • Because Fee lawsuits can drain resources even when they fail. Reviewing earlier cases involving public-sector unions, Hodges reports that they “impose substantial litigation costs on unions that could otherwise dedicate these resources to representing workers” [17].
  • So Compulsory hearings and new legal fights can consume money for wages, benefits, and representation. Challenges to funding and workplace access also put the tools of collective protection at risk. Protecting people with little individual power gives [NAME] a reason to preserve those resources and tools.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s letters overstate the legal defects, and referral need not lead to a full hearing on every term.

  • Because Referral need not lead to a full hearing on every contract term.
