original.title: Helping finish construction brings noise that can hide warnings of danger.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Helping finish construction brings noise that can hide warnings of danger.

  • Because Construction takes place near everyday public and residential settings: “All AVC alignments would be routed through or near rural towns, businesses, or residential neighborhoods.” [15]
  • Because The review predicts loud noise at some sites: “Construction noise levels would temporarily exceed maximum allowable levels” [15], “outlined in state noise ordinances at some locations” [15].
  • Because FHWA explains how construction noise can block communication: “Loud noises from construction activities can create situations where people cannot effectively communicate” [16].
  • Because FHWA treats this as a possible safety issue when noise can “prevent people from hearing important local noises such as approaching traffic, emergency warning devices, alerts from other people” [16].
  • So Helping noisy work proceed near homes and public places can add the risk of missed danger warnings for people nearby. Avoiding that risk serves [NAME]’s wish to stay personally safe to the extent [NAME] is near the work.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The conduit’s service area is the Lower Arkansas River Valley east of Pueblo, with 39 participating systems and a service population of about 50,000. Both the benefits and the construction hazards fall mainly on people in or passing through that area. The district is the repayment entity. The EPA household-bill findings and the CDC hospital warning are national statements, and the record gives no estimate for a household bill here. CDC’s “Particle pollution can affect anyone” describes who can be harmed, not who meets this dust. Sources: [3], [10].

Evidence note: The EIS lists air quality among resources with minimal effects, describes traffic disruption as short-term and localized, uses borings for major crossings, and says noise would decrease away from the source and would not be anticipated to last longer than 2 to 4 weeks in any specific area outside more complicated work such as in Pueblo. The FHWA text says speech interference may be merely an annoyance in certain situations. The EIS reports construction equipment typically up to 90 decibels against residential ambient levels up to 50, and FHWA’s Table 3.2 lists 66 dB for normal-voice communication at 1 meter. The passages cited do not measure masked warnings at a specific site. Sources: [15], [16].

original.title: It helps protect communities from contaminated drinking water.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps protect communities from contaminated drinking water.

  • Because The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation found groundwater with “cancer-causing radioactive contaminants including naturally occurring radium and uranium.” [5]
  • Because On January 8, the House Natural Resources Committee chair reported: “18 of those communities are currently failing to meet Federal drinking water standards due to these contaminants.” [3]
  • Because The finished conduit will deliver clean water to “39 rural communities across southeastern Colorado.” [6]
  • Because Protecting shared drinking water serves societal security. The federal plan for water security calls the water sector “a lifeline sector” [7] and states: “Safe drinking water is a prerequisite for protecting public health and all human activity” [7].
  • So Helping finish a shared safe-water system strengthens the government's ability to defend U.S. communities against a documented health threat. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a country that protects its citizens.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: Sources differ on key counts. Reclamation’s ROD and 2024 testimony refer to twelve providers under orders or exceeding standards, while the chair and the district refer to 18. Municipal Sewer & Water reports about 39,000 residents in the 39 communities, while most sources say about 50,000. Sources: [5], [10], [3], [11].

original.title: It helps secure enough water to keep communities and essential services running.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps secure enough water to keep communities and essential services running.

  • Because Some local sources run short: “springs that supply some of the underground water sources can dry up periodically.” [11]
  • Because The conduit supplies water from elsewhere: “It will transport water that originates in the Fryingpan River basin on the western slope of the Continental Divide” [11]. Reclamation says it will “help meet existing and future municipal and industrial water demands” [5].
  • Because The services supplied include “water for hospitals in towns such as La Junta” [12] and “water for rural schools in communities such as Lamar” [12].
  • Because Water shortages threaten services beyond household drinking needs. The federal plan for water security identifies “fire protection, healthcare, and heating and cooling processes” [7] as critical services disrupted by interrupted water service.
  • So Easier financing helps meet water needs despite local shortages and future demand. Keeping communities, schools, and hospitals supplied supports the United States' ability to protect people and maintain stable daily life.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: The 2022 EA states that the project would not increase Fryingpan-Arkansas Project water diversions. The conduit delivers water by pipe rather than adding river diversions. Sources: [13].

Evidence note: Sources differ on key counts. Reclamation’s ROD and 2024 testimony refer to twelve providers under orders or exceeding standards, while the chair and the district refer to 18. Municipal Sewer & Water reports about 39,000 residents in the 39 communities, while most sources say about 50,000. Sources: [5], [10], [3], [11].

original.title: It strengthens water providers' ability to sustain an essential public service.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It strengthens water providers' ability to sustain an essential public service.

  • Because Local providers face tight budgets: “Rural water providers in our area often struggle to secure the funding needed to meet the needs of the communities they serve.” [14]
  • Because The parties paying for the conduit must also keep it working. The bill requires “the assumption by the contracting parties of the care, operation, maintenance, and replacement of the conduit.” [2]
  • Because County commissioners say completing the conduit would “help reduce the financial burden on these providers and enhance their ability to deliver a higher quality and a more reliable water supply” [14].
  • So Reducing the yearly repayment burden makes the shared supply more affordable for strained providers. Helping them sustain water service strengthens the public capacity needed to protect citizens.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: Secondary accounts describe the bill’s hardship clause differently from its text. The district’s post-veto message says it “Provides an opportunity for a federal decision on debt forgiveness based on economic hardship,” and the Colorado Sun says it may have allowed Reclamation to forgive some loan payments. The bill text ties a term of up to 75 years at half the Treasury rate to a demonstration of financial hardship and does not use the word forgiveness. Sources: [8], [15], [2].

original.title: It helps protect the pipes and equipment that keep water flowing.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It helps protect the pipes and equipment that keep water flowing.

  • Because Dissolved minerals in existing supplies cause physical damage. Reclamation found “corrosion and scaling effects that lead to premature deterioration of distribution pipes, water treatment equipment” [5].
  • Because Its updated assessment retains the conduit's benefits from “reducing total dissolved solids concentrations” [13], meaning less dissolved mineral material in supplied water.
  • So Helping deliver less damaging water slows wear on essential water systems. Preserving those systems strengthens the United States' ability to maintain services its communities depend on.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

original.title: It helps protect a shared river from polluted treatment waste.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It helps protect a shared river from polluted treatment waste.

  • Because In Las Animas, treating polluted well water creates another problem. The water district's president described “contaminated waste water that is a byproduct of treatment.” [16] He said: “We can discharge that back to the river, but we can’t do that in perpetuity.” [16]
  • Because That waste poses a pollution risk to a shared river: “the Arkansas River’s own water quality problems, which can be worsened by the discharges.” [16]
  • Because Reclamation says the conduit will “supplement or replace existing poor-quality groundwater sources” [13].
  • So Replacing polluted well water reduces the need for the local treatment that produces this waste. Helping finance that change protects a shared U.S. water resource from this source of pollution. Protecting essential water resources serves [NAME]'s concern for a secure country.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: The district president said the state will not allow Las Animas to discharge indefinitely. The 2013 EIS assumed zero liquid discharge under all alternatives. La Junta is seeking grants to reduce concentrate volume. The timing of any requirement is not stated in the record. Sources: [16], [17], [18].

original.title: It helps rural communities maintain viable local economies.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It helps rural communities maintain viable local economies.

  • Because The region faces “low income, and its shrinking population and economy” [16].
  • Because Existing water limits business activity. The water district's president explained: “If we try to do anything in Las Animas that requires a new water supply, we can’t do it.” [16]
  • Because Reclamation's experience with other rural water projects supports the link to stability: when clean water becomes available, “businesses can turn their attention to new opportunities” [5] and “communities can gain stability” [5].
  • Because These communities also house food producers: they “support families who ranch and raise livestock.” [3]
  • So Helping finance a usable new supply removes a water barrier to business activity and supports viable towns, including ranching communities. Sustaining U.S. communities directly serves [NAME]'s concern for a stable country.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. After the veto, the district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would carry construction about three to five years, and quote the district president that repayment becomes challenging in the second half of the project. Sources: [8], [9].

original.title: The added financing cost draws on federal resources available for defense and emergencies.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 The added financing cost draws on federal resources available for defense and emergencies.

  • Because The existing interest rate is tied to Treasury’s borrowing costs: “computed average interest rate payable by the Treasury upon its outstanding marketable public obligations” [1].
  • Because Receiving the same payment later is worth less. CBO explains that “an amount received or paid today is more valuable than the same amount received or paid in the future.” [19]
  • Because CBO’s July 2025 table lists the bill’s effect on direct spending as “Increase by Less Than $500K” [20].
  • So The cheaper financing adds a federal cost. Keeping the current terms preserves the federal resources that cover it.
  • Because Federal financing costs compete with defense spending. A report by the Joint Economic Committee’s chair states: “Interest costs use revenue that could be used for other government outlays, such as national defense.” [21]
  • Because CBO identifies “respond to unforeseen events” [22] as another purpose of federal tax and spending policy.
  • Because [NAME] values a state with the means to defend its citizens and protect them against new threats.
  • So Preserving funds available for defense and emergency action serves that value and gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added subsidy.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO treats higher promised repayments as funds that keeping the current terms would preserve, but the record reports a payment problem under those terms. This response does not dispute that CBO lists a small direct-spending increase, and it does not reach the PRO’s reasoning from a federal cost to resources for other uses.

  • Because The bill makes the easier repayment terms depend on hardship: “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2].
  • Because In 2024 testimony on an earlier bill, the repayment district assessed whether income from contracts to use project facilities could cover its share after construction costs rose: “Repayment can now be accomplished only if the interest rate is reduced to at least half the current project rate and the repayment period is at least 75 years, 25 years longer than the currently authorized 50 years.” [23]
  • Because Reclamation confirmed the payment problem under the existing law: “Given this increase, the project beneficiaries are again faced with challenges to repay their share of construction of the project, as directed under P.L. 111-11.” [10]
  • Because The PRO’s own CBO source accounts for missed payments when valuing loans. It describes “the expected cost of default, which CBO accounts for in projected cash flows rather than in the discount rate.” [19]
  • So An interest rate tied to federal borrowing costs and an earlier due date set what is owed. They do not show what would be collected. Comparing the value of the promised payments leaves out the payment problem. The PRO has not shown that keeping the old terms preserves the higher repayments it counts as available funds.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Secondary accounts describe the bill’s hardship clause differently from its text. The district’s post-veto message says it “Provides an opportunity for a federal decision on debt forgiveness based on economic hardship,” and the Colorado Sun says it may have allowed Reclamation to forgive some loan payments. The bill text ties a term of up to 75 years at half the Treasury rate to a demonstration of financial hardship and does not use the word forgiveness. Sources: [8], [15], [2].

Evidence note: The bill’s only cost figure in the record is CBO’s July 2025 listing of “Increase by Less Than $500K” in direct spending and no effect on revenues, in a table CBO says was prepared with limited review time. Sponsors say the bill “does not authorize any additional Federal funding.” The JEC and CBO statements cited concern the national debt in general. The JEC statement concerns net interest on the national debt, and the CBO statement concerns deficit-financed policy under a large debt. Neither names a program this bill would reduce. Sources: [20], [21], [3].

catalog.retirement_reason: Safe water and care for people are the substantive goals. Religious support for those goals does not independently establish Tradition fit.

original.title: Helping deliver safe water follows the Christian duties to serve the thirsty and protect life.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 Helping deliver safe water follows the Christian duties to serve the thirsty and protect life.

  • Because Communities awaiting the pipeline face a health threat: “The drinking water sources they rely on are often contaminated with unsafe levels of radium, uranium, and other pollutants.” [4]
  • Because Jesus's teaching praises giving water to those in need: “I was thirsty and you gave Me drink.” [5]
  • Because The Baptist Faith and Message calls Christians to “contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death.” [6]
  • Because Evangelical teaching also applies water provision to public action. The National Association of Evangelicals says, “We urge governments” [7] to “provide safe drinking water” [7].
  • So Helping finance a safer water supply puts those inherited teachings into practice through public policy. [NAME]'s wish to follow Christian tradition therefore supports this relief.
original.con_html:
Response The personal service the PRO invokes is not carried out by supporting public loan terms. This response does not answer the PRO’s separate appeal to the National Association of Evangelicals’ public-policy call.

  • Because The family following Jesus’s teaching describes its service as “giving and sacrificing our time and resources” [5]. Christian writer Robert Sirico distinguishes public aid from that duty: “What is required of us as individuals may or may not translate into a civic policy priority.” [8] He adds: “a government program effects nothing toward fulfilling the Gospel requirement that we give of our own time and income toward assisting the poor.” [8]
  • Because The National Association of Evangelicals calls on governments to “provide safe drinking water” [7]. That is a public-policy goal, separate from the personal giving in the passage the PRO quotes.
  • So The “thirsty” teaching and the personal duty to serve do not by themselves make favoring these terms an inherited Christian practice. That step needs the public-policy teaching and not the duty of personal service.
original.retirement_reason: Safe water and care for people are the substantive goals. Religious support for those goals does not independently establish Tradition fit.

original.title: Affordable water can help sustain the town where a Christmas caroling tradition continues.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Affordable water can help sustain the town where a Christmas caroling tradition continues.

  • Because Unsafe water “forces many families to rely on bottled water or expensive filtration systems” [4]. H.R.131 addresses local affordability by “cutting local costs by lowering the interest rate and providing more flexible repayment terms.” [9]
  • Because The district's spokesman identifies water quality as a barrier to living in valley towns: “It's a great lifestyle and one of the big drawbacks is the water quality.” [10]
  • So Easing the cost of a safer supply supports the households and towns where these families can keep living.
  • Because The district lists “Town of Swink” [12] among conduit participants. Its church keeps a shared religious custom: “The Swink United Methodists Shared Their Annual Tradition of Christmas Caroling with the Community.” [13]
  • So By easing a stated cost and water-quality barrier to remaining in these towns, the bill can help sustain the community in which this annual Christmas caroling custom is practiced. Continuing that named religious custom, rather than water quality alone, supplies the Tradition connection.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The same district spokesman passage says “the decline of a lot of the communities in the Lower Arkansas Valley is directly related to the poor quality of water.” The farm article’s stated water threat concerns irrigation water being purchased and diverted, which the bill does not address. Sources: [10], [14].

catalog.retirement_reason: Mercy in public debt terms is a general moral justification, without a particular inherited debt observance or practice affected by the bill.

original.title: Hardship relief follows Christian mercy toward borrowers while helping communities meet their repayment duties.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Hardship relief follows Christian mercy toward borrowers while helping communities meet their repayment duties.

  • Because The difficulty is an inability to pay: “the communities that it will serve do not have the financial capacity to meet the traditional repayment obligations.” [4]
  • Because The bill ties easier repayment to “a demonstration of financial hardship” [2] for a project serving “communities and households that do not have reliable access to domestic water supplies” [2].
  • Because Kevin DeYoung's account of Christian lending judges loans by their effect on borrowers: “It depends on whether the loan will help the borrower or most likely hurt them.” [16]
  • Because Christian concern for people in need is an express duty: “We should work to provide for the orphaned, the needy, the abused, the aged, the helpless, and the sick.” [6]
  • Because Repayment is also a Christian duty in public finance. Joe Carter explains that elected representatives take on “contractual debt obligations” [17] and concludes, “For this reason, I believe as Christians we should not refuse to pay for the legal obligations that we have authorized.” [17]
  • So A lower rate and more time make repayment fit hardship while retaining the required share. [NAME] can honor both mercy toward borrowers in need and responsibility for paying debts by favoring these terms.
original.con_html:
Response DeYoung’s help-or-hurt test sets loans for urgent personal needs apart from other lending, so it does not establish that mercy toward borrowers covers this water district’s construction debt. This response does not reach the PRO’s separate appeal to repayment duty.

  • Because DeYoung’s test concerns which loans count as usury. He explains, “But not every sort of interest-bearing loan has been considered usury.” [16] He distinguishes loans for urgent personal needs from another kind: “But a loan as a business venture or investment risk has historically been considered a different kind of loan.” [16]
  • Because The bill requires “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. That condition concerns the project’s financing, not a loan for a person’s urgent needs.
  • Because The broader duty is addressed to Christians: “We should work to provide for the orphaned, the needy, the abused, the aged, the helpless, and the sick.” [6] It does not say that easing a public project’s debt is how that duty is carried out.
  • So The PRO’s sources do not establish that easing this public construction debt falls within the mercy they describe. Its appeal to repayment duty is not answered here.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: DeYoung’s article describes Old Testament loans as given to the destitute and says that in such cases one must not charge interest, while distinguishing loans of capital. The article does not discuss public water-project repayment. Carter says an individual must pay “to the best of their ability” and writes about the debt ceiling. H.R.131 keeps the 35 percent share while changing the rate and the deadline. Sources: [16], [17].
original.retirement_reason: Mercy in public debt terms is a general moral justification, without a particular inherited debt observance or practice affected by the bill.

catalog.retirement_reason: Keeping a public commitment is the substantive justification; invoking an inherited promise does not turn ordinary promise-keeping into Tradition.

original.title: Making the longstanding federal water pledge workable honors the Christian duty to keep one's word.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 Making the longstanding federal water pledge workable honors the Christian duty to keep one's word.

  • Because The commitment reaches back generations: “Over six decades ago, President John Kennedy came to Pueblo, CO, and famously promised to build the Arkansas Valley Conduit.” [9]
  • Because Financing relief helps carry out that pledge: “it would fulfill a decades--many decades--old promise on which they have relied.” [9]
  • Because Christian teaching treats promises as binding: “Jesus here stresses that the word of a Christian should be such that a “yes” or a “no” carries binding force.” [18]
  • Because That moral standard can guide public conduct. The Baptist Faith and Message says, “Every Christian should seek to bring industry, government, and society as a whole under the sway of the principles of righteousness, truth, and brotherly love.” [6]
  • So Favoring terms that help the government carry out its pledge lets [NAME] uphold an inherited moral standard in public life.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The 1962 Act authorized the project and made a repayment contract a condition precedent to construction. Congress reduced the conduit’s required share to 35 percent in 2009. Reclamation’s 2024 testimony says completing the conduit “fulfills a commitment the federal government made decades ago.” H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. The 1962 repayment clause runs “as rapidly as is consistent with the contracting parties' ability to pay, but in any event, within fifty years.” Senator Bennet says Kennedy “famously promised to build” the conduit, and the Project Management Plan says completion “will fulfill a project authorization from 1962.” The text of the 1962 Pueblo address is not in the record. Sources: [19], [20], [1], [9], [21].
original.retirement_reason: Keeping a public commitment is the substantive justification; invoking an inherited promise does not turn ordinary promise-keeping into Tradition.

catalog.retirement_reason: Productive spending and stewardship are general prudential duties here, not an identified inherited practice or way of life.

original.title: Helping turn existing construction into a working water supply follows Christian stewardship.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 Helping turn existing construction into a working water supply follows Christian stewardship.

  • Because Public resources are already committed: “More than $249 million has already been spent on the AVC” [22].
  • Because Completing the project gives that work a useful purpose: “Once completed, the Arkansas Valley Conduit will deliver clean water to over 50,000 people in 39 rural communities across southeastern Colorado.” [9]
  • Because Christian stewardship means using what God entrusts to people well: “A thoughtful stewardship of all that we have is part of our Christian discipleship.” [23] Its purpose includes others' welfare: “We, in turn, are thus responsible for using his blessings for his glory, our benefit and the welfare of others.” [23]
  • So By easing the repayment obstacle to completion, the bill helps put existing work and public money to their intended use. [NAME] can favor that productive use of resources as an expression of inherited Christian stewardship.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The 1962 Act authorized the project and made a repayment contract a condition precedent to construction. Congress reduced the conduit’s required share to 35 percent in 2009. Reclamation’s 2024 testimony says completing the conduit “fulfills a commitment the federal government made decades ago.” H.R.131 appropriates no construction funds. The 1962 repayment clause runs “as rapidly as is consistent with the contracting parties' ability to pay, but in any event, within fifty years.” Senator Bennet says Kennedy “famously promised to build” the conduit, and the Project Management Plan says completion “will fulfill a project authorization from 1962.” The text of the 1962 Pueblo address is not in the record. Sources: [19], [20], [1], [9], [21].

Evidence note: The veto message reports “More than $249 million has already been spent on the AVC” and “total costs are estimated to be $1.3 billion,” so the larger part of the estimated cost lies ahead. H.R.131 appropriates none of it. The stewardship source speaks of personal resources. Sources: [22], [23].
original.retirement_reason: Productive spending and stewardship are general prudential duties here, not an identified inherited practice or way of life.

catalog.retirement_reason: The objection is fiscal prudence or responsibility to descendants; religious endorsement alone does not establish a distinct Tradition stake.

original.title: The interest discount shifts financing costs from users to the public, against the inherited Christian ethic of responsibility and thrift.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 The interest discount shifts financing costs from users to the public, against the inherited Christian ethic of responsibility and thrift.

  • Because This is public financing: existing law provides “100 percent federal construction financing” [1].
  • So For the same unpaid balance and time, users would owe half the interest charged at the existing benchmark. The public supplies that financing discount.
  • Because Chuck Colson links responsibility to Christian heritage: “As heirs to the Christian work ethic, we Americans value liberty and self-reliance. Hard work. Paying our bills. Delaying our gratification.” [24]
  • Because Colson applies restraint to public finances: “It's a moral issue. Living within our means, caring about our children and grandchildren, saving our society.” [24]
  • Because Concerned Women for America calls for a return to “historically-proven, time-honored principles” [25], including “individual freedom and responsibility” [25].
  • Because Writing about government loan relief, Jeremiah Greever applies Christian teaching directly to public lending: “he doesn’t call us to lend someone else’s money and then change the terms of the lending agreement.” [26]
  • So Keeping this inherited ethic in public lending gives [NAME] a reason to oppose shifting more of users’ financing costs to the public.
  • Note The sponsor says the bill “does not authorize any additional Federal funding” [4]. The objection concerns the discounted price of public lending, which the bill changes.
original.con_html:
Response An interest discount on public lending does not establish the failure of responsibility the PRO infers from it. This response does not answer Greever’s separate objection to changing the terms of a loan made with others’ money.

  • Because Existing law requires “payment in an amount equal to 35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [1]. The bill keeps “35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2] and assigns the contracting parties “the care, operation, maintenance, and replacement of the conduit.” [2]
  • Because Crown explains the repayment teaching this way: “The implication of this Scripture is that the wicked can repay but will not, as opposed to those who want to repay but cannot.” [27]
  • Because Focus on the Family publishes Crown’s advice that borrowers unable to make minimum payments ask creditors to “reduce the interest and/or accept what you can afford to pay.” [28] It adds, “If they accept your proposal, pay that amount faithfully until it is totally repaid.” [28]
  • So In this teaching, lower interest can be part of faithful repayment. A hardship discount does not itself show that borrowers are shirking their duties.
  • Because Colson’s account of Christian responsibility also recognizes government, family, church and business as institutions that “all have vital and proper roles to play in society, balancing each other.” [24]
  • Because The National Association of Evangelicals’ civic platform urges governments to “provide safe drinking water” [7]. Existing law requires evidence that “it would be infeasible for the communities involved to construct the works themselves, singly or jointly.” [1]
  • So The work ethic does not settle how the cost of this government task should be shared. The PRO’s general appeals to self-reliance supply no further reason why the old interest charge better reflects Christian responsibility in this hardship case.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO’s July 2025 listing shows direct spending “Increase by Less Than $500K.” Colson, Perkins and CWA wrote about national spending and debt, not this contract. Sources: [29], [30].
original.retirement_reason: The objection is fiscal prudence or responsibility to descendants; religious endorsement alone does not establish a distinct Tradition stake.

catalog.retirement_reason: The objection is fiscal prudence or responsibility to descendants; religious endorsement alone does not establish a distinct Tradition stake.

original.title: The longer repayment limit permits debt to bind later generations, against Christian teaching to limit long-term debt and provide for descendants.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 The longer repayment limit permits debt to bind later generations, against Christian teaching to limit long-term debt and provide for descendants.

  • Because The bill lifts the repayment limit by 25 years. The committee describes “increasing the repayment period from 50 years to 75 years” [1].
  • So Repayment claims could remain in years 51–75, after the existing legal deadline.
  • Because Albert Mohler identifies the inherited teaching: “The Christian tradition has been very suspicious of credit and borrowing.” [31]
  • Because Crown Financial Ministries makes the rule about duration explicit: “Do not accumulate long-term debt” [27].
  • Because Focus on the Family warns that borrowing reaches into an uncertain future: “it does warn us against making assumptions about the future” [32].
  • Because Family Research Council president Tony Perkins applies biblical money teachings “both as individuals and collectively as communities and countries” [30].
  • Because Perkins grounds his warning about passing public debt to descendants in Proverbs: “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children” [30].
  • So Allowing repayment claims for another 25 years puts later generations’ resources within reach of the debt. Maintaining Christian caution about long commitments and the duty to provide for descendants gives [NAME] a reason to oppose lifting the limit.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that a longer hardship repayment plan falls under its sources’ warnings against accumulating debt and passing overspending to descendants.

  • Because The bill keeps the construction share at “35 percent of the cost of the conduit” [2]. Extra time depends on “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. The committee reports that inflation caused project costs “to nearly double from $640 million to $1.3 billion.” [1]
  • Because Crown’s rule, “Do not accumulate long-term debt” [27], discusses lengthening home loans through “expansion through taking on debt” [27]. Perkins warns about “continuing to amass trillions of dollars in debt, debt that is going to be passed to future generations.” [30]
  • Because The same Crown ministry advises hardship borrowers to seek payments they can afford and says, “If they accept your proposal, pay that amount faithfully until it is totally repaid.” [28]
  • Because Mohler’s historical account says, “Usury laws and a bias against borrowing and lending dissuaded most Christians from borrowing except in a dire emergency.” [31] This project addresses unsafe water: Chairman Westerman reported that “18 of those communities are currently failing to meet Federal drinking water standards due to these contaminants.” [4]
  • Because Focus on the Family says, “Sometimes we must take on debt so that we can care for our loved ones.” [32] Its repayment standard is “a moral obligation to repay his or her creditors to the best of their ability.” [32]
  • So These teachings distinguish taking on debt from handling a repayment hardship, and require attention to essential needs and ability to pay. The extra time addresses repayment of the existing construction share. Payments reaching years 51–75 do not by themselves show the debt accumulation or passing on of overspending the PRO’s examples condemn. The PRO supplies no further link from that longer window to neglect of descendants.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Crown’s text states that the longest term of debt God’s people took on in the Bible was about seven years, and criticizes 30-year and longer home loans. It addresses household mortgages. Sources: [27].

Evidence note: CBO’s July 2025 listing shows direct spending “Increase by Less Than $500K.” Colson, Perkins and CWA wrote about national spending and debt, not this contract. Sources: [29], [30].
original.retirement_reason: The objection is fiscal prudence or responsibility to descendants; religious endorsement alone does not establish a distinct Tradition stake.

catalog.retirement_reason: Impartial treatment in repayment is a justice concern. Its religious endorsement does not establish preservation of a particular tradition.

original.title: The bill gives one conduit special hardship terms, against the biblical rule of impartial government.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill gives one conduit special hardship terms, against the biblical rule of impartial government.

  • Because Existing law already adjusts repayment speed to need: “as rapidly as is consistent with the contracting parties' ability to pay” [1]. It still imposes the 50-year deadline quoted above.
  • Because The act’s ordinary interest rule covers water supplied to towns and homes: “municipal, domestic, and industrial water supply allocations” [1]. Its ordinary cost-recovery rule requires repayment “within not more than fifty years” [1].
  • Because The bill gives the discounted rate and longer term specifically to “the contract for the Arkansas Valley Conduit” [2], “notwithstanding the reclamation laws or any other provision of this Act” [2].
  • So Hardship in this conduit qualifies for half its applicable Treasury benchmark and up to 75 years. Other hardship cases under the act would still face its ordinary full benchmark and 50-year limit.
  • Because WORLD’s biblical account of government calls for “public impartiality” [33] and says “extra sensitivity to abuse of the poor does not warrant prejudice in their favor” [33].
  • So Applying this inherited rule to public lending calls for common rules for hardship. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose an exception whose relief also depends on which project a community uses.
original.con_html:
Response Project-specific hardship terms do not by themselves establish the favoritism barred by the cited teaching.

  • Because WORLD says, “In this way godly justice and righteousness focus on process.” [33] Its rule is to “judge your neighbor fairly” [33].
  • Because The bill bases relief on “a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2]. The committee identifies a concrete repayment problem: inflation caused costs “to nearly double from $640 million to $1.3 billion.” [1]
  • So The exception has a reason tied to repayment capacity. Its project-specific scope alone does not show the biased judgment WORLD condemns.
  • So The PRO compares legal deadlines and rates, but supplies no comparison showing the same repayment capacity, cost increases, and water-access problems. Sharing a legal deadline does not establish the same financial need. The rule against favoritism therefore does not establish that these different hardship terms treat comparable cases unfairly.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Reclamation testified that the conduit is “unique within Reclamation’s authorized projects” in keeping repayment of a large upfront cost while serving only municipal and industrial purposes. GAO reported in 1996 that reclamation law does not require irrigators to pay interest on repayment obligations. Sources: [20], [34].
original.retirement_reason: Impartial treatment in repayment is a justice concern. Its religious endorsement does not establish preservation of a particular tradition.

original.title: It gives nature defenders evidence to challenge pressure on officials enforcing habitat protections.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It gives nature defenders evidence to challenge pressure on officials enforcing habitat protections.

  • Because Epstein’s islands contain protected habitats. The Virgin Islands’ lawsuit described “native coral and wildlife protected by federal and territorial law and enforcement authorities.” [3]
  • Because Officials reported construction continuing despite an order to stop work, including “additional roadways that have been carved out on the island, there have been two jetties, fill material has been placed into the submerged lands” [4].
  • Because DOJ’s files record Governor Bryan telling Epstein that he had asked an official to step aside and give way on permits: “I asked him to recuse himself and concede on all previous permit requests.” [4]
  • Because Public environmental information supports action. The UN Environment Programme explains: “Access to information empowers citizens and incentivizes them to participate in decision and policy making processes in an informed manner.” [5]
  • So Releasing the exchanges gives [NAME] and local nature groups evidence to compare private requests with public enforcement decisions and challenge pressure to relax habitat protections.
  • So That supports [NAME]’s wish to take part in defending nature by demanding that officials protect coral and wildlife when landowners seek special treatment.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Later messages in the same DOJ record have Epstein reporting that the official wanted “80k plus plus remediation plus” and “Not issuing permit until they give us a deficiency list to clear.” In a 2023 deposition Bryan said he never gave Epstein special treatment. The source does not identify a permit decision made in response to Bryan’s request. Sources: [6], [4].

Evidence note: A Virgin Islands settlement announced before November 18, 2025 required Epstein’s estate to pay $450,000 to remediate damage around Great St. James, sell both islands to independent third parties and wind down its local business operations. Sources: [7].

original.title: It opens records for checking how money raised for ocean protection was spent.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It opens records for checking how money raised for ocean protection was spent.

  • Because Maxwell’s TerraMar Project claimed to “give a voice to the least protected, most ignored part of our planet – the high seas.” [8]
  • Because Its results needed checking. The Independent reported that it “produced no tangible examples of successful ocean conservancy projects.” [8]
  • Because The released Maxwell banking records include “emails and bank statements” [9]. A 2016 bank email requests “an external transfer in the amount of $182.00 from the TerraMar account” [10]. These give payment details for checking past spending.
  • Because Financial records help assess whether charitable resources serve their purpose. National Philanthropic Trust explains: “Nonprofit reporting provides insight into how an organization employs funds raised—and how it measures success.” [11]
  • So The bill supplies bank records for checking TerraMar’s past spending against its aim of protecting oceans.
  • So [NAME]’s concern for oceans gives [NAME] a reason to support access to evidence for checking whether conservation money served nature and demanding proof of results from conservation work.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect the added details of TerraMar’s past payments to checking conservation results or making better choices about conservation work.

  • Because The warning about TerraMar’s results was already public in 2021: it “produced no tangible examples of successful ocean conservancy projects.” [8] The same report states: “The charity was disbanded in both the US and Britain soon afterwards.” [8]
  • Because The specific bank email records “an external transfer in the amount of $182.00 from the TerraMar account” [10]. It names a recipient and invoice, but gives no account of any ocean protection achieved with that payment.
  • Because The donor guidance distinguishes spending from results. It says to “look at the metrics for success that an organization has established for themselves” [11] and recommends reviewing “their financial documents and impact reports” [11].
  • So A payment record shows a transaction, not its conservation result. The PRO supplies no link between these added entries and work protecting oceans, and no lesson they add for judging an active conservation effort. Its move from inspecting a closed charity’s payments to helping conservation money serve nature is unsupported.

original.title: It supplies material for nature defenders challenging climate misinformation.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It supplies material for nature defenders challenging climate misinformation.

  • Because The files show Epstein sending physicist Lawrence Krauss a video titled “Nobel Laureate Smashes the Global Warming Hoax” [12].
  • Because They also record replies to misleading claims. Krauss answered a question about Antarctic ice by explaining that the “west Antarctic ice sheet is melting at an unprecedented rate.” [12]
  • Because A climate scientist has already used the released emails this way. Climatologist Michael Mann told Fast Company: “The Epstein Files is almost an advertisement for Science Under Siege because we see all of the key promoters of climate denial and anti-science that we talk about in the book” [12].
  • Because Public communication helps build support for cutting warming emissions. The UN panel on climate change (IPCC) explains: “Media can be a useful conduit to build public support to accelerate mitigation action” [13].
  • Because Climate action protects nature. The IPCC reports that heatwaves, droughts and floods are driving “mass mortalities in species such as trees and corals.” [14]
  • So Publishing these exchanges gives advocates a documented account of climate myths being shared, their sources and the replies. [NAME] can use that material in climate education and advocacy.
  • So Access to evidence for this work supports [NAME]’s wish to defend wildlife and habitats against warming.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The video Epstein sent was public on YouTube, and NASA reported in 2014 that glaciers in a section of West Antarctica were “melting faster than most scientists had expected.” Sources: [12], [15].

original.title: The required review makes work against pollution and wildlife crime compete for prosecutors’ time.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 The required review makes work against pollution and wildlife crime compete for prosecutors’ time.

  • Because Compliance takes up ordinary workdays. DOJ reported “plans to divert 400 attorneys across the department to dedicate all or most of their workdays to complying with the Epstein Files Transparency Act.” [16]
  • Because South Florida criminal prosecutors are among the reviewers: “these attorneys are being pulled from the Florida office’s criminal and national security divisions.” [17]
  • Because That division includes prosecutors who protect nature: “This group of specially trained, experienced prosecutors investigates and prosecutes federal criminal violations of environmental and wildlife protection laws.” [18]
  • Because The demand reaches across another prosecutors’ office. In Manhattan, “Nearly every single prosecutor, even those working on high-profile cases, as well as some top-ranking executive staff, is assisting in reviewing files.” [19]
  • Because Manhattan’s criminal prosecutors also enforce pollution laws. In a 2024 case, a contractor admitted “negligently causing the release of asbestos into the ambient air” [20]. The release states: “The prosecution of this case is being handled by the Office’s Civil Rights Unit in the Criminal Division.” [20]
  • So The bill adds a large, urgent task to offices that prosecute pollution and wildlife crime. Those cases must compete for staff time assigned to disclosure work.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose that pressure on enforcement because enforcing these laws helps protect nature from pollution and destruction.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The reported 400 attorneys is a department-wide total. The Miami Herald names the Florida office’s criminal and national security divisions but not its Environmental Crimes Unit. The cited asbestos case dates from 2024. Reports describe DOJ plans to redact beyond what the Act requires. A December 9, 2025 court order adds a pre-release certification under Section 2(c)(1)(A) of the Act, requiring review by SDNY attorneys, for Maxwell discovery records only. Sources: [17], [21], [20].

Evidence note: Bloomberg reported that lawyers could seek approval to exempt urgent matters, and quoted a statement that attorneys were working “around the clock.” DOJ’s December 2025 letter said most items offices supplied were non-responsive and that a judge’s order added review layers at SDNY. Sources: [16], [22].

original.title: Putting promises of secrecy at risk discourages the tips needed to fight crimes against nature.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Putting promises of secrecy at risk discourages the tips needed to fight crimes against nature.

  • Because The law in force already protected confidential sources under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). A July 2025 appeals decision upheld withholding because “witnesses provided information to the FBI ‘under implied assurances of confidentiality.’” [23]
  • Because A promise of secrecy to a source who is not a victim is not a separate ground for withholding under the bill. Its investigation exception covers information that “would jeopardize an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution, provided that such withholding is narrowly tailored and temporary” [1].
  • So The bill puts secrecy at risk for sources in the covered files whose information meets none of its withholding exceptions.
  • Because Exposing cooperation makes future witnesses less willing to help. The July decision accepted the FBI’s explanation that “witnesses are more likely to ‘hedge or withhold information’ if they believe ‘their cooperation with the FBI will later be made public.’” [23]
  • Because Nature protection needs inside information. The FACT Coalition reports that “identifying illicit financial flows associated with environmental crimes is extremely difficult without somebody on the inside tipping off an enforcement official.” [24]
  • Because Federal wildlife enforcement uses confidential sources. In a turtle-trafficking case, agent Ryan Bessey received a tip: “A confidential informant let him know he’d been contacted about supplying turtles.” [25] The source introduced him to the trafficker: “The informant connected Bessey to Kang through social media, introducing him as another supplier.” [25]
  • So Undercutting trust in federal promises of secrecy threatens the cooperation needed to uncover environmental crime. [NAME] has a reason to oppose that threat to nature protection.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that disclosure of Epstein records would make environmental sources less willing to cooperate.

  • Because The bill's release categories concern Epstein and Maxwell, including “Entities (corporate, nonprofit, academic, or governmental) with known or alleged ties to Epstein's trafficking or financial networks.” [1] They do not require release of unrelated environmental case files.
  • Because For unrelated law-enforcement records, the Freedom of Information Act still permits withholding information whose release “could reasonably be expected to disclose the identity of a confidential source” [26]. The bill does not remove this protection from unrelated environmental sources.
  • Because The FBI explanation the court accepted turns on what future sources expect: “witnesses are more likely to ‘hedge or withhold information’ if they believe ‘their cooperation with the FBI will later be made public.’” [23] That condition does not establish that an Epstein-specific disclosure rule would change environmental sources' expectations.
  • So The PRO needs evidence that exposing sources in these files would undermine trust among environmental sources still covered by existing protections. Showing why environmental enforcement needs tips does not establish that change in trust or the resulting loss of cooperation.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ’s January 2026 attorney review protocol under the Act lists “Names of confidential sources or cooperating witnesses” among required Privacy Act redactions. It concerns names rather than all information a source provided, and neither of these PROs’ packets cites it. Sources: [27].

original.title: Publicizing donor ties puts conservation funding at risk.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Publicizing donor ties puts conservation funding at risk.

  • Because The bill requires disclosure despite damage to reputations: “No record shall be withheld, delayed, or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity” [1].
  • Because The risk reaches an environmental grantmaker. Reporting on Earthshot states: “The Charity Commission is assessing concerns about sources of funding to a charity founded by Prince William after the head of one of its partners was included in the recently released Epstein files.” [28]
  • Because Earthshot funds concrete nature protection: “Winning The Earthshot Prize will go towards helping enable the establishment of the first High Seas protected area.” [29]
  • Because Donor controversies put money at stake. Charity Commission guidance tells trustees to consider “the risk of reduced support for your charity or harm to its reputation” [30] when keeping donations, and “the financial loss that will result from refusing or returning the donation” [30].
  • So Scrutiny sparked by disclosure creates risks of lost support and rejected donations. Less support leaves fewer resources for work such as protecting marine habitats, giving [NAME] another reason to oppose the mandate.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Epstein’s 2017 email exchange with Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem was reported on November 13, 2025 from House Oversight Committee emails. The Earthshot complaint came from the anti-monarchy group Republic, whose figure of “at least £1m” from DP World is its own. Third Sector states that no findings have been made and that inclusion in the files is not a sign of wrongdoing. Sources: [31], [28].

Evidence note: Charity Commission guidance says “Your starting point should be to accept and keep a donation,” and tells trustees they can refuse or return one in the charity’s best interests. It says “You shouldn’t make assumptions about what their views will be” regarding donors. The regulator’s statement describes an assessment “to determine any next steps,” and the cited report identifies no donation refused, returned or lost. Sources: [30], [28].

original.title: It opens evidence for pursuing abuse regardless of a suspect's wealth, office, or country.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It opens evidence for pursuing abuse regardless of a suspect's wealth, office, or country.

  • Because Status and reputation cannot justify hiding covered records: “No record shall be withheld, delayed, or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity, including to any government official, public figure, or foreign dignitary.” [1].
  • Because The duty covers records about how cases ended: “Any immunity deals, non-prosecution agreements, plea bargains, or sealed settlements involving Epstein or his associates.” [1].
  • Because Public access puts evidence within reach of investigators outside the United States. In February 2026, Reuters reported that French prosecutors' new probes “will rely on publicly available material” [3] and that “One will focus on human trafficking” [3].
  • So Victims, advocates, and investigators gain evidence to examine favored treatment and pursue abuse across borders. Seeking accountability without favoring powerful suspects serves [NAME]'s concern for justice for every victim, including vulnerable strangers abroad.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Before the vote, DOJ and the FBI stated: “We did not uncover evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties.” AP’s later review reported “scant evidence” of a trafficking ring serving powerful men, while adding that “it is possible those records contain evidence overlooked by investigators.” French prosecutors called their work “titanic work, without knowing what will come of it.” Sources: [4], [5], [3].

original.title: It gives survivors evidence to pursue compensation from those responsible.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It gives survivors evidence to pursue compensation from those responsible.

  • Because The bill covers DOJ records about organizations “with known or alleged ties to Epstein's trafficking or financial networks” [1].
  • Because A lawyer for survivors is using new revelations to examine civil claims. Arick Fudali said: “We’re also looking at other potential avenues of civil suits against perhaps some of his enablers that are now being revealed, his facilitators” [6].
  • Because Federal trafficking law already lets victims sue people who knowingly benefit from trafficking they knew or should have known about: “whoever knowingly benefits, or attempts or conspires to benefit, financially or by receiving anything of value from participation in a venture which that person knew or should have known has engaged in an act in violation of this chapter” [7]. Victims “may recover damages and reasonable attorneys fees” [7].
  • So Access to evidence about abuse and its support makes an existing route to compensation more usable. Helping survivors identify whom to sue and build their claims serves [NAME]'s concern that people harmed by abuse receive a just remedy.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A Section 1595 claim against an enabler requires a knowing benefit from a venture the person knew or should have known violated the trafficking chapter, and must be brought within 10 years of the cause of action or, if later, within 10 years of a minor victim turning 18. A financial tie alone does not establish those facts. The cited lawyer speaks of “potential avenues.” Sources: [7], [6].

original.title: It gives the public evidence to demand better government protection.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It gives the public evidence to demand better government protection.

  • Because The bill opens internal DOJ communications about “decisions to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate Epstein or his associates.” [1]. It also covers records about the “destruction, deletion, alteration, misplacement, or concealment of documents” [1].
  • Because DOJ's 2020 review concluded that “the victims were not treated with the forthrightness and sensitivity expected by the Department” [8].
  • Because Reviewing those failures has a direct use in victim protection. DOJ said the review “will inform our implementation of the Crime Victims Rights’ Act and the Attorney General’s Guidelines on Victim and Witness Assistance.” [8].
  • Because Former FBI agent Brian Fitzpatrick identifies a further use for disclosure: “to instruct law enforcement on future human trafficking and exploitation investigations.” [9].
  • Because The bill also opens underlying jail records: “Documentation of Epstein's detention or death, including incident reports, witness interviews, medical examiner files, autopsy reports, and written records detailing the circumstances and cause of death.” [1].
  • Because DOJ's prison watchdog found that “MCC New York staff falsified count slips and round sheets” [10] and stressed that “these failures have been recurring ones at the BOP” [10]. MCC New York was Epstein's federal jail; BOP is the federal prison agency.
  • So Public access lets advocates and watchdogs check official accounts and demand better treatment of victims and safer jails. It also gives future trafficking investigators a case to learn from. These tools serve [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable victims and people who depend on prison staff for their safety.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ changed its victim-assistance guidelines effective March 31, 2023, including earlier notice of plea and non-prosecution agreements. The DOJ inspector general’s published jail review made eight recommendations, which the BOP accepted, and identified staffing shortages and disregard of policies among causes. Sources: [11], [10].

original.title: It gives survivors fairer access to answers and evidence supporting their own accounts.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It gives survivors fairer access to answers and evidence supporting their own accounts.

  • Because Survivors asked Congress to take responsibility for disclosure. Anouska De Georgiou said: “Now it is the responsibility of Congress to pass a bill so that we don't have to carry the baton of being the ones to enforce this” [12].
  • Because The publication duty includes reasons for blacked-out text: “All redactions must be accompanied by a written justification published in the Federal Register and submitted to Congress.” [1].
  • So DOJ must make the covered records publicly available without requiring each survivor to bring a separate request. Survivors gain records they can search and reasons for redactions they can question.
  • Because Disclosure has supplied this kind of recognition. ABC reported the release of “a September 1996 complaint filed with the FBI's Miami office” [13], which Maria Farmer confirmed was hers. After the release, she said: “I'm just really grateful. I'm finally able to be vindicated. I feel redeemed.” [13].
  • So Giving survivors access to answers and documentary support for their earlier reports treats them as people whose suffering and accounts matter. That serves [NAME]'s concern for just treatment of vulnerable people.
  • Note The bill permits removing victims' identifying information from public records: “contain personally identifiable information of victims” [1]. This permits access to the rest of a record while withholding those details.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: NPR reported that the Act “contains no penalties or enforcement mechanism.” The required notices explain redactions, not why any complaint went unanswered, and Farmer’s quoted reaction does not report an explanation from the FBI. Sources: [14], [1].

original.title: It gives people evidence to challenge unsupported blame.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It gives people evidence to challenge unsupported blame.

  • Because Covered records become public “in a searchable and downloadable format” [1], giving readers documents they can check and keep.
  • Because Public records have enabled independent checks. AP examined newly released FBI emails about a supposed client list; an agent wrote that “investigators did not locate such a list during the course of the investigation.” [5].
  • Because The records also show how investigators assessed other accusations. AP reported: “Some allegations couldn’t be verified, investigators wrote.” [5] It reported that a 2019 memo’s review of payments to entities linked to influential figures “found no connection to criminal activity” [5].
  • So Readers gain evidence to distinguish allegations from findings and challenge claims the records do not support. Treating accused strangers according to evidence serves [NAME]'s concern that everyone receive just treatment.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ wrote that the production “may include fake or falsely submitted images, documents or videos, as everything that was sent to the FBI by the public was included.” Khardori warned that interview summaries could include “false leads and derogatory information.” Sources: [15], [16].

original.title: Mass publication risks exposing survivors to danger and renewed trauma.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 Mass publication risks exposing survivors to danger and renewed trauma.

  • Because In July 2025, DOJ had decided against further disclosure: “no further disclosure would be appropriate or warranted.” [17]
  • Because Removing names alone cannot protect survivors. DOJ explained: “Sensitive information relating to these victims is intertwined throughout the materials. This includes specific details such as victim names and likenesses, physical descriptions, places of birth, associates, and employment history.” [17]
  • Because Preparing this archive for release needs repeated manual work. DOJ's later account explains that “the document identification process was substantially manual and iterative” [18] and warns that inconsistencies would “likely exist in how reviewers applied redactions.” [18]
  • Note The bill lets officials block out information in portions that “contain personally identifiable information of victims” [1]. That protection depends on finding the identifying details before publication.
  • Because A separate congressional release shows why missed details matter. Victims' lawyers reported that “some victims warned that releasing their names would put them in physical danger.” [19] One survivor said: “I have been unable to mentally and emotionally function or sleep” [19].
  • Because The release under the Act, which came after the 30-day date, then did expose survivors. MS NOW reported that “survivors’ names and contact information were left unredacted and appear more than 500 times.” [6] Their lawyer said: “That was really, really revictimizing, really traumatizing for the survivors.” [6]
  • So Ordering broad, searchable publication creates a risk of exposing survivors through missed clues. The 30-day limit leaves less review time, though this record does not show that the limit caused the reported errors. [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people gives a reason to oppose imposing that danger and trauma on them.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: DOJ’s protocol under the Act directed redaction of other names or details that would reveal a victim’s identity. FBI review to prepare for possible publication was reported in March 2025. The congressional release predates the bill. The 30-day date passed on December 19, 2025, and DOJ’s main production came on January 30, 2026, with “virtually all of the time and attention” of reviewers described as going to protecting victim information. Sources: [20], [21], [18].

Evidence note: DOJ told the court on February 2, 2026 that, out of a January 30 upload of more than 3 million pages, it “now has taken down several thousands of documents and media that may have inadvertently included victim-identifying information due to various factors, including technical or human error.” This is an attributed DOJ account, not an independent audit or judicial finding. Several thousand removed items are not several thousand distinct victims or confirmed disclosure events. January 30 was after the 30-day date, so the letter does not establish that the deadline caused the errors, and it does not show the counterfactual extent of disclosure without the Act. Sources: [22].

original.title: Publishing unproved accusations and names linked only by contact exposes innocent strangers to unfair suspicion and lost opportunities.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Publishing unproved accusations and names linked only by contact exposes innocent strangers to unfair suspicion and lost opportunities.

  • Because Existing public-records law lets DOJ withhold investigative information whose release “could reasonably be expected to constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy” [23]. A court upheld that protection in the Epstein files for people including “third parties mentioned as part of the FBI’s investigative efforts or who provided information” [24].
  • Because Investigative files are not findings of guilt. Legal analyst Ankush Khardori describes “FBI summaries of witness interviews that could include false leads and derogatory information that the government was unable to corroborate.” [16]
  • Because The bill bars withholding for the harm such publication does to a person's good name: “No record shall be withheld, delayed, or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity, including to any government official, public figure, or foreign dignitary.” [1] This rule covers ordinary people too.
  • Because Mention in such a file can itself draw suspicion. In a 2025 appeal, the court accepted the FBI’s explanation that disclosure could subject third parties merely mentioned “to possible harassment or criticism and focus derogatory inferences and suspicion” on them [25]. Lost work or income can follow from that suspicion.
  • So The bill removes a ground for protecting people from being treated as guilty because of an unproved claim or mere contact with Epstein. [NAME]'s concern for everyone's just treatment and equal opportunities gives a reason to oppose exposing strangers to damaged reputations and lost income without proof of wrongdoing.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Act separately requires release of records on decisions “to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate.” DOJ and the FBI had said they found no evidence predicating investigation of uncharged third parties. A Privacy Act duty requires reasonable efforts at accuracy for some dissemination. DOJ’s protocol lists certain PII redactions but not ordinary third-party names generally. Sources: [1], [17], [26], [20].

original.title: Exposing confidential helpers risks retaliation and makes future abuse harder to uncover.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Exposing confidential helpers risks retaliation and makes future abuse harder to uncover.

  • Because Existing public-records law protects information whose release “could reasonably be expected to disclose the identity of a confidential source” [23] or “could reasonably be expected to endanger the life or physical safety of any individual” [23].
  • Because These files contain real promises of secrecy. A court found that FBI labels in the Epstein records showed “these sources provided information under an express grant of confidentiality.” [24] It also accepted the risk that disclosure “could subject the sources to reprisal.” [24]
  • Because The bill has no separate exception for a helper's confidentiality or safety. Its investigation exception covers material that “would jeopardize an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution, provided that such withholding is narrowly tailored and temporary” [1]. For unclassified information about helpers who are not victims, outside its other exceptions, a promise of secrecy alone would no longer justify withholding.
  • So The bill puts helpers at risk even after a case closes. Breaking a promise made to secure their help also treats them unjustly.
  • Because That breach affects future cooperation. The court accepted the FBI's warning of “great detriment to the FBI’s ability to recruit and maintain reliable confidential sources.” [24] These sources had provided information about “the trafficking and prostituting of children.” [24]
  • So Losing that cooperation weakens a way to uncover child abuse. [NAME] has a reason to oppose endangering helpers and undermining protection for vulnerable people who need others to speak up.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO overlooks an existing privacy law that the Justice Department applies to confidential-source names independently of FOIA.

  • Because The Privacy Act limits release of personal records retrieved by name or another identifier, unless consent or a listed exception allows it: “No agency shall disclose any record which is contained in a system of records” [26]. Its protection covers U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, including helpers who are not victims.
  • Because The department’s protocol applies that law to these files. Under “Privacy Act Redactions” [20], it directs reviewers to remove “Names of confidential sources or cooperating witnesses” [20]. This instruction relies on an existing statute, not a new court order or a helper’s status as a victim.
  • So Ending one FOIA reason for secrecy does not by itself require disclosure of these protected identities. The PRO’s chain from the bill to exposed helpers, broken promises, and lost cooperation omits this independent protection.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A June 25, 2026 district-court opinion in Phang v. Blanche granted preliminary relief and explained that the Act requires disclosure beyond ordinary FOIA production. The government did not respond to merits arguments and the court treated them as conceded under its local rule. The passages read do not decide whether the Privacy Act or source-identity protections bind against the Act. This does not settle the open confidentiality question. A September opinion is after the evidence cutoff and excluded. Sources: [27].

original.title: Revealing secret investigative methods helps future offenders avoid detection.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 Revealing secret investigative methods helps future offenders avoid detection.

  • Because Existing public-records law allows withholding information that “would disclose techniques and procedures for law enforcement investigations or prosecutions” [23]. These files contain such information: a court described “collection methods, analysis of investigative information, sensitive file numbers, types and timing of investigations, information about targets, dates, and the scope of surveillance” [24].
  • Because The bill's investigation exception is limited to an “active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution” [1]. Its national-security exception covers information that is “in fact properly classified” [1]. It provides no separate exception for unclassified methods whose release would help offenders evade future investigations.
  • Because The court accepted a concrete risk from these records: “releasing investigative techniques could help criminals evade the law, employ countermeasures, and avoid criminal activities in a particular area to evade detection.” [24]
  • So The bill removes protection for methods whose usefulness extends beyond the current case. Helping future offenders avoid detection weakens protection for people vulnerable to exploitation, giving [NAME] a further reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The Act allows temporary narrowly tailored withholding where release would jeopardize an active federal investigation. On November 14, 2025, the Attorney General said she assigned an Epstein-related inquiry to Jay Clayton. Sources: [1], [28].

Evidence note: Courts have recognized a qualified law-enforcement privilege that can apply after an investigation ends, and statutes are read with a presumption retaining established principles unless a contrary purpose is evident. No packet source shows that privilege being applied under the Act. DOJ’s protocol lists deliberative-process, work-product and attorney-client privileges. Sources: [29], [30], [31], [20].

original.title: It helps [NAME] understand survivors across differences in background and experience.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps [NAME] understand survivors across differences in background and experience.

  • Because The investigative material the bill would open includes “FBI summaries of witness interviews” [3].
  • Because Those witnesses include survivors. Annie Farmer recalled that the FBI “finally interviewed us, and asked us both to be witnesses against Epstein.” [4]
  • Because Some survivors faced poverty and unstable housing. Reporter Julie Brown explained: “some of them lived in foster homes. Several of them were one step away from homeless, if not truly homeless.” [5]
  • Because Their differences also include religion, race, and politics. Survivor Danielle Bensky said: “We have different religions. We are different races, different creeds, different ethnicities. We have different political affiliations.” [4]
  • Because Brown described officials who “treated them as prostitutes, and never fully understood that they were victims.” [6]
  • Because Survivors tied release to whether their accounts had been heard. Liz Stein said: “We have told our stories over and over and over. Now it's time to see who was listening.” [4]
  • Because The bill allows removing victims’ identifying details from released records, covering portions that “contain personally identifiable information of victims” [2].
  • So Making these accounts available responds to survivors’ challenge about who was listening and gives [NAME] a way to understand their experiences beyond dismissive labels. [NAME]’s wish to listen to and understand different people supports that access.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A federal judge’s guidelines on trial use of FD-302s say a 302 is an agent’s notes, “is not presumed to be a verbatim transcript,” and may differ by how much detail an agent includes and whether it includes “facts learned elsewhere as part of the investigation or editorial content.” Those guidelines address hearsay and impeachment at trial, not public reading. The bill permits withholding victims’ personal and medical files and similar files. Bensky and Stein’s cited statements were public before the vote. Sources: [7], [2], [4].

retirement.reason: Editorial issue HR4405_UNT_support_02. The argument runs from release to help-seeking to compassionate support. Calling survivors people with different experiences and counseling an opportunity to be heard does not show a connection to understanding or accepting people across relevant differences. Care and emotional support alone do not supply it. This is a value-fit defect, not a demand for an observed future effect. Remove from Tolerance as written, without moving it to another value or recasting help-seeking as acceptance across differences.
