  • Because A comparison of keeping and losing the larger credits links their loss to “lower revenue for health care providers and fewer services rendered” and an “increase in uncompensated care sought by the uninsured”. Uncompensated care means care for which providers are not paid. [9]
  • Because Revenue losses at rural hospitals “could force hospitals to reduce costs by eliminating services that would affect all members of their community.” [10]
  • Because Small rural hospitals “are called upon to respond to a wide range of emergency situations in their communities”. Their emergency plans cover natural disasters and “Terrorism and bioterrorism events – bombings, use of biological agents such as anthrax”. [11]
  • So Supporting payments for care helps preserve hospitals and services that emergency responders need. That protects the country’s response capacity during disasters and attacks, including care for residents with other insurance.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The rural hospital estimate assumes 4.8 million more people uninsured in 2026. CBO, assuming January 2026 enactment, projects 0.1 million more insured in 2026 and 3.0 and 4.0 million in 2027 and 2028. Sources do not identify which emergency services would change. Sources: [10], [2].

original.title: Broader coverage strengthens the country’s response to the opioid crisis.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Broader coverage strengthens the country’s response to the opioid crisis.

  • Because Marketplace plans must “offer substance use disorders benefits at parity with medical and surgical benefits”, meaning comparable insurance protections for addiction treatment. [6]
  • Because Insurance helps people reach treatment. A study identifies “Financial barriers such as lack of insurance coverage” as an obstacle. In its long-term study of Baltimore residents who injected drugs, private insurance “was associated with receipt of buprenorphine and having a regular source of medical care.” Buprenorphine is a medicine for opioid addiction. [7]
  • Because Medicines for opioid addiction, including buprenorphine, have “proven effectiveness at reducing mortality risks.” [12]
  • Because An earlier ACA study, covering states with and without Medicaid expansion, found: “Areas with higher uninsurance rates prior to the ACA saw larger reductions in opioid-related ED visits after the ACA took effect.” These are emergency department visits; the study found the effect emerged over several years. [8]
  • Because The national health-security strategy identifies substance use disorder as a challenge to communities’ ability to withstand crises and states: “Community resilience plays a significant role in national health security.” [13]
  • So Making treatment coverage more affordable strengthens the response to a deadly drug threat and supports communities’ ability to withstand further emergencies. Both serve [NAME]’s concern for a secure country.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The COVID testing study measures insurance at the time of interview and warns that observational studies cannot prove causality. The pandemic paper models universal coverage eliminating patient costs. The addiction-benefit paper did not assess effects on treatment use. The Baltimore study notes that income changes can affect both insurance eligibility and treatment use. The emergency-department study covers the broader 2014 ACA expansions, including Medicaid. Sources: [5], [4], [6], [7], [8].

original.title: Better access to care helps preserve the workforce the country depends on.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 Better access to care helps preserve the workforce the country depends on.

  • Because Research on the larger credits describes improved access to care, including “primary and preventive care visits”, which “can both help prevent and manage costly chronic diseases.” Chronic diseases are long-lasting illnesses. [14]
  • Because These illnesses affect the wider economy. CDC researchers identify “lost productivity in the workforce” among their burdens. [15]
  • So Supporting care that prevents and manages illness helps preserve people’s ability to work. That supports the country’s ability to produce goods and provide services, strengthening its stability.

original.title: Maintaining health-care spending supports jobs, economic stability, and public services.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 Maintaining health-care spending supports jobs, economic stability, and public services.

  • Because Coverage losses cut provider income: “Health care providers that lose revenue must reduce how much they can spend on their staff and goods purchased from vendors”. [16]
  • Because The effects spread beyond health care: “Reductions in labor expenses mean that some jobs are lost and some staff may be paid less. Thus, staff must restrict their purchases of consumer goods”. [16]
  • So Restoring the credits supports payments to providers, workers, and suppliers, reducing a source of economic disruption across the country.
  • Because Falling incomes also weaken public finances: “The combined reductions in individual and business incomes inevitably lead to lower state and local tax revenues.” [16]
  • Because The resulting budget pressure hinders public services: “This means that state and local governments will have more difficulties balancing their budgets and paying for health, human service, and other government functions.” [16]
  • So Supporting employment and incomes also protects the revenue governments use to serve residents. This chain supports both national stability and the state’s capacity to protect its people.
original.con_html:
Response The spending study does not establish that the bill preserves jobs and tax revenue across the country, rather than supporting a particular flow of spending.

  • Because It uses the “IMPLAN economic modeling system” [16]. USDA’s guidance warns: “Results of the analysis, whether output or jobs, should not be reported as net, new, or additional.” [17] Jobs supported by spending are not a count of jobs the country would otherwise lose.
  • So The model’s provider, supplier, and worker spending chains do not establish the claimed national employment and tax gains from this bill. The further claim about protecting public services rests on those unestablished gains. This does not deny that the affected providers and workers would receive the payments.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The jobs study's spending assumptions were aligned with the cost of extending the credits and reversing other changes in 2026, so its comparison does not isolate H.R.1834. Sources: [16].

original.title: Lower premium bills support household spending and economic stability.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 Lower premium bills support household spending and economic stability.

  • Because An analysis of the credits’ expiration links higher insurance bills for people who stay covered to less spending elsewhere: “This reduces their ability to purchase other goods and services, further dampening state economies.” [16]
  • So By lowering premiums for eligible policyholders, the bill preserves money for other purchases. That supports households and the businesses that depend on their spending, strengthening economic stability across the country.
original.con_html:
Response More purchasing power for policyholders does not by itself establish a more stable national economy.

  • Because The model’s own guidance says: “Input-Output models do not account for general equilibrium effects such as offsetting gains or losses in other Industries or geographies or the diversion of funds from other projects.” [18] These are changes elsewhere when money and work shift between uses.
  • So Policyholders do keep more money for other purchases. Following that purchasing power alone leaves out the changes needed to establish the claimed national effect.

original.title: Federal premium help reduces pressure to divert limited state funds to replace it.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 Federal premium help reduces pressure to divert limited state funds to replace it.

  • Because Connecticut committed its own money to replace lost federal help before the January vote: “Connecticut allocated an additional $51 million after a November 2025 special legislative session”. [19]
  • Because Filling that gap competes with other health protection. California and Colorado shifted state subsidies away from reducing deductibles and copayments to reducing premiums: “switching from a program that lowered out-of-pocket cost sharing (by reducing or eliminating deductibles and copayments) to one that lowers monthly premiums to help people purchase and maintain comprehensive coverage.” [19]
  • So Restoring federal help meets more of that premium need and reduces pressure on states to fund replacements. That protects states’ ability to use limited health funds for other needs, serving [NAME]’s concern for a capable state.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The April 2026 report says seven states modified their subsidy programs in response and that the new state investments were for 2026 only. It also reports Massachusetts adding $250 million. Connecticut's allocation came after a November 2025 session. Sources: [19].

original.title: A more affordable insurance system outside work helps the country withstand economic downturns.
original.pro_html:
Point 8 A more affordable insurance system outside work helps the country withstand economic downturns.

  • Because Job losses can remove health protection: “Because insurance coverage in the U.S. is closely tied to employment, economic downturns pose a serious threat to Americans’ access to affordable health care.” [20]
  • Because People losing job-based coverage can use the Marketplace outside its yearly enrollment window. CMS explains: “You’ll have 60 days to enroll in a Marketplace plan from the time your coverage ends, which may or may not be the last day of employment.” [21]
  • Because CBO projects lower prices before tax credits for the plans used to set subsidy amounts in 2027–2029 because “on average, the people who enroll in the marketplaces would be healthier than would be the case” without the extension. [2]
  • Because This wider sharing of medical costs benefits people without subsidies too: “Even those not eligible for PTCs see lower premiums with enhanced PTCs because the additional enrollment has improved the nongroup market risk pool.” PTCs are premium tax credits; a risk pool is the group whose medical costs insurance shares. [22]
  • So The bill makes an available route to coverage outside work more affordable, through larger credits and lower insurance prices. That helps the country absorb job losses without also losing as much health protection, strengthening its ability to withstand economic shocks.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO substitutes lower prices and higher enrollment for evidence of fewer coverage gaps when people lose jobs.

  • Because CBO’s forecast of lower prices in 2027–2029 rests on the expectation that “on average, the people who enroll in the marketplaces would be healthier than would be the case” [2] without the extension. That is a forecast about the mix of enrollees, not coverage transitions during a downturn.
  • Because Research on the earlier ACA using 2014–2019 data found that “the risk of losing insurance remained virtually unchanged with the introduction of the landmark ACA.” [23] It draws the distinction explicitly: “These results underscore how policies that increase the share of people with insurance at a point in time do not necessarily increase the stability and certainty associated with having insurance.” [23] It studies the earlier ACA, not the enhanced credits.
  • So A price and enrollment forecast cannot substitute for evidence about keeping or quickly replacing coverage after job loss. The closest evidence cited here does not show that subsidized Marketplace access reduced that risk.

original.title: The added debt puts more pressure on funding for defense and emergencies.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 The added debt puts more pressure on funding for defense and emergencies.

  • Because More debt raises the government's exposure to interest costs: “the larger debt is, the more an increase in interest rates raises debt-service costs.” [24]
  • Because CBO connects debt to limits on national protection: “Lawmakers might feel constrained from using federal tax and spending policies to respond to unforeseen events or for other purposes, such as to promote economic activity or strengthen national defense.” [24]
  • Because CBO also warns of harm to the U.S. role abroad if lawmakers become “reluctant to increase spending to prepare for or respond to an international crisis” [24].
  • So The bill adds debt and interest demands that put defense and crisis response under greater budget pressure. Preserving the state's ability to prepare for threats and defend citizens gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added pressure.
original.notes_html: Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

original.title: The added borrowing increases exposure to a financial crisis that would threaten national stability.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 The added borrowing increases exposure to a financial crisis that would threaten national stability.

  • Because An August 2025 budget update from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget included the July budget law and new tariffs. It projected debt growing faster than national output: “Debt held by the public will rise from about 100 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ($30 trillion) today to 120 percent of GDP ($53 trillion) by 2035.” [25]
  • Because CBO explains the risk of that path: “The likelihood of a fiscal crisis would increase if federal debt continued to grow faster than GDP, because mounting debt could erode investors’ confidence in the U.S. government’s fiscal position.” [24]
  • Because A loss of confidence would raise interest rates and lower the value of existing government bonds. CBO says losses to banks and other investors “could be large enough to cause some financial institutions to fail.” [24]
  • Because The damage could spread as banks lend less: “such a crisis could spread globally as liquidity declined and financial institutions reduced their lending, leading to an economic contraction.” [24]
  • So The bill adds to the debt burden behind this crisis risk. Protecting the country against financial breakdown and economic disruption gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added exposure.
original.notes_html: Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

original.title: The added debt threatens financial tools the United States uses to protect its interests.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 The added debt threatens financial tools the United States uses to protect its interests.

  • Because Growing debt creates risks beyond a sudden crisis. CBO identifies “a gradual decline in the value of Treasury securities and other domestic assets, heightened expectations of inflation, and a loss of confidence in the U.S. dollar as the dominant international reserve currency.” [24] This includes the dollar's role as the main currency other countries hold in reserve.
  • Because CBO explains the funding consequence: “Such developments would make it more difficult to finance public and private activity.” [24]
  • Because The national security strategy calls U.S. financial markets “pillars of American influence that afford policymakers significant leverage and tools to advance America’s national security priorities.” [27]
  • So Adding debt adds risks to stable funding and financial influence that support U.S. security. [NAME]'s concern for a strong, secure country gives a reason to oppose those risks.
original.notes_html: Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

original.title: The added borrowing competes with investment that supports military strength.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 The added borrowing competes with investment that supports military strength.

  • Because CBO explains the mechanism: “The increased federal borrowing associated with larger amounts of debt reduces the resources available for private investment.” [24]
  • Because Less investment weakens production over time: “That reduction in private investment would slow economic growth.” [24]
  • Because The national security strategy calls the economy “the necessary foundation of our military.” [27]
  • So The bill's borrowing puts pressure on investment and production that sustain national defense. Protecting that economic foundation gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html: Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

original.title: Interest paid abroad reduces the national income available to sustain U.S. strength.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 Interest paid abroad reduces the national income available to sustain U.S. strength.

  • Because CBO identifies a separate cost of growing debt: “Rising interest costs associated with federal debt would drive up interest payments to foreign holders of that debt and thus decrease national income.” [24]
  • Because The national security strategy identifies the economy as a source of resources for security: it “generates wealth we can invest in strategic interests” [27].
  • So Added borrowing carries an income cost through interest paid abroad, beyond its effect on domestic investment. Retaining national resources that support the country's strength gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that cost.
original.notes_html: Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

original.title: The larger subsidies put more public money within reach of organized fraud.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 The larger subsidies put more public money within reach of organized fraud.

  • Because The enhanced credits expand fully paid coverage for eligible low-income households: “The reduction in applicable percentages allows households with incomes between 100% and 150% of FPL to receive full subsidies, reducing consumers' premium contributions to zero dollars.” [28] FPL means the federal poverty level.
  • Because CMS links this feature to abuse: “the widespread availability of $0 premium plans created the incentive and opportunity for fraudulent and improper enrollments at scale” [29].
  • Because Income-check gaps remained in the rules for 2026. CMS explained that a planned check was paused: “Income DMIs will not be opened for applicants when the Marketplace attempts to verify an applicant’s attested projected annual household income with the IRS, but the IRS returns no tax data.” [30] That means missing tax records would not trigger this extra income check.
  • Because A November 2025 conviction shows an actual loss from organized enrollment fraud. The Justice Department reported a scheme seeking “over $233 million in fraudulent ACA plan subsidies for which the federal government paid at least $180 million.” [31]
  • So Restoring larger subsidies expands the money and incentives exposed to a proven fraud mechanism. A strong state must keep public resources from financing crime. [NAME] therefore has a reason to oppose this added exposure.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO carries an older fraud warning into 2026 without separating larger credits from a monthly signup route that had ended.

  • Because The agency running the federal insurance Marketplace (CMS) links abuse to repeated signups: “By fully subsidizing the premium for these plans, individuals could be enrolled into these plans once every month through a special enrollment period (SEP) by predatory agents and brokers without the individual's knowledge.” [29]
  • Because Before the vote, CMS listed “Removal of Monthly Special Enrollment Period (SEP)” [30] among the rules already in force. This was the signup route for people with income at or below 150 percent of the federal poverty level.
  • Because The 2025 law also bars tax credits for special signups based on income alone from 2026. Congress's research service describes the bar on “an SEP on the basis of expected household income” [32] that is “not connected to a change in circumstances specified by the HHS Secretary.” [32] It “applies to plan years beginning after December 31, 2025.” [32]
  • Because H.R.1834 extends the credit rules. Its credit changes concern “Extension of Rules To Increase Premium Assistance Amounts” [1] and “Extension of Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [1].
  • So Extending the credit amounts does not reopen that route. A past theft and larger lawful payments do not establish extra money reaching criminals under those rules. This response does not answer the PRO’s point that an income check was paused for 2026.
original.notes_html:
Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

Evidence note: KFF analysis finds that almost all (98%) adults who qualified for a free silver plan with enhanced credits would still qualify for a free bronze plan without them. CMS estimates that about 200,000 consumers had a desired plan changed without consent in 2025, after the July 2024 control. CMS says it worked with issuers to restore those selections. Sources: [33], [34].

original.title: Expanding fully paid plans makes unauthorized enrollment harder to notice and exposes citizens to disrupted care.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 Expanding fully paid plans makes unauthorized enrollment harder to notice and exposes citizens to disrupted care.

  • Because CMS explains how fully paid plans conceal unauthorized signups: “Because these enrollees do not receive a monthly premium bill requiring action on their part, they may not be aware they are enrolled.” [29]
  • Because A planned $5 charge on automatic renewal had been paused before the January vote. CMS stated: “Qualifying consumers will continue to be automatically re-enrolled with no premium responsibility following application of Advance Payments of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC).” [30]
  • Because GAO documented the scale of reported unauthorized signups and switches: CMS received “approximately 275,000 complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35]
  • Because GAO explains that these practices can cause “loss of access to medical providers and medications” [35]. The November 2025 conviction also established harm: “some of these consumers experienced serious disruptions in their medical care and often lost their prior insurance coverage under Medicaid or other programs.” [31]
  • So By expanding plans that hide unauthorized enrollment, the bill increases exposure to organized abuse that can interrupt care. Protecting citizens from that threat through a reliable national insurance system gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.con_html:
Response The complaint history does not establish added hidden enrollment or disrupted care from this extension under the consent controls already in place.

  • Because CMS changed controls for existing coverage on the federal Marketplace: “Beginning July 19, 2024, CMS began blocking agents and brokers from making changes to a consumer’s FFM enrollment unless the agent or broker is already associated with the consumer’s enrollment.” [36]
  • Because CMS provides a way for a new broker to act with the consumer's involvement: “the consumer must conduct a three-way call with the Marketplace Call Center” [36].
  • Because Congress's audit agency, GAO, combines “complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.” [35] That period includes months before these controls began.
  • So The control acts before an unassociated broker can switch existing coverage; it does not depend on a premium bill exposing the switch afterward. The complaint total mixes initial enrollments and switches across different safeguards. It does not establish added harmful switches from this extension under the rules in force on January 8. This response concerns switches of existing coverage; it does not address new unauthorized enrollments.
original.notes_html:
Brief context note: CBO's warnings concern the government's total long-term debt, and CBO says crisis risk depends on more than the amount of debt and that it cannot reliably quantify the probability. CBO scores this bill at $80.582 billion in added deficits over 2026–2035, with most of it in 2026–2029. CRFB projects public debt of $53 trillion by 2035 without this bill. Federal Reserve researchers tie the dollar's role also to the U.S. economy's size and strength, its openness and the rule of law. Sources: [24], [2], [25], [26].

Evidence note: KFF analysis finds that almost all (98%) adults who qualified for a free silver plan with enhanced credits would still qualify for a free bronze plan without them. CMS estimates that about 200,000 consumers had a desired plan changed without consent in 2025, after the July 2024 control. CMS says it worked with issuers to restore those selections. Sources: [33], [34].

catalog.retirement_reason: Access to care for poor and sick people is the substantive benefit. Religious endorsement does not create a distinct Tradition reason.

original.title: It puts the inherited Christian duty to care for sick and poor neighbors into practice.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It puts the inherited Christian duty to care for sick and poor neighbors into practice.

  • Because The Southern Baptist confession teaches: “We should work to provide for the orphaned, the needy, the abused, the aged, the helpless, and the sick.” [3]
  • Because The National Association of Evangelicals applies that duty to public funding: “Adequate funding for food, shelter and health care should be maintained so that those who cannot care for their families and themselves receive the support they need.” [4]
  • Because The larger credits bring coverage within reach of low-income households: “With the enhanced subsidies, most enrollees at the lowest income level — under 150 percent of poverty — pay little or nothing for their plan.” [5]
  • Because Coverage helps people receive care: “health insurance is essential to getting timely health care in the United States” [5].
  • So Restoring this help carries an established Christian duty into public policy, giving [NAME] a reason grounded in following religious tradition.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The premium tax credit itself continues without the bill; only the enhancements lapse. The U.S. Catholic bishops' October 2025 letter urges Congress to extend the enhanced credits while barring their use for plans covering elective abortion. H.R.1834 extends them without that bar. Sources: [6], [7], [2].
original.retirement_reason: Access to care for poor and sick people is the substantive benefit. Religious endorsement does not create a distinct Tradition reason.

catalog.retirement_reason: Maternal and prenatal health are the substantive benefits; this argument does not connect them to continuing a particular religious observance or family custom.

original.title: It helps families practice the Christian duty to protect life before and after birth.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps families practice the Christian duty to protect life before and after birth.

  • Because The coverage made more affordable includes care during pregnancy and after birth: “Maternity care and newborn care — services provided before and after a child is born — are essential health benefits.” [8]
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession teaches: “We should speak on behalf of the unborn and contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death.” [3]
  • So Making this coverage easier to keep helps families obtain care for mothers and babies, putting their inherited belief in the protection of life into practice.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: All qualified health plans must cover maternity and newborn care under either option, and Medicaid pays for nearly half of U.S. births. Sources: [8].
original.retirement_reason: Maternal and prenatal health are the substantive benefits; this argument does not connect them to continuing a particular religious observance or family custom.

original.title: It lowers a cost of keeping a mother at home for children’s religious upbringing.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It lowers a cost of keeping a mother at home for children’s religious upbringing.

  • Because Insurance costs compete with household needs. An enrollee warned that losing the larger credits would mean “digging into basic necessities, like, food, car, gas, rent.” [9]
  • Because Caring for children at home is a practice the religious right values: “Focus on the Family has always taken pains to express and provide support for mothers who choose to stay home with their young children.” [10]
  • Because Focus on the Family connects that role to passing on faith: “God created us to have relationship with Him. The most effective place for us to learn that is not at church — it’s at home!” [11]
  • So For eligible families using ACA insurance on one wage, the bill lowers the cost of keeping a mother at home to care for children and teach the faith.

original.title: It reduces a loss of insurance help that marriage can trigger at the income cutoff.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It reduces a loss of insurance help that marriage can trigger at the income cutoff.

  • Because The income cutoff can penalize two people who qualify separately but cross the married cutoff when their incomes combine. Heritage explains that “the FPL for a couple is less than twice that for a single person” [12]. FPL means the poverty line used to set the cutoff.
  • Because The bill extends the “Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” [2].
  • So For otherwise eligible couples whose insurance costs qualify for help above that limit, marrying no longer causes all aid to disappear merely because their combined income crosses it.
  • Because The comparison must also count what the couple would receive unmarried. Consider two childless adults, each with $46,950 in annual income counted for the credit: 300% of the “$15,650” [13] one-person amount. Married, their $93,900 is 443% of the “$21,150” [13] two-person amount, above the cutoff. Hold their plans fixed, with benchmark premiums totaling $20,000 a year. Under ordinary 2026 credits, the table reads “At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” [14], so they pay about $9,352 unmarried and the full $20,000 married: a $10,648 cost of marrying. Under the restored schedule, “300 | 0.0600” [15] means about $5,634 unmarried, and “400 or more | 0.0850” [15] means about $7,982 married: a $2,348 cost. For this couple the bill lowers the cost of marrying by about $8,300.
  • Because Evangelical teaching opposes “creating economic disincentives to marriage.” [4]
  • So Reducing this financial obstacle for such couples supports the traditional practice of marriage.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that premium credits can produce both marriage penalties and bonuses. Under the bill, the cost of marrying falls for some couples crossing the income cutoff (support point 4's example: about $8,300 lower) and rises for some couples below it (oppose point 9's example: about $1,729 higher). Both examples rest on stated assumptions. Sources: [16], [14], [15].

catalog.retirement_reason: Helping relatives care for elderly people is a general care justification here; no particular inherited arrangement or observance supplies an additional premise.

original.title: It helps families fulfill the biblical duty to honor aging parents.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It helps families fulfill the biblical duty to honor aging parents.

  • Because Removing the income cutoff particularly helps older people who rely on ACA insurance: “The cliff—and therefore this disparate treatment—falls disproportionately on older people, those in high-premium areas (which are heavily rural areas), and small business owners.” [17]
  • Because Focus on the Family explains the duty this way: “Honor implies choosing to give great respect and care to our elders” [18].
  • Because That care includes material help: “This might mean sharing your home and offering financial support.” [18]
  • So Lower insurance bills for these parents reduce the cost they and their families must meet, helping families carry out the inherited duty to honor and care for them.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Focus on the Family names financial support as one possible way to honor a parent and also says, 'There is no verse in Scripture that obligates you to take aging parents into your home or cancel your vacation plans to pay for their prescriptions.' The cliff source identifies older buyers as an age group and does not report how often their children help with these costs. Sources: [18], [17].
original.retirement_reason: Helping relatives care for elderly people is a general care justification here; no particular inherited arrangement or observance supplies an additional premise.

original.title: It supports church giving and paid ministry, helping congregations continue worship and teaching.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It supports church giving and paid ministry, helping congregations continue worship and teaching.

  • Because Small churches use ACA coverage for staff: “Among the most affected are small congregations that usually can’t afford group plans and instead provide salary stipends to staff members for use in the ACA Marketplace” [19].
  • Because A Christian clergy relief fund tied its proposed emergency aid to the larger credits: “If Congress renews the subsidies at the 2025 levels, the program will not move forward.” [20]
  • So Restoring those credits eases the strain on pastoral families and churches that help pay their insurance costs.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession makes regular giving a religious duty: “According to the Scriptures, Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.” [3]
  • Because Higher insurance bills also squeeze giving. A pastor reported: “Riverside Church is projecting 20% attendance growth but flat giving for 2026 as more dollars go to health insurance instead of tithing” [19].
  • So Lower bills leave members more room to continue customary giving and support their congregation.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession says Sunday observance should include “exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.” [3]
  • So Easing these pressures on church budgets helps sustain the clergy, worship, and teaching through which congregations practice and pass on their faith.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The clergy relief fund's program is a one-time $2,500 stipend for up to 1,000 clergy. The Riverside Church figure is one congregation's forecast of 20% attendance growth with flat giving for 2026. Sources: [20], [19].

original.title: It helps Christian health ministries continue their healing work.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It helps Christian health ministries continue their healing work.

  • Because The Catholic Health Association links lost coverage to unpaid care: “the loss of coverage would put additional stress on local health care providers as they face more uncompensated care and bad debt.” [21] These are bills providers do not collect.
  • Because Church clinics also face added demand for free care. Reporting from Bread of Healing at Cross Lutheran Church explains: “They are bracing for higher demand as more residents are expected to forgo insurance as a crucial tax credit is set to expire and premiums spike.” [22]
  • Because Catholic providers identify care for those in need as their religious mission: “Our health ministry is especially committed to serving those most in need, recognizing that our mission is not complete until quality, affordable, and accessible health care is a reality for all.” [21]
  • So Keeping more patients insured eases unpaid bills and the added demand for free care, helping Christian institutions carry on an established ministry.

original.title: It reduces financial pressure to give up inherited family farms and rural ways of life.
original.pro_html:
Point 8 It reduces financial pressure to give up inherited family farms and rural ways of life.

  • Because Minnesota Farmers Union warned that higher insurance costs were “forcing some to choose between buying health insurance, making their operating loan payments or in some cases, putting food on the table” [23].
  • Because In a 2003 statement on agriculture, U.S. Catholic bishops identify the threatened inheritance: “They are about a way of life for farm families in the United States who are unable to meet debt payments and face selling a farm that has been in the family for generations.” [24]
  • Because The bishops defend preserving this life: “We stand with farmers, particularly those who own small and family farms here and abroad, in their struggle to live with dignity, to preserve a way of life, and to strengthen rural communities.” [24]
  • So Lower insurance costs leave farm families more money to meet farm debts, helping them keep the land and work through which they pass on family and rural customs.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The bishops' statement on family farms dates from November 2003 and concerns farm debt, not insurance. The Minnesota Farmers Union statement is from October 2025 and refers to independent family farmers generally. Sources: [24], [23].

original.title: It makes plans covering a practice rejected by the religious rule against abortion easier to buy.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It makes plans covering a practice rejected by the religious rule against abortion easier to buy.

  • Because Some states have “laws that require all fully-insured group plans and individual plans (including Marketplace plans) to include abortion coverage.” [25]
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession directs believers to “speak on behalf of the unborn and contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death” [26].
  • So Larger credits lower the price of entering plans with abortion benefits. For [NAME], continuing the particular religious rule against abortion supplies a reason to oppose making coverage of that practice easier to obtain. This justification concerns that religious observance, rather than a general appeal to protect vulnerable life.
  • Note Federal credits cannot pay the abortion portion of the premium beyond the rape, incest, and life-endangerment exceptions: “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” [25] The objection concerns cheaper entry into plans that include those benefits.

original.title: It increases public payments to plans that religious teaching tells taxpayers not to support.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It increases public payments to plans that religious teaching tells taxpayers not to support.

  • Because The Catholic bishops object to paying for the plan itself: “federal taxpayer dollars are still paying for the plans that cover abortion” [27]. Their October 2025 letter asks Congress to pair extension with a limit: “We urge Congress to extend the enhanced PTCs while amending all PTCs to disallow their being used for plans that cover elective abortion.” [7] H.R.1834 contains no such limit.
  • Because The Southern Baptist public-policy commission says “no taxpayer’s conscience should be violated by being forced—even indirectly—to pay for abortions.” [26]
  • So Larger credits increase public support for the plans these religious bodies reject. Preserving their rule against indirect support gives [NAME] a reason to oppose those added payments, regardless of whether abortion numbers rise.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The premium tax credit itself continues without the bill; only the enhancements lapse. The U.S. Catholic bishops' October 2025 letter urges Congress to extend the enhanced credits while barring their use for plans covering elective abortion. H.R.1834 extends them without that bar. Sources: [6], [7], [2].

original.title: It increases the financial pressure to accept a personal payment for abortion coverage.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It increases the financial pressure to accept a personal payment for abortion coverage.

  • Because Plans covering abortions beyond those exceptions must collect an abortion-coverage payment of “at least $1 per enrollee per month” [28] and “deposit these separate payments into segregated accounts” [28].
  • Because Where state law requires Marketplace plans to cover abortion, buying one includes that payment. KFF describes the mandate as covering “individual plans (including Marketplace plans)” [25].
  • Because Christian health-sharing ministries state the religious concern as getting care “without being forced to fund procedures or drugs that violate their conscience.” [29]
  • So Where every Marketplace option includes this charge, refusing it means giving up Marketplace aid. The bill increases the aid a believer must forgo. Preserving the practice of refusing payments that violate religious teaching gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that pressure.
original.con_html:
Response A state coverage mandate alone does not establish that an objecting buyer has no subsidized plan without elective abortion coverage.

  • Because Washington law says, “No individual or organization with a religious or moral tenet opposed to a specific service may be required to purchase coverage for that service or services if they object to doing so for reason of conscience or religion.” [30]
  • Because A 2023 survey of Marketplace plans identifies an actual exception: “Oregon, one of the states requiring that abortion be covered, has granted an exemption to plans sponsored by religious health systems.” [31]
  • So The PRO must establish its no-acceptable-plan condition for the relevant buyer and coverage year. A count of states with mandates does not establish that condition. These examples do not show that every buyer has an acceptable option.

original.title: It broadens access to plans with gender-transition benefits that traditional Christian teaching opposes.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It broadens access to plans with gender-transition benefits that traditional Christian teaching opposes.

  • Because Washington’s required benefits still include this care: its benchmark plan “requires individual and small group health plans to cover gender-affirming treatment.” [32]
  • Because Southern Baptists teach that “gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [33] and declare that “we oppose efforts to alter one’s bodily identity” [33].
  • So Cheaper enrollment opens access to these plans’ transition benefits. Maintaining this religious understanding of sex gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
  • Note The 2026 federal rule shifts the excluded benefit’s cost to the state: “the state is required to defray the cost of the benefit.” [32] Washington appropriated money “so that the benefit can continue to be offered.” [32] Larger federal credits still make the plan carrying that state-funded benefit easier to buy.

catalog.retirement_reason: The stated objection is protection of embryonic life, rather than the distinct marital-conception rule in the next point. Religious endorsement of protection alone is insufficient.

original.title: It widens access to IVF practices that endanger embryos protected by the tradition.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It widens access to IVF practices that endanger embryos protected by the tradition.

  • Because Illinois includes in vitro fertilization (IVF), fertilizing eggs outside the body, in its required individual-plan benefits: “IVF and other fertility treatments are covered on individual and small-group plans” [34].
  • Because IVF can leave embryos frozen in storage. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine describes a route to their destruction: “Facilities may dispose of unclaimed embryos by removing them from storage and thawing without transfer.” [35]
  • Because Southern Baptists teach that human beings deserve protection “from the moment of fertilization until natural death” [36] and object to the “continued freezing, stockpiling, and ultimate destruction of human embryos” [36].
  • So Larger credits make coverage of IVF easier to obtain, widening access to practices that expose embryos to this danger. Following the inherited duty to protect embryonic life gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].
original.retirement_reason: The stated objection is protection of embryonic life, rather than the distinct marital-conception rule in the next point. Religious endorsement of protection alone is insufficient.

original.title: It widens access to IVF that Catholic tradition rejects for replacing the spouses’ sexual union.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It widens access to IVF that Catholic tradition rejects for replacing the spouses’ sexual union.

  • Because The Illinois Marketplace benefits described above include IVF: “IVF and other fertility treatments are covered on individual and small-group plans” [34].
  • Because The Catholic bishops describe IVF as “joining egg and sperm in a glass dish, not in the mother’s body” [39].
  • Because Their teaching draws the moral line at replacing the marital act: “procedures that assist the marital act in being procreative are morally acceptable, while those that substitute for it are not.” [39]
  • So Cheaper access to IVF expands access to a substitute for marital intercourse. Preserving this Catholic teaching on how spouses should conceive children gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose the bill, apart from embryo destruction.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].

original.title: It expands access to contraception rejected by traditional Catholic teaching on marriage.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It expands access to contraception rejected by traditional Catholic teaching on marriage.

  • Because Most private plans must “cover, without any cost sharing, the full range of FDA-approved contraceptives and services” [40]. Covered birth control therefore comes without a separate patient charge under the rule.
  • Because The Catholic bishops teach that “every act of intercourse must remain open to life and that contraception is objectively immoral.” [41]
  • So Larger credits expand access to plans with these benefits. Within Catholic traditionalism, maintaining this teaching about married sex gives [NAME] a reason to oppose widening access to contraception for preventing pregnancy.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].

original.title: It gives Marketplace insurance a larger price advantage over Christian mutual aid.
original.pro_html:
Point 8 It gives Marketplace insurance a larger price advantage over Christian mutual aid.

  • Because The credits pay for “health insurance obtained through the marketplaces established by the Affordable Care Act.” [1] Health care sharing ministries (HCSMs) fall outside that insurance system: “HCSMs are not health insurance” [42].
  • Because For eligible buyers, subsidies can make Marketplace coverage “significantly less expensive than an HCSM membership” [42].
  • Because These ministries practice religious mutual aid: “Members affirm shared faith commitments and contribute to each other’s medical bills, supported by prayer and mutual encouragement.” [29] Christian Healthcare Ministries links this practice to “the command of Galatians 6:2” [43].
  • So For households receiving larger credits, the bill cuts Marketplace payments while ministry dues receive no credit. This gives them a stronger financial reason to choose insurance instead of contributing through a ministry. Preserving the religious practice of sharing medical bills, giving, and prayer gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added incentive.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Baptist resolution permits reproductive technologies consistent with its affirmation, especially on the number of embryos generated. Catholic bioethics guidance allows some insurance payments under protest, given a proportionately serious reason, lack of suitable alternatives and ongoing opposition. Samaritan's rules recognize insurance payments alongside ministry membership. Sources: [36], [37], [38].

original.title: It increases the financial cost of marriage for some couples buying Marketplace insurance.
original.pro_html:
Point 9 It increases the financial cost of marriage for some couples buying Marketplace insurance.

  • Because Marriage combines the couple’s incomes for the credit. The law requires that “the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year.” [44]
  • Because For 2026 coverage in the 48 contiguous states, the poverty-line amounts used for credits are “$15,650” [13] for one person and “$21,150” [13] for two. Two married adults therefore face a lower poverty-line amount than two separate one-person tax households.
  • Because The ordinary 2026 premium-share table reads: “At least 250% but less than 300% 8.44% 9.96% At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” [14]. Thus the share is 8.44% at 250% of poverty and 9.96% at 369%.
  • Because The bill restores the enhanced schedule. Its IRS table gives “250 | 0.0400” [15] and “369 | 0.0773” [15]: shares of 4% and 7.73%. To find the income percentage, IRS instructions say to “drop any numbers after the decimal point.” [15]
  • So Consider two childless adults, each with $39,125 in annual income counted for the credit. Compare being unmarried throughout 2026 with being married throughout 2026. They are otherwise eligible all year. Hold their plans and full premiums fixed, with premiums high enough to receive credits. Separately, each is at 250% of poverty; married, their $78,250 is counted at 369%. Under ordinary 2026 credits, their combined annual premium share rises from about $6,604 to $7,794 when married—a $1,190 cost. Under the restored schedule, it rises from $3,130 to about $6,049—a $2,919 cost. The bill adds about $1,729 to this couple’s annual cost of being married rather than unmarried.
  • Because The Southern Baptist confession calls marriage “the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime” [45] and “the framework for intimate companionship, the channel of sexual expression according to biblical standards” [45].
  • So Maintaining this marriage tradition gives [NAME] a reason to oppose increasing the money such couples lose by marrying.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that premium credits can produce both marriage penalties and bonuses. Under the bill, the cost of marrying falls for some couples crossing the income cutoff (support point 4's example: about $8,300 lower) and rises for some couples below it (oppose point 9's example: about $1,729 higher). Both examples rest on stated assumptions. Sources: [16], [14], [15].

original.title: It protects female athletes’ access to team projects that remove pollution and improve waste practices.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It protects female athletes’ access to team projects that remove pollution and improve waste practices.

  • Because The bill would allow males to practice with female teams only if “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1].
  • Because Team membership provides an organized way to remove pollution. Fordham rower Caitlin Boyle reported: “In the cleanup, 50 of my teammates on Fordham Rowing assisted me with picking up trash along the shores and streets of City Island in bags and then disposing of the waste properly.” [4]
  • Because Those projects also spread knowledge: “Additionally, I held a presentation for the team educating them on basic environmental knowledge and the importance of proper waste management.” [4]
  • Because Teammates help launch wider efforts. Wisconsin rower Grace Latz said: “I started all of this because my teammates were taking similar classes to me and shared the same values, so it made it easier.” [5]
  • Because The recycling group Latz helped start reached other institutions: “Since then, REthink has expanded beyond the UW athletic department to work with the UW campus, the hospital, the Wisconsin unions, dining services and UW housing.” [5]
  • So Protecting female athletes’ places on teams that do this work protects their access to cleanup, environmental teaching and wider recycling campaigns. Preserving these ways to defend nature gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Boyle organized her City Island cleanup in partnership with the New York Department of Sanitation. REthink grew to about 60 members and worked with campus units beyond athletics. Sources: [4], [5].

Evidence note: At the comparison date the NCAA regulated transgender participation sport by sport, with a U.S. Rowing testosterone threshold listed for rowing. Rep. Bonamici told the House that about 10 of roughly 510,000 NCAA athletes were transgender. Sources: [2], [3], [6].

original.title: It protects female rowers’ time on the water, where seeing environmental harm prompts care and action.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects female rowers’ time on the water, where seeing environmental harm prompts care and action.

  • Because The bill’s safeguard for male practice also protects a female athlete’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • Because Rowing gives athletes firsthand knowledge of the waters they use. Wisconsin rower Alexandra Bogner said: “I’ve rowed on both Lake Mendota and Lake Monona and have been able to see the ecological challenges that they face” [7].
  • Because Seeing litter while rowing helped prompt Boyle’s research on school waste management: “Rowing on Long Island further inspired this thesis due to the plethora of trash that is floating around in the ocean.” [4]
  • Because Practice also gave Boyle chances to act: “For the past four years, I have tried to grab every piece of waste out of the ocean at practice that I can reach.” [4]
  • So Protecting female rowers against losing practice time keeps open a route from seeing pollution to removing litter and studying ways to reduce waste. That serves [NAME]’s wish to care for nature and protect it from pollution.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: At the comparison date the NCAA regulated transgender participation sport by sport, with a U.S. Rowing testosterone threshold listed for rowing. Rep. Bonamici told the House that about 10 of roughly 510,000 NCAA athletes were transgender. Sources: [2], [3], [6].

original.title: It protects female athletes’ access to scholarship support for environmental study.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects female athletes’ access to scholarship support for environmental study.

  • Because The bill would allow males to train or practice only if no female lost a “scholarship” [1].
  • Because Athletic aid supports students doing environmental work. Notre Dame described rower Anna Kottkamp as “an environmental science major” [8] who “went on to earn a full athletic scholarship.” [8]
  • Because Kottkamp was “an undergraduate research assistant for Jennifer Tank” [8], studying “the impact of cover crops on agricultural streams.” [8]
  • Because Tank’s research tests ways to protect water from pollution: “Her research combines the wide-scale planting of cover crops in winter with innovative drainage strategies that can reduce fertilizer runoff to streams and rivers.” [9]
  • So Protecting athletic aid for female students doing this work protects financial support for learning how to prevent water pollution. Supporting that way to protect nature gives [NAME] a further reason to favor the bill.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Kottkamp began as a walk-on without previous competitive rowing experience and later earned a full athletic scholarship. Her environmental education curriculum work took place during a 2013 Peru internship supported by a Kellogg Institute fellowship. Sources: [8].

Evidence note: At the comparison date the NCAA regulated transgender participation sport by sport, with a U.S. Rowing testosterone threshold listed for rowing. Rep. Bonamici told the House that about 10 of roughly 510,000 NCAA athletes were transgender. Sources: [2], [3], [6].

original.title: It removes women’s outdoor competition as a way to develop care for nature.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes women’s outdoor competition as a way to develop care for nature.

  • Because Women’s school teams compete in natural places. At a Malden River cleanup involving Tufts’ women’s rowing team, an athletics coordinator explained that “our rowing athletes train and compete on it almost every day.” [12]
  • Because On the comparison date, NCAA rules could admit transgender women to women’s teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2]
  • Because Outdoor activities can strengthen concern for the environment. In a study of teenagers at a 15-day outdoor camp, “Pairwise comparisons for affective beliefs revealed that scores for the experimental group increased after the intervention (p < .01), whereas scores for the control group underwent no significant change.” [13]
  • Because College sailing gives a concrete example of this link. Harvard describes a sailor’s drive to protect the environment: “It's that time in the water with her teammates that has driven Hogan-Lopez to learn more about the environment and how to protect it.” [14]
  • So The ban would remove women’s outdoor competition from the opportunities available to otherwise eligible transgender students. It would cut off competition’s time in nature and shared experiences as a way to build that care.
  • Note The exception allowing students to “train or practice” [1] does not restore access to competition.
  • So [NAME]’s concern for nature gives [NAME] a reason to preserve this way of developing care for it, and therefore to oppose the bill.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The camp study measured a 15-day programme with about 6-10 hours of activity daily, including trekking, biking, climbing and canoeing. It did not measure school racing. Sources: [13].

Evidence note: College sailing rules for fall 2024 listed open events for all genders, men's events for men or non-binary sailors, and women's events for women or non-binary sailors. H.R.28 restricts programs designated for women or girls, so open events remain, and it allows practice under stated conditions. Harvard's feature credits time on the water with teammates and does not separate racing from practice. Sources: [11], [15], [14].

original.title: It restricts posts for leading environmental work within women’s teams.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It restricts posts for leading environmental work within women’s teams.

  • Because Yale places environmental leaders within individual teams: “each participating varsity and club team has a sustainability captain. That person leads the efforts within their team and tailors the certification program to the schedule and structure of their team.” [16]
  • Because These posts include a “sustainability captain of the varsity women’s swimming and diving team” [16]. That captain described practical care for nature: “We volunteered together at a New Haven Land Trust garden last year and performed manual labor to prepare for spring planting.” [16]
  • Because On the comparison date, NCAA rules could admit transgender women to such teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2]
  • Because Team service also removes pollution and prompts sign-ups for further conservation work. At the Tufts cleanup, “Participants collected 33 bags of trash, which included 16 bags of sorted single use plastic bottles (over 1500 bottles)!” [17] and “many students signed up to continue to be involved with the Friends of the Malden River.” [17]
  • So A post for leading a women’s team’s environmental work is an opportunity tied to participation in that team and a way to bring teammates into practical care for nature.
  • Because The bill expressly reaches “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Note Its exception lets students “train or practice” [1]; it does not preserve a separate environmental leadership post within a women’s program.
  • So The bill would restrict access to these posts for otherwise eligible students it excludes from women’s programs. That cuts off a way for those students to organize practical care for nature.
  • So [NAME] values taking part in defending nature. Keeping these opportunities to lead environmental work open gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose the bill.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Tufts cleanup included about 20 athletes from men's and women's rowing and women's track and field, plus community volunteers. Sources: [17].

original.title: It protects women's fair chance to earn sporting wins and recognition.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It protects women's fair chance to earn sporting wins and recognition.

  • Because Male puberty builds strength: “increases in testosterone due to puberty promote muscular strength” [5].
  • Because A review of 24 studies of transgender women who were not athletes found that, after 12–36 months of hormone treatment, they likely retained a strength advantage over women who were not transgender: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5]
  • Because Strength matters in speed and power events: “In sports demanding speed and power, muscular strength and the ability to generate high rates of force are recognised as key determinant in athletic success.” [5]
  • So In strength-dependent events, the bill would keep retained male-puberty strength advantages out of the female category. Giving women a meaningful chance to earn sporting rewards serves [NAME]'s concern for equal opportunity and just treatment.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s evidence does not settle whether trained transgender women keep the advantage in speed and power events that its fairness claim needs.

  • Because Its review leaves the effects of hormone treatment in trained people unresolved: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [5]
  • Because The review does not report whether the compared groups had similar training: “The levels of physical activity of the transwomen compared with cisgender women in the studies were not reported.” [5] Here, cisgender women means women who are not transgender.
  • Because A 2024 cross-sectional study of athletes found mixed results. Compared with cisgender women athletes, transgender women athletes had “higher absolute handgrip strength” [6] but “lower relative jump height” [6].
  • So Strength retained by non-athletes does not establish an advantage in a speed or power event among trained athletes, and the one athlete study points in both directions. The authors say that study is not sufficient to guide policy. This response does not show that no advantage exists, and it does not address settings without hormone limits.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. CRS reports that some states and school districts allowed participation with no particular requirements or restrictions. Sources: [4], [7].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

original.title: It protects girls' places in sport and their chances to gain education, health, and leadership benefits.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects girls' places in sport and their chances to gain education, health, and leadership benefits.

  • Because Former college swimmer Paula Scanlan testified to actual lost places: “I know women who have lost roster spots and spots on the podium.” [10]
  • Because The bill allows male training or practice only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where places or sports aid are limited, the competition ban and the practice condition protect female athletes from losing them to male participants. For a girl who needs sports aid to attend college, protecting that aid preserves a route into education.
  • Because Girls in positive sports programs report better mental health. A 2024 study found: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because A 2024 survey of U.S. adults who had played girls' or women's sports found reported gains in leadership skills: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So Keeping a girl's place in a good program preserves her chance to gain these benefits. Protecting routes into education, well-being, and adult leadership serves [NAME]'s concern for equal opportunities in life.
original.con_html:
Response The place-protection reason depends on the fairness claim in reason 1; it does not independently show that reserving places advances equal opportunity.

  • Because The bill's practice exception requires that “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where a place is limited, the bill decides which student holds it. That shows who keeps the benefit, not that the allocation is fairer.
  • Because The mental-health finding concerns access to a good program: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because The leadership finding concerns benefits attributed to participation: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So These benefits follow whoever holds the place, so they do not resolve who has a fair claim to it. This reason adds to [NAME]’s equal-opportunity concern only so far as the fairness claim in reason 1 holds. This response does not dispute that some female athletes would keep places and their benefits under the bill.

original.title: It protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and the lost games that safety concerns can cause.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and the lost games that safety concerns can cause.

  • Because World Rugby links contact-sport risk to “the size, force- and power-producing advantages conferred by testosterone during puberty and adolescence, and the resultant player welfare risks this creates” [13].
  • Because Its review explains the danger to a smaller player: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.” [13]
  • Because World Rugby's review of 12 months of testosterone suppression concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.” [13]
  • So In school contact competition such as rugby, excluding male competitors who have gone through male puberty removes this source of size and force mismatch. That protects athletes who are less able to withstand those forces.
  • Because Safety concerns have also cost whole teams games. After Payton McNabb's 2022 volleyball injury, her school board voted “to forfeit the remaining varsity and junior varsity volleyball games against Highlands School” [14], which the report describes as “attended by the transgender player.” [14] The report states: “The board cited safety concerns for players.” [14] That player's status is unconfirmed: “It is not possible to verify this athlete was trans.” [15]
  • So Where covered competition would otherwise include male competitors, the bill also removes that reason for a school to withdraw its girls' team. Protecting athletes from added collision risks and removing that ground for forfeits serves [NAME]'s concern for the weak and vulnerable, including girls [NAME] does not know.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: World Rugby's October 2020 summary states that there were no direct studies on trans women rugby players. Its collision estimate models typical male mass against typical female mass. The review cited by the PRO says hormone-naive transgender women may not on average have the same athletic attributes as cisgender men. Sources: [16], [13], [5].

Evidence note: The McNabb injury occurred on September 1, 2022. North Carolina's state ban took effect August 16, 2023 and applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [14], [17].

Evidence note: Snopes (March 2025) states that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender, and that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. It reports that the school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence, that the board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players while several coaches spoke for continuing, and that North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, with their sports unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [15], [2], [18].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

original.title: It takes away a route to learning and educational opportunities that other students keep.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It takes away a route to learning and educational opportunities that other students keep.

  • Because Sports teach useful skills: “Sports provide meaningful opportunities for kids to feel confident in themselves and learn valuable life lessons about teamwork, leadership, and communication.” [2]
  • Because Team participation also brings educational openings. The bill itself names “scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • Because The ban reaches beyond matches to “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because The same birth-based rule also restricts nonbinary students it classifies as male. Nonbinary students do not identify only as girls or boys. The Equality Caucus explains: “It would also limit the ability of non-binary and intersex students to participate in these programs as well.” [20]
  • Because Girls born with variations in sex traits also face uncertain eligibility. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [2]. They describe the resulting barrier: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [2]
  • So Blocking team competition and the activities tied to it takes away chances to learn and advance. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities includes transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students, giving a reason to oppose these barriers.
  • Note Permission for “males to train or practice” [1] restores neither eligibility to compete nor equal access to team places and benefits. Even practice is conditional: it is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1], among other protected opportunities.
original.con_html:
Response For students past male puberty, listing the benefits of a lost team place does not show that the eligibility rule denies equal opportunity.

  • Because Fair opportunity can require limits on entry to a sports category. In Clark, a court upheld excluding boys from girls’ volleyball because “due to average physiological differences, males would displace females to a substantial extent if they were allowed to compete for positions on the volleyball team.” [21] The reason was a real difference affecting fair competition, rather than the mere existence of separate teams.
  • Because Previous eligibility under a testosterone limit does not establish equal competitive conditions. Reviewing physical traits after male puberty, Hilton and Lundberg reported that “the muscular advantage enjoyed by transgender women is only minimally reduced when testosterone is suppressed.” [22]
  • So Equal opportunity requires a fair basis for eligibility, not preservation of every existing route to scholarships, learning, or admission. For these students, the PRO must show why the boundary unfairly blocks comparable students; naming benefits and affected identities does not supply that step. This response does not reach students who have not gone through male puberty, sports where no advantage has been shown, or eligible girls deterred by uncertainty about intersex variations.
