original.notes_html: Evidence note: NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. CRS reports that some states and school districts allowed participation with no particular requirements or restrictions. Sources: [4], [7].

original.title: It replaces individual protection against unfair treatment with automatic exclusion.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It replaces individual protection against unfair treatment with automatic exclusion.

  • Because The rule makes no distinction by age or sport: “this bill is a blanket ban that treats every age student in every sport the same.” [2]
  • Because On the comparison date, Fourth Circuit law protected an individual girl’s participation, while nationally “Courts have reached different conclusions” [7]. In its April 2024 B.P.J. decision, the Fourth Circuit noted that puberty-blocking treatment meant “B.P.J. has never experienced elevated levels of circulating testosterone.” [23]
  • Because The court held that applying West Virginia’s ban would “treat her worse than people to whom she is similarly situated, deprive her of any meaningful athletic opportunities, and do so on the basis of sex.” [23]
  • So H.R.28 would make birth sex decisive even in cases where a court had held, under the law then in force, that exclusion treated an individual girl worse than comparable students. Replacing that Title IX protection with a duty to exclude conflicts with treating everyone justly. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: B.P.J.'s court found a genuine dispute of material fact on competitive advantage and left her equal-protection claim for further proceedings. In September 2024 the Ninth Circuit upheld a preliminary order on equal-protection grounds in Doe v. Horne. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in B.P.J. and Hecox on July 3, 2025, after the comparison date. On June 30, 2026 the Supreme Court reversed the B.P.J. and Hecox judgments (see note LAW-01). Sources: [23], [24], [7], [25].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [26].

original.title: It removes support and adds stigma for students already facing serious distress and isolation.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It removes support and adds stigma for students already facing serious distress and isolation.

  • Because CDC’s national 2023 high school survey found greater distress and less belonging among transgender students and those unsure whether they were transgender than among peers whose gender matched their sex assigned at birth: “Transgender and questioning students experienced a higher prevalence of violence, poor mental health, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and unstable housing, and a lower prevalence of school connectedness than their cisgender peers.” [27]
  • Because School sports offer health and belonging: “Sports participation is linked to increased academic achievement and fosters in students increased emotional, mental, and physical well-being and a sense of community.” [2]
  • Because Denying team membership also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference describes that exclusion as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [2]
  • So Taking away this source of support while adding stigma burdens students who already need protection. [NAME]’s concern for vulnerable people gives a reason to oppose that harm.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The CDC figures come from a cross-sectional school survey and do not compare outcomes under different sports eligibility rules. The bill permits practice under its stated conditions. Sources: [27], [1].

original.title: It removes a safe way for some girls to compete.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It removes a safe way for some girls to compete.

  • Because A boys’ team is not a safe substitute for every excluded girl. In B.P.J.’s case, the court explained: “By participating on boys teams, B.P.J. would be sharing the field with boys who are larger, stronger, and faster than her because of the elevated levels of circulating testosterone she lacks.” [23]
  • Because The court identified the resulting risk: “It also would expose B.P.J. to the same risk of unfair competition—and, in some sports, physical danger—from which the defendants claim to be shielding cisgender girls.” [23]
  • So H.R.28 removes girls’ team eligibility even in these circumstances. For girls seeking to keep competing on a sex-separated school team, the alternative brings this added danger. Protecting vulnerable students gives [NAME] a reason to oppose shifting that risk onto them.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: B.P.J.'s dispute concerned girls' cross country and track teams. The court referred to physical danger "in some sports". Sources: [23].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [26].

original.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity, and bodily safety at risk.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity, and bodily safety at risk.

  • Because Schools must apply the rule without a set verification process. Representative Hayes notes: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [28]
  • Because A comparable Florida ban led to inquiries into a child’s private history. AP reported: “They interviewed officials at Monarch and at the daughter's middle and elementary schools, seeking to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29]
  • Because The inquiry also reached teammates’ knowledge of her body: “When investigators interviewed the Monarch volleyball players, they said the team did not change clothes or shower together, so they were never disrobed with Norton's daughter.” [29]
  • Because The inquiry was followed by the girl’s withdrawal from school. AP reported, “That all ended when the investigation began and the girl left Monarch.” [29] It added, “The girl now attends school online.” [29]
  • Because Women’s rights organizations warn that sex verification may involve “forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2]. They identify a further danger from such procedures: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2].
  • So A nationwide duty to enforce birth-sex eligibility creates grounds for the same kind of intrusive inquiries, with risks of exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling, and, as those organizations warn, abuse. Protecting children from these harms gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule.
  • Note The supporter’s reply, “There is no requirement for inspections” [2], does not answer the risk. The documented records checks and interviews already invaded privacy. An exam mandate is not needed for that harm.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s evidence does not establish that the bill would lead to bodily examinations or resulting sexual abuse.

  • Because H.R.28 restricts participation in programs “designated for women or girls.” [1] Its text adds no requirement for bodily examinations.
  • Because AP describes an inquiry into records and knowledge: investigators sought “to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29] That account reports no bodily examination.
  • Because Florida’s birth-sex law provides a records-based way to decide eligibility: a birth certificate is accepted if its sex statement “was filed at or near the time of the student's birth.” [30]
  • So The step to bodily examinations and sexual abuse rests on an organizational warning, not on a documented case in the PRO’s evidence. This response does not answer the PRO’s documented privacy harms from records checks and interviews, or the disrupted schooling that followed.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The Florida inquiry also examined staff handling of records, and the student's mother faced discipline. NCAA policy already required annual eligibility documentation from transgender women athletes. FERPA regulations limit officials' access to records in which they have legitimate educational interests. Sources: [29], [19], [31].

Evidence note: Idaho's statute included a separate sex-dispute verification process, which the Ninth Circuit described as allowing gynecological exams. The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [32], [1].

original.title: It exposes students to appearance-based accusations and unequal burdens from enforcing the rule.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It exposes students to appearance-based accusations and unequal burdens from enforcing the rule.

  • Because Enforcing birth-sex eligibility invites suspicion of girls who do not fit stereotypes. Women’s rights organizations warn that verification practices “are especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity, other women and girls who do not conform to sexist stereotypes, and nonbinary and gender nonconforming students.” [2]
  • Because Such accusations have harmed girls who are not transgender. Describing a Utah basketball player targeted for short hair and baggy clothes, the same letter reports: “As a result, the student was subjected to harassment, bullying, and threats of violence, necessitating police protection for her and her family.” [2]
  • Because Utah’s school board independently confirmed harm from the public accusation, recording “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” [33]. Public accusations themselves expose children to abuse.
  • So Extending this eligibility rule nationwide exposes students to harassment for their appearance and, as those organizations warn, unequal scrutiny tied to race and gender stereotypes. That conflicts with treating everyone justly and protecting vulnerable children.
  • So Facing accusations, threats, or humiliating checks also creates a barrier to playing for girls who remain eligible. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities supplies a further reason to oppose this effect of enforcing the rule.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A court had blocked Utah's categorical ban before the February 2024 episode. Utah's fallback commission was then deciding transgender girls' eligibility. The official censure attributed the harm to the board member's public post and comments. Sources: [34], [35], [33].

original.title: It puts educational aid serving other students at risk when schools retain inclusive teams.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It puts educational aid serving other students at risk when schools retain inclusive teams.

  • Because The bill makes inclusion a new Title IX violation: “It shall be a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] to permit the participation it bars.
  • Because Existing enforcement law allows “the termination of or refusal to grant or to continue assistance under such program or activity” [36] after an “express finding on the record, after opportunity for hearing, of a failure to comply with such requirement” [36]. It also requires a finding “that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means.” [36]
  • Because That aid supports education beyond the individual athlete. CRS explains: “The Department of Education (ED) distributes substantial funding to elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions” [7].
  • So Schools that keep including these students would put aid for the affected program at risk, exposing other students to losses too. [NAME]’s concern for students’ equal opportunities gives a reason to oppose making inclusion grounds for withdrawing that support.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Section 1682 requires a hearing, an express finding and a failed attempt at voluntary compliance, and limits termination to the particular program. In 2025 a court restrained a USDA freeze of Maine funds on procedural grounds and the parties settled; Maine and California refused to change their policies and DOJ sued. Sources: [36], [7].

original.title: The bill removes a barrier to participation for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes who are male under its definition.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes a barrier to participation for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes who are male under its definition.

  • Because Such an objection has led a team to give up a game: “A Vermont Christian high school forfeited a girls basketball game because the opposing team had a transgender player, the head of school said.” [4]
  • Because The school's complaint explains the religious basis of its objection: “sex is immutable.” [5] It says competing in that matchup would affirm the opposite, “in violation of its beliefs.” [5]
  • So In covered girls' competitions, the bill removes the matchup that triggers this objection. Girls with that conviction can compete without giving it up.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement includes accepting girls whose religious or other beliefs differ from [NAME]'s. Keeping a way for them to play puts that acceptance into practice.
  • So [NAME] has a reason grounded in tolerance to favor removing this cost of disagreement.
  • Note Acceptance also has room for cooperation across the competition boundary. The bill allows “males to train or practice with an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1] if no female loses a place, opportunity, scholarship, admission, or other sports benefit. Shared training remains a way to work together across differences.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO confuses accepting girls who object to a matchup with accepting their rule for who else may compete.

  • Because The complaint explains the school's religious objection to playing the matchup: “it would be affirming that sex is mutable, in violation of its beliefs.” [5] That explains the objection; it does not make meeting the school's demand an act of accepting people across differences.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement does not mean adopting their demands about others. UNESCO's declaration on tolerance makes the distinction explicit: “It means that one is free to adhere to one's own convictions and accepts that others adhere to theirs.” [6]
  • Because H.R.28 would make it unlawful for federally funded programs to allow “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It would apply the same rule across covered programs, whether anyone objects or not. Its definition rests on “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]
  • So The forfeit explains why the school wants a different rule for who may compete. It does not show why respecting these girls gives [NAME] a reason based on tolerance to impose that rule on other participants.
  • Because The training exception begins, “Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to prohibit” [1]. It leaves shared training possible under stated conditions; it requires no cooperation across differences.
  • So Permission to train together does not supply the missing link between enforcing the objection and accepting people despite disagreement.

original.title: Protecting girls' team places preserves opportunities to practise understanding and acceptance.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Protecting girls' team places preserves opportunities to practise understanding and acceptance.

  • Because The competition rule prevents male competitors from taking female roster places. Even shared training is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1], among other protected benefits.
  • Because Girls' teams can offer a setting for learning to work with different people. A player in a study of two multiethnic high school teams described her own learning: “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” [7]
  • So Protecting girls against this loss of places and practice access preserves their access to those shared learning experiences.
  • So [NAME]'s wish for people to listen to, understand, and accept others gives a reason to protect girls' opportunities to practise those habits with teammates.
original.con_html:
Response The cited study does not establish that the team places protected by the bill offer practice in accepting different people.

  • Because The change the study reports from team play is that it “made players more collectivistic in response to a values questionnaire.” [7] The questionnaire's example of that outlook was “I agree with Emily, learning to play as a team is more important.” [7] That measures the weight given to team goals, a different outcome from acceptance of people with different beliefs. It neither shows nor rules out such acceptance.
  • Because The player's statement, “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” [7], appears in an account of what she learned about group dynamics. In the same passage she complains about team cohesion and says, “I think we need team bonding.” [7]
  • So The link from a team place to practice in accepting different people rests on one player’s unelaborated use of the word tolerance, in a passage about team cohesion. This response does not dispute that she names tolerance as something she learned, or that the teams were multiethnic.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The girls' basketball study reports that its workshops, a three-session intervention, did not have the intended effect of increasing understanding of a different value system. That result concerns the intervention, not team play. The study's measured seasonal change was toward collectivistic responses; it did not measure acceptance of others. It covered two Los Angeles-area teams. Sources: [7].

retirement.reason: The current Tolerance standard requires a substantive understanding or acceptance connection across relevant differences and says generic access to information is insufficient. The bill’s study orders documentation of adverse results to girls and lost benefits of single-sex sports, delivered to two congressional committees. It requires no listening, understanding or acceptance across differences, and it does not study the experiences of the students the rule excludes. Calling this understanding people with different experiences relabels an information duty as tolerance. The preserved note already records that the mandate is directed to listed adverse consequences and is not a balanced inquiry.

accepting and understanding those with life-styles and beliefs different from one’s own

clarified_text_if_main_declines_retireme.title: The required study makes girls’ experiences part of the evidence lawmakers must receive.
clarified_text_if_main_declines_retireme.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
clarified_text_if_main_declines_retireme.pro_html:
Point 3 The required study makes girls’ experiences part of the evidence lawmakers must receive.

  • Because The bill orders the Comptroller General, the federal official it assigns to this study, to document “adverse psychological, developmental, participatory, and sociological results to girls” [1] from male participation, including “displacement or discouragement from sports participation” [1].
  • Because This study concerns the benefits protected by the shared-training rule. It studies “benefits to women or girls of participating in single sex sports that would be lost by allowing males to participate.” [1]
  • Because The findings must reach the House and Senate education committees in “a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So The bill requires an official study of these experiences and delivery of the findings to lawmakers. [NAME]’s wish to understand people with different experiences gives a reason to favor this duty to study and report.

paths.original_excerpt: The bill requires official examination of these experiences and delivery of the findings to lawmakers.
paths.necessity_reason: Local route resting on the study provision; with this argument active, the study provision would have two users and Main may separate it.

fragments.body_html: Evidence note: The report mandate is directed to listed adverse consequences for girls and the meaning of benefits protected by the practice exception. It does not require a balanced inquiry into all experiences of shared sport. That limits the report's scope; it does not remove the PRO's narrower information route. Sources: [1].
fragments.reason: Limits the study route; no response exists and none is created.

original.pro_html:

  • Because The bill orders Congress's audit office to document “adverse psychological, developmental, participatory, and sociological results to girls” [1] from male participation, including “displacement or discouragement from sports participation” [1].
  • Because This inquiry concerns the benefits protected by the shared-training rule. It studies “benefits to women or girls of participating in single sex sports that would be lost by allowing males to participate.” [1]
  • Because The findings must reach the House and Senate education committees in “a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So The bill requires official examination of these experiences and delivery of the findings to lawmakers. [NAME]'s wish to understand people with different experiences gives a reason to favor this duty to investigate and report.

  • Because The bill orders Congress's audit office to document “adverse psychological, developmental, participatory, and sociological results to girls” [1] from male participation, including “displacement or discouragement from sports participation” [1].
  • Because This inquiry concerns the benefits protected by the shared-training rule. It studies “benefits to women or girls of participating in single sex sports that would be lost by allowing males to participate.” [1]
  • Because The findings must reach the House and Senate education committees in “a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So The bill requires official examination of these experiences and delivery of the findings to lawmakers. [NAME]'s wish to understand people with different experiences gives a reason to favor this duty to investigate and report.

original.title: It replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.

  • Because As of January 14, 2025, Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, protected participation in at least some cases. In a 2024 case, “The Fourth Circuit ruled that application of the West Virginia law to the plaintiff violated Title IX, because it treated her worse than those similarly situated based on her sex and caused her harm.” [8]
  • Because Individual differences mattered to that ruling. The court criticized a ban that applied “regardless of whether a particular student has any genuine athletic advantages” [8]. H.R.28 would instead make birth biology and genetics decisive for every student it classifies as male.
  • Because [NAME] values accepting people even when they disagree. That gives weight to including a classmate despite disagreement about that classmate’s gender, and to hearing the student’s circumstances before ruling them out.
  • So The bill would close a route to acceptance that the law then in force protected. Hearing individual students or choosing inclusion as a school community could no longer change eligibility under its birth-based rule.
  • Because The restriction also reaches activities tied to team membership. The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Shared sports offer chances to know people. Researchers describe “regular social interaction; opportunities to build positive relationships with teammates and coaches” [9].
  • Because Exclusion also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that “denying transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth the chance to participate only serves to deny them an opportunity to be part of that community, further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10]
  • Note The limited permission for “males to train or practice” [1] does not restore eligibility to compete on girls’ and women’s teams.
  • So Required exclusion takes away shared competition and team-linked opportunities to build understanding, while reinforcing stigma against these classmates. [NAME]’s wish to accept and understand different people gives a reason to preserve those opportunities and resist that treatment.
original.con_html:
Response Accepting a person does not require agreeing on team eligibility, so losing eligibility is not by itself a loss of acceptance.

  • Because Accepting people across disagreements leaves room to disagree about rules. [NAME] can listen to a student, understand their circumstances, and accept them while reaching a different view about team eligibility. The research defining this value says it concerns “accepting and understanding those with life-styles and beliefs different from one’s own.” [11]
  • Because The bill sets a rule for sports eligibility: “For the purposes of this subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] A decision under that rule does not establish how classmates regard or listen to the student.
  • So Treating eligibility itself as acceptance assumes the point at issue. This response does not answer the PRO’s claims that exclusion reduces contact and team-linked chances to build understanding, adds stigma, or removes a school’s choice to include.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The cited study compared any sports team participation with none. It did not compare acceptance with and without access to girls' competition. The bill allows conditional training or practice. Sources: [9], [1].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [12].

original.title: Its unclear birth-based test puts girls with intersex traits at risk of exclusion.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Its unclear birth-based test puts girls with intersex traits at risk of exclusion.

  • Because Intersex variations are differences in sex traits. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [10].
  • Because These groups report exclusion under comparable rules: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [10]
  • Because Accepting all kinds of people includes accepting people born with different bodies. Their sex traits give [NAME] a reason to make room for them in shared school life.
  • So Exposing these girls to exclusion because their bodies do not fit a simple birth-based test conflicts with that acceptance. [NAME] has a reason to oppose this risk.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The letter names no specific ban or exclusion and gives no worked example of how conflicting traits would be treated. During debate the bill manager said the bill "deals with men in sports" when asked about intersex children. Sources: [10], [10].

original.title: It gives sex-based accusations more power to threaten girls’ places on teams.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It gives sex-based accusations more power to threaten girls’ places on teams.

  • Because Schools would have to follow a rule making birth sex decisive. The bill applies to “a recipient of Federal financial assistance who operates, sponsors, or facilitates athletic programs or activities” [1].
  • So Where schools have included transgender girls, the bill would make a claim that a girl was born male grounds to challenge her eligibility. This gives such accusations a route to exclusion.
  • Because That route has already operated under Utah’s school sports eligibility rules. Associated Press reported that Utah’s athletics association “secretly investigated a female athlete — without telling her or her parents — after receiving complaints from the parents of two girls she had defeated in competition questioning whether the girl was transgender.” [13] The complaint was “among several the association had looked into in its efforts to comply with the Utah law” [13].
  • Because Public accusations can also bring harassment. In a separate 2024 case, Utah’s education board found that a member’s post insinuated “that one of the female students in the picture may not be female” [14]. It recorded “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” [14] resulting from the post and comments.
  • Because Girls who look different face a particular risk. The women’s rights and sports groups warn that sex checks are “especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity” [10].
  • Note The bill’s manager says, “There is no requirement for inspections” [10]. Sex challenges and public accusations do not require physical exams.
  • So The bill creates grounds for exclusion that can turn differences in bodies, appearance, and gender expression into sources of suspicion and harassment. [NAME]’s tolerance toward different people gives a reason to oppose that risk, including, as those groups warn, an added risk for girls of color.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Salt Lake Tribune dates the Utah complaint to the year before the ban took effect in July 2022, when the association let registered transgender athletes compete after a year of hormone blockers. An association spokesman said many parents raised such complaints and none was verified. The state had one registered transgender female athlete on a girls' team that year. AP separately reported that the complaint was among several examined in efforts to comply with the law. Sources: [15], [13].

original.title: It removes a source of serious injury risk in female contact sports.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes a source of serious injury risk in female contact sports.

  • Because Hormone-based eligibility allowed these matchups in U.S. college sports. The NCAA’s May 2024 rules included women’s rugby and stated: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [4]
  • Because A review of studies of non-athletic transgender women found higher strength and muscle measures than in women female at birth after hormone treatment: “values remain above that observed in cisgender women, even after 36 months.” [5]
  • Because World Rugby links size and speed differences to injury: “When two opponents in a tackle are significantly different with respects to mass or speed, these risk factors increase significantly.” [6] The passage concerns head and neck injury risks.
  • Because Its review of testosterone reduction concluded that “safety and fairness cannot presently be assured for women competing against transwomen in contact rugby.” [7]
  • So Where hormone-based rules allowed these matchups, H.R.28 would prevent them in covered female competitions. This removes the collision hazard from those matchups.
  • So Safer conditions for an ordinary way to exercise serve [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury and danger.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Snopes (March 2025) states that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender, and that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. It reports that the school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence, that the board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players while several coaches spoke for continuing, and that North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, with their sports unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [8], [9], [10].

Evidence note: World Rugby's estimate models typical male mass against typical female mass. A 2024 athlete study recommends evaluating transgender women athletes as their own group rather than using cisgender men as proxies. The hormone review did not report activity levels of the groups compared. Sources: [6], [11], [5].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [12], [13].

original.title: It protects girls’ opportunities to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects girls’ opportunities to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.

  • Because Limited places can mean lost participation. ABC7 reported that Taylor Starling was moved to junior varsity when a transgender runner joined a seven-place varsity team, “causing Starling to miss a varsity cross-country meet.” [14] After a Title IX complaint she “was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet.” [14]
  • Because The bill reserves female competition for females at birth. It also conditions male practice on protecting each female’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • So It prevents that source of exclusion from female competition and practice. Where a girl has no other team place, that keeps her chance to exercise on a team open.
  • Because The federal health department explains that sports “participation is one way for youth to get the physical activity they need to be fit and healthy.” [15]
  • Because A U.S. study compared girls with boys during Title IX’s expansion of girls’ sports. It reported that the expansion “resulted in greater physical activity and improved weight and body mass.” [16]
  • Because CDC states that “regular physical activity prevents risk factors for various health conditions like heart disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes.” [17]
  • Because CDC also reports that active youth have “stronger bones and muscles.” [17] Its listed brain-health benefits include “reduced symptoms of depression.” [17]
  • So Keeping sports opportunities open protects a route to exercise and its physical and mental health benefits. Protecting that route serves [NAME]’s wish to protect health and avoid disease.
original.con_html:
Response The roster example does not show lost access to healthy exercise.

  • Because Starling “was bumped down to the JV team.” [14] JV means junior varsity.
  • Because The report adds that “she was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet. ML remains on the team as well.” [14]
  • So Starling retained access to school sports, and both runners ultimately participated on varsity. Losing varsity status for one meet does not establish reduced exercise or lost health benefits.
  • Because The health study concerns an expansion of participation: “Title IX caused a significant increase in girls’ sports participation.” [16]
  • So That research concerns girls added to sports, while the PRO’s example concerns a girl who stayed active. The evidence does not supply the step from displacement to less exercise. This response does not address a girl cut from a capped team with no other place to play.

original.title: It protects bodily privacy in female changing activities tied to team participation.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects bodily privacy in female changing activities tied to team participation.

  • Because The bill’s reach includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • So A changing activity designated for women or girls and made conditional on team participation falls within its female-only participation rule.
  • Because Unwanted shared undressing can damage a sense of security. Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines saying, “We did not give our consent to be exploited and exposed to a 6-foot-4 fully naked man.” [9] She added, “You allowed college women to be traumatized” [9].
  • So Applying the rule to those changing activities removes that route to unwanted shared undressing. Privacy in intimate settings supports feeling personally secure, which [NAME] values.
original.con_html:
Response The bill’s text and the quoted account do not show that shared changing is a covered activity.

  • Because The bill limits its new definition of sex to “the purposes of this subsection” [1].
  • Because Its definition of athletic activities “includes, but is not limited to, all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Walberg quotes Gaines describing the exposure: “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” [9]
  • So That account does not establish that access depended on team participation or that the shared changing was itself a covered athletic activity. A room's connection to sports does not establish the condition on which the PRO's legal argument rests. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.

original.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse, and trauma.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse, and trauma.

  • Because The bill sets a birth-sex rule but leaves the checking method open. Representative Hayes noted that it provides “neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” [18].
  • Because Idaho enacted an intrusive sex-check rule. The Ninth Circuit described it as allowing “intrusive medical procedures to verify her sex, including gynecological exams” [19].
  • Because The National Women's Law Center and Women's Sports Foundation warn that H.R.28 invites “invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [9] that “make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [9].
  • Because Such checks also threaten mental health. The court explained: “The psychological burden of these searches falls not only on transgender women like Lindsay but also on all women and girls who play female athletics.” [19]
  • Because Fear of checks threatens participation too. Representative Randall warned that intrusive questions and examinations would be “dissuading girls' participation in sports” [9].
  • So The new federal eligibility rule creates risks of bodily intrusion, abuse, and distress in an ordinary school activity. It also threatens the health benefits of exercise described in reason 3. Avoiding these dangers serves [NAME]'s aim to stay safe and healthy.
original.con_html:
Response Idaho's separate medical-testing rule does not establish that H.R.28 would expose girls to intrusive exams.

  • Because H.R.28 defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without ordering medical inspections. Its House manager described the intended method: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [9]
  • Because The Idaho court tied intrusive checks to that state's separate “sex dispute verification provision” [19]. It also reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [19]
  • So The PRO's own court source supplies a working alternative to intrusive exams under comparable restrictions. Idaho shows that a legislature can choose exams, but it does not show that schools under H.R.28 would choose them over records. The PRO’s claims of exam-related abuse and trauma depend on that step. This response does not address records-based inquiries, or fear and withdrawal caused by the possibility of challenges.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: Idaho's statute included a separate sex-dispute verification process, which the Ninth Circuit described as allowing gynecological exams. The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [19], [1].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [20].

original.title: Public challenges to girls' sex expose them to harassment and threats of violence.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Public challenges to girls' sex expose them to harassment and threats of violence.

  • Because The Leadership Conference warns that H.R.28 “will invite scrutiny and harassment of any other student perceived by anyone as not conforming to sex stereotypes” [9].
  • Because This kind of accusation has already put a girl in danger. After a Utah school board member questioned a basketball player's sex, the board found that her post “created a substantial risk of harm” [21].
  • Because The girl was not transgender. The National Women's Law Center and Women's Sports Foundation report that the resulting threats required “police protection for her and her family” [9].
  • So Making birth sex a federal condition for playing gives these accusations a new role in decisions about who can play. Threats against girls who are not transgender and their families make this a safety concern in ordinary school sports, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Existing Title IX rules allowed separate sex-based teams. The Utah board treated the post as a breach of existing duties, including respecting student privacy and preventing harassment. H.R.28 creates no procedure for publicly disputing a student's sex. Sources: [22], [21].

original.title: The exclusion cuts off a route to exercise, mental health support, and health checkups.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 The exclusion cuts off a route to exercise, mental health support, and health checkups.

  • Because The ban reaches recreational school sports as well as elite competition. As Representative Bonamici explained, “this bill applies to every student of every age in every sport the same way” [9].
  • Because Federal health guidance links youth sports with “Increased physical activity levels” [15] and physical activity with “Reduced risk of cancer and diabetes” [15].
  • Because A Colorado survey linked playing on three or more sports teams, versus none, to “reduced likelihood of depression” [23] among transgender students.
  • Because Sports also supply supportive relationships. The study cites research showing that “increased social support in adolescence, including that provided by team sports participation, protects against depression” [23].
  • Note The bill's conditional permission “to train or practice” [1] leaves the competition ban in place.
  • Because Boys' teams do not keep every excluded girl in sports. Surveyed transgender girls reported avoiding sports because they feared being “forced to play on a team or use a facility that does not align with their gender identity” [24].
  • Because Leaving sports also risks losing a reason to see a doctor. In a study of providers who care for transgender youth, one warned that patients who no longer need sports exams “may miss health issues and immunizations due to not coming in” [25].
  • So Closing access to competition removes a way to sustain exercise and supportive relationships. For students driven out of sports, it also puts sports-linked checkups at risk. Protecting physical and mental health gives [NAME] a reason to oppose these losses.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Colorado study measured the number of sports teams played and states that it cannot assess whether team participation directly reduces adverse mental-health outcomes. The missed-checkup statement is one provider's prediction, and the provider study notes that its prompt lacked precision because many bills do not ban participation outright. Sources: [23], [25].

original.title: Official rejection threatens mental health beyond students who lose a team place.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 Official rejection threatens mental health beyond students who lose a team place.

  • Because Denying students a place in school athletics marks them as outsiders. The Leadership Conference describes this as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth” [9].
  • Because Medical researchers warn that these laws can “worsen the mental health of those who aren't directly targeted by these laws (e.g., trans youth who don't play sports)” [25].
  • Because The effects may reach teammates too. A suggested advocacy letter from the American Psychological Association warns that “excluding any subset of girls from sports can encourage divisiveness and compromise group cohesion, undermining the benefits all youth deserve from team sports” [26].
  • Because Supportive school relationships matter for health. CDC's research review describes school communities “lessening emotional distress, anxiety, and depression” [27].
  • So The law's rejection of some students threatens the supportive school ties that protect mental health, even without anyone leaving a sport. Protecting health in everyday school life gives [NAME] another reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The APA divisiveness language appears in suggested advocacy text asking legislators to oppose a bill, and it cites an ACLU document. It reports no study of a sports eligibility rule. CDC lists other school supports, including student-led clubs, enforced antiharassment policies and caring student-teacher relationships. H.R.28 does not address those. Sources: [26], [27].

retirement.reason: A national rule against individual sports injuries does not by itself protect the safety or stability of society as a whole. Federal enforcement and durability do not supply the missing collective-security mechanism. The injury argument remains under Personal Security and Concern.

original_mapping.title: It gives the United States an enforceable, lasting safeguard against injury risks from physical mismatches in women’s contact competition.
original_mapping.pro_html:
Point 1 It gives the United States an enforceable, lasting safeguard against injury risks from physical mismatches in women’s contact competition.

  • Because Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, had no express rule for transgender athletes: “Neither the statute nor the regulations currently address how Title IX applies to transgender athletes.” [3] A statute is a law. Regulations are rules written by a government agency.
  • Because May 2024 rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, allowed transgender women to qualify for women’s rugby through a limit on testosterone, a hormone. Transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women. The rules state: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [4] The rugby line sets its blood testosterone limit at “<10 nmol/L” [4], meaning below that level.
  • Because A 2021 review of studies of transgender women who were not athletes found evidence of strength retained after hormone treatment: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5] Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.
  • Because World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, explains how size and speed differences affect injury risk in tackles: “the discrepancy in mass and speed of direct opponents in tackles predicts neck forces, moments and head accelerations.” [6] It adds: “Since these factors contribute directly to injury risk, it is clear that large discrepancies create greater risks for smaller and slower players, particularly when size and speed exist in combination.” [6] A discrepancy is a difference.
  • Because World Rugby’s review connects advantages kept after hormone treatment to that risk: “The lowering of testosterone removes only a small proportion of the documented biological differences, with large, retained advantages in these physiological attributes, with the safety and performance implications described previously.” [6]
  • So In covered women’s rugby, the bill would exclude competitors who went through male puberty and keep those advantages. That removes this source of risk in competition, rather than relying on a testosterone limit to remove it.
  • Because Title IX already has ways to enforce the new duty: “Title IX is primarily enforced in two ways: through private litigation in federal court and by federal agencies that distribute funding to education programs.” [3] Private litigation means lawsuits brought by people or groups.
  • So Making that participation an express Title IX violation gives federal agencies and affected students a legal basis to demand that covered schools follow the rule. This includes places where state rules allow the participation.
  • So Writing the eligibility test into the law also prevents a future president’s administration from reversing that duty simply by changing how an agency reads Title IX.
  • Note The January 2025 ruling had already removed the 2024 Title IX regulations: “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [3] Vacated means canceled. Removing those regulations did not create the bill’s express national eligibility duty.
  • So Enforceable, lasting protection against this physical risk strengthens the country’s ability to defend its citizens through federal institutions. That serves [NAME]’s wish for a strong U.S. state that protects citizens against threats.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response Making protection from rugby injuries a lasting federal duty does not establish the gain in societal security this argument claims.

  • Because This value separates society’s safety from personal safety: “Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety.” [7]
  • Because World Rugby’s injury argument is about impacts on players’ bodies: “the discrepancy in mass and speed of direct opponents in tackles predicts neck forces, moments and head accelerations.” [6]
  • So That evidence is about players’ safety. It does not show how the risk threatens the country’s security or stability.
  • Because The ways to enforce the law already exist: “Title IX is primarily enforced in two ways: through private litigation in federal court and by federal agencies that distribute funding to education programs.” [3]
  • So A new eligibility duty changes what those institutions enforce. Its national reach and protection from reversal do not show that those institutions become better able to meet threats to society.
  • So The argument needs a link from this sports protection to a safer, more stable country or a stronger state able to defend its citizens. Federal enforcement and a lasting rule do not supply that link.
original_mapping.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

original_mapping.title: It gives Congress evidence to check the safeguards in the sports rule.
original_mapping.pro_html:
Point 2 It gives Congress evidence to check the safeguards in the sports rule.

  • Because The bill connects a federal study to the training and practice exception: “The Comptroller General shall carry out a study to determine the meaning of the phrase `any other benefit' as used in subsection (d)(4)” [1]. The Congressional Research Service describes this as a report by the Government Accountability Office [2]. These are benefits the exception must protect for female athletes.
  • Because The study must examine harms and lost benefits, including “deprivation of the benefit of an environment free of hostility based on sexual assault or harassment” [1].
  • Because The bill requires the study’s results to reach the education committees of both the House and Senate in “a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So Congress would receive a required review of harms and benefits related to the rule’s safeguards. This gives lawmakers information to check whether those safeguards protect girls and where more action is needed.
  • So A state better able to find gaps in its protections is better able to defend citizens. That gives [NAME] a separate reason to favor the bill’s required review.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response Information about sports benefits does not supply the missing link to the state’s ability to protect society.

  • Because The study’s assigned purpose is “to determine the meaning of the phrase `any other benefit' as used in subsection (d)(4)” [1], which sets the training and practice exception.
  • Because Its subject is “benefits to women or girls of participating in single sex sports that would be lost by allowing males to participate.” [1]
  • Because The bill sends the results to Congress: “the Comptroller General shall submit to the Committee on Education and the Workforce of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions of the Senate a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So These provisions explain what lawmakers would learn about the benefits the exception must protect. They do not explain how that knowledge improves the country’s security or stability, or its ability to meet threats to society.
  • So Calling Congress better able to find gaps in sports protections repeats the unsupported step in Point 1. The argument still needs to show why better oversight of those protections serves societal security.

original_mapping.title: The birth-sex rule creates pressure for invasive checks that expose girls to sexual abuse.

  • Because Schools must meet the new rule without a clear way to check sex. Representative Hayes explains: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [11]
  • Because Another birth-sex sports ban shows the enforcement risk. In 2024, a federal appeals court described Idaho’s law as allowing sex challenges and checks “including gynecological exams.” [12] A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs.
  • Because The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that checks under H.R.28 “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [10]. They name the danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [10].
  • Note The House member managing the bill proposes checking “a person's birth certificate.” [10] The bill does not make that document the final answer. Its test remains “reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] That assurance does not prevent schools from adopting invasive checks.
  • So Creating a risk of abuse in schools weakens the state’s protection of its citizens. [NAME]’s commitment to a strong state that can defend them gives a reason to oppose this rule.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response The evidence does not show that H.R.28 would push schools toward invasive checks and more exposure to sexual abuse, or how such a risk would weaken societal security.

  • Because Idaho added a specific rule for medical checks: “A dispute regarding a student’s sex shall be resolved by the school or institution by requesting that the student provide a health examination and consent form or other statement signed by the student’s personal health care provider that shall verify the student’s biological sex.” [12]
  • Because The same court reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [12] It also said that, among the other 24 states with restrictions, “none has authorized a similar sex verification process.” [12]
  • Because H.R.28 defines sex through “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without adding Idaho’s procedure for medical checks. The House member managing the bill proposed using records: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [10]
  • So Idaho’s added procedure explains the risk of invasive checks in that example. The wider comparison shows an established way to check sex through records. The argument does not show why H.R.28’s definition, or its failure to make birth certificates final, would replace that approach. Its warning therefore does not establish the added pressure its abuse claim needs.
  • Because This value also separates society’s safety from personal safety: “Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety.” [7]
  • So Even if some girls faced this risk, the argument would still need to show how it weakens the country’s stability or the state’s ability to protect its people. Saying that a school harm weakens state protection does not supply that link.
