original.title: The birth-sex rule creates pressure for invasive checks that expose girls to sexual abuse.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 The birth-sex rule creates pressure for invasive checks that expose girls to sexual abuse.

  • Because Schools must meet the new rule without a clear method for checking sex. Representative Hayes explains: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [11]
  • Because Another birth-sex sports ban shows the enforcement risk. In 2024, a federal appeals court described Idaho’s law as allowing sex challenges and checks “including gynecological exams.” [12]
  • Because The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that checks under H.R.28 “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [10]. They identify the danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [10].
  • Note The floor manager proposes checking “a person's birth certificate.” [10] The bill gives that document no final say. Its test remains “reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] His assurance does not prevent schools from adopting invasive checks.
  • So Creating an abuse risk in schools weakens the state’s protection of its citizens. [NAME]’s commitment to a strong state that can defend them gives a reason to oppose this rule.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s evidence does not show that H.R.28 would push schools toward invasive checks and increase exposure to sexual abuse.

  • Because Idaho added a specific rule for medical checks: “A dispute regarding a student’s sex shall be resolved by the school or institution by requesting that the student provide a health examination and consent form or other statement signed by the student’s personal health care provider that shall verify the student’s biological sex.” [12]
  • Because The same court reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [12] It also said that, among the other 24 states with restrictions, “none has authorized a similar sex verification process.” [12]
  • Because H.R.28 defines sex through “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without adding Idaho’s procedure for medical checks. Its floor manager proposed using records: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [10]
  • So Idaho’s added procedure explains the risk of invasive checks in that example. The wider comparison shows an established way to check sex through records. The PRO does not show why H.R.28’s definition or its failure to make birth certificates final would displace that approach. Its warning therefore does not establish the added pressure needed for its abuse claim.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [13].

original.title: The rule invites public accusations that threaten students and their communities.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 The rule invites public accusations that threaten students and their communities.

  • Because The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights coalition warns that H.R.28 “will invite scrutiny and harassment of any other student perceived by anyone as not conforming to sex stereotypes” [10]. The risk reaches girls whose bodies or appearance prompt suspicion, whether they are transgender or not.
  • Because Such accusations already threaten school safety. The Salt Lake Tribune reported: “A Utah high school student needs police protection after a state school board member publicly singled out and suggested the student was transgender — without evidence — inciting threats from her followers on social media.” [14]
  • Because Hostility aimed at a group can intimidate a whole community. The Justice Department explains this wider harm in discussing hate crimes: “They represent an attack not just on the individual victim, but on the victim's community.” [15]
  • So Extending birth-sex eligibility rules to federally funded schools nationwide creates more occasions for this intimidation. Protecting citizens and their communities from threats gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: The Salt Lake Tribune reports the same board member was reprimanded in fall 2021 after a post that led some followers to threaten violence, before Utah's 2022 ban. It also reports a "slew of accusations" from parents and others after the law passed. Sources: [14].

original.title: Exclusion cuts access to sports as a way to build safer communities.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Exclusion cuts access to sports as a way to build safer communities.

  • Because Ordering transgender students onto teams based on sex at birth drives some out of sport. A 2025 study summarizes earlier research: “policies requiring youth to play on teams with their assigned sex, dissuade youth from participating” [16].
  • Because The loss also reaches girls born with variations in sex traits, often called intersex variations. The women’s sports organizations report: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [10]
  • Note The conditional practice exception permits “males to train or practice” [1]. It guarantees no place in practice and leaves the competition ban intact.
  • So Where schools now include them, the bill cuts off a route into sport for students it excludes or deters.
  • Because Sports also provide a setting linked to less use of illegal drugs. A review of 17 studies that followed young people over time reports: “Sport participation was associated with reduced illicit drug use during adolescence.” [17]
  • Because The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) describes organized sports as a tool for violence prevention: “Research shows that organized sport participation can reduce youth violence” [18].
  • Because School sports build community ties. The civil rights coalition explains that “School athletics are very often the centerpiece of communities across the country” [10] and that exclusion means “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10] HHS links sports with “Improved teamwork, social skills, and social responsibility” [19].
  • Because Community ties are associated with public safety. The Surgeon General links stronger community ties with “lower levels of community violence” [20].
  • So Exclusion closes a route to cooperation, community ties, less illegal drug use and, on HHS’s account, violence prevention. Preserving those forms of protection helps the United States protect its people. That serves [NAME]’s goal of a secure, stable country.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s research does not establish that changed eligibility would reduce violence prevention or community safety.

  • Because HHS cites “McMahon S, Belur J. Sports-based Programmes and Reducing Youth Violence and Crime.” [18] That review states: “None of the evaluations present robust enough evidence to directly establish causal links between interventions and outcomes.” [21] It reports some correlational evidence, not proof of cause.
  • Because A separate review of studies on youth crime concludes that “in general, sports involvement is not reliably related to more or less juvenile delinquency” [22]. HHS itself says: “Coaching, program design, and funding affect these outcomes” [18].
  • So Fewer sports places cannot simply stand for lost crime prevention. The PRO has not linked the affected programs to the features that provide that protection.
  • Because The Surgeon General’s discussion of lower crime concerns residents’ “willingness to act” [20] for community members.
  • So Losing a school sports tie and losing neighborhood trust are different outcomes, and the PRO does not connect them. This response does not address the PRO’s drug-use route.
original.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: The mental-health study compared any team participation with none, and its authors say they could not deduce causal relationships and that depression can make participation harder. HHS introduces its mental-health and disease findings with "is associated with". The suicide figure describes existing risk among transgender and questioning students. HHS associates youth sports with reduced suicide risk and physical activity with reduced cancer and diabetes risk, and one study found lower depressive and anxiety symptoms among team athletes. CDC reports that about 26% of transgender and questioning students attempted suicide in the past year. Sources: [16], [19], [23].

Evidence note: The Surgeon General's advisory reports that people in neighborhoods connected to community institutions prepare for and recover from natural hazards more quickly. That passage does not address school sports. Sources: [20].

original.title: It applies a particular inherited Christian understanding of sex in school sports.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It applies a particular inherited Christian understanding of sex in school sports.

  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention affirmed in 2014 that “gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [3].
  • Because The bill uses that distinction for female sports eligibility: “sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]
  • So The bill makes a public sports rule follow the understanding of sex [NAME] wants to maintain.
  • Because The same faith statement says, “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [4].
  • Because The Family Research Council tells Christian parents to teach that “God created each of us either male or female” [5].
  • So Using birth sex for sports eligibility makes that public practice follow the male-and-female understanding parents are instructed to transmit. The bill does not regulate classroom teaching; the claimed connection is consistency between the sports rule and that particular inherited belief.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill's definition of sex applies "for the purposes of this subsection". It does not regulate what schools teach about gender identity. Sources: [1].

original.title: It preserves the established practice of separate female competition.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It preserves the established practice of separate female competition.

  • Because Separate school sports have a long legal history: “Long-standing Title IX regulations permit separation of the sexes in school sports programs provided schools offer equal athletic opportunities.” [6]
  • Because The Southern Baptist Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission identifies the cultural practice it wants to preserve: “Maintaining separate categories for males and females is essential to preserve the integrity and essence of women’s sports.” [7]
  • So Reserving female competition and its titles for female athletes preserves this form of women’s sports. [NAME]’s wish to honor cultural practices supports keeping it.
  • Note The January court ruling did not create the bill’s national requirement. CRS reports that “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [6] That removed the 2024 regulations; the longstanding sports rule quoted above permitted separate teams. H.R.28 would add an express requirement to exclude male competitors from female sports.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: NCAA policy from 2011 allowed transgender athletes in sex-separated sports subject to hormone-therapy conditions. On the comparison date the NCAA regulated eligibility sport by sport, with women's teams retained. Sources: [8], [6].

catalog.retirement_reason: Protecting daughters' safety and opportunities is the substantive benefit. Calling it a father's religious duty does not independently establish a particular traditional practice.

original.title: It gives families a way to carry out their traditional duty to protect women and girls.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It gives families a way to carry out their traditional duty to protect women and girls.

  • Because The Southern Baptist faith statement assigns the husband a protective role: “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.” [4]
  • Because Its Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission applies Christian duty to sports opportunities: “Christians should uphold biological reality, protect women’s opportunities, and preserve the sanctity of women’s sports by supporting such bans.” [7]
  • Because A 2021 review studied hormone treatment in transgender women who were not athletes. After one to three years of treatment, it found evidence of a lasting strength advantage over women born female: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [9]
  • Because The bill reserves female competition for female athletes and allows male practice only while protecting each female’s “roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So The bill protects female places and awards from going to male competitors and removes the risk of facing those competitors’ lasting strength advantages in female competition. Supporting this protection for daughters puts the inherited family duty into practice, giving [NAME] a reason grounded in Tradition to favor it.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s strength evidence is contested, so it does not establish the lasting strength advantage it says the bill would keep out of female competition.

  • Because The 2021 review studied hormone treatment to match gender identity, called GAHT, in “non-athletic transgender women” [9]. It limits its reach: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [9]
  • Because A 2026 review compares transgender women after hormone treatment with women whose gender identity matches their birth sex, called cisgender women. It reports: “While transgender women exhibited higher lean mass than cisgender women, their physical fitness was comparable.” [10] It concludes: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” [10] The July correction removed three studies, added one and states: “The main conclusions and key messages remain unchanged.” [11]
  • So The evidence does not establish the claimed lasting strength advantage in female competition, although its low certainty means it does not rule one out. This response does not address the PRO’s reason concerning places and awards, which rests on the duty its tradition states rather than on this evidence.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [10], [11].
original.retirement_reason: Protecting daughters' safety and opportunities is the substantive benefit. Calling it a father's religious duty does not independently establish a particular traditional practice.

retirement.reason: The cited religious resolution asserts a privacy concern, not an inherited practice or a reason to preserve continuity with the past. Generic religious endorsement does not turn a privacy argument into Tradition.

original_mapping.title: It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.
original_mapping.pro_html:
Point 4 It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.

  • Because Southern Baptists, a large Christian denomination, defend “the privacy concerns women rightly have about sharing sleeping quarters and intimate facilities with members of the opposite sex” [12]. Intimate facilities are places for changing clothes or washing.
  • Because Competition can bring access to changing areas. The 2024 manual for a women’s swimming championship of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, provides “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. It connects athlete access to credentials, which are passes: “Team staff will receive numbered wristbands and student-athletes will receive labeled credentials. No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13]
  • Because Such access has been reported. Representative Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines: “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” [14]
  • Because The bill covers activities beyond the contest itself, including “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • So A male athlete excluded from female competition cannot gain access to its private team activities through a place as a female competitor. Removing that way into shared intimate facilities supports the religious custom of privacy between the sexes that [NAME] wants to uphold.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response The argument does not establish that a place in female competition itself gives shared intimate access, that the bill covers those facilities, or that the cited statement describes an inherited custom.

  • Because The swimming manual describes “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. That passage does not say which users may use which room, or that those rooms are shared across sexes.
  • Because Its credential rule says: “No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13] This makes identification necessary to enter the building. It does not make a competition pass permission to change or shower with women.
  • Because The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Applying that clause to the claimed intimate access requires evidence that the access is a benefit that depends on team participation. The manual does not establish that condition for sharing intimate facilities with women.
  • So The legal path to these facilities is not established.
  • Because The Baptist resolution lists “the privacy concerns women rightly have” [12] among its reasons to oppose a civil-rights bill. It does not describe an inherited custom or ask people to keep one because of continuity with the past.
  • So Religious support for a privacy concern does not by itself establish a Tradition reason. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.

original.title: It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.

  • Because Southern Baptists defend “the privacy concerns women rightly have about sharing sleeping quarters and intimate facilities with members of the opposite sex” [12].
  • Because Competition can bring access to changing facilities. The NCAA’s 2024 women’s swimming manual provides “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. It ties athlete access to credentials: “Team staff will receive numbered wristbands and student-athletes will receive labeled credentials. No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13]
  • Because Such access has been reported. Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines saying, “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” [14]
  • Because The bill covers activities beyond the contest itself, including “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • So A male athlete excluded from female competition cannot gain access to its private team activities through a place as a female competitor. Removing that route to shared intimate facilities supports the religious custom of privacy between the sexes that [NAME] wants to uphold.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that a female competition place itself grants shared intimate access, or that the bill covers those facilities.

  • Because The swimming manual describes “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. That passage does not identify which users may use which room or say those rooms are shared across sexes.
  • Because Its credential rule says, “No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13] This makes identification necessary for venue entry. It does not make a competition credential permission to change or shower with women.

The manual does not establish that condition for sharing intimate facilities with women.
  • So The PRO’s legal route to these facilities is not established. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.

catalog.retirement_reason: General virtue formation and care through school teams are not shown to continue an inherited Christian practice; the religious ministry example does not establish that link for the covered teams.

original.title: Barring children from their existing girls' competitions removes a shared way to pass on Christian virtues.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 Barring children from their existing girls' competitions removes a shared way to pass on Christian virtues.

  • Because The rule also reaches activities reserved for team participants: “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Christian teaching values sports for building good habits, including self-control: “the virtues of temperance, humility, courage, patience can be fostered” [15].
  • Because This practice also has an American Christian ministry tradition: Upward Sports describes competition as “working together toward excellence with Christ-like love.” [16]
  • Because School teams provide these shared relationships: “Teams provide a place for kids to make friends and build relationships.” [14]
  • So Barring a child from the girls' games they already play removes shared competition with that team, a chance to practice these virtues together.
  • Because Seeking transgender children's good is part of the Southern Baptist Convention's teaching: “we love our transgender neighbors, seek their good always” [3]. The same resolution affirms that “gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [3], so this duty of care does not itself endorse girls' team placement.
  • Because The National Women's Law Center and Women's Sports Foundation warn that exclusion would “harm these students, who because of stigma and discrimination are already especially vulnerable to isolation and decreased academic performance” [14].
  • Because Uncertainty about the bill's definition of sex also threatens girls born with variations in sex traits, called intersex variations: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [14].
  • Because That warning concerns lost opportunities: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [14]
  • Because Christian teaching includes these children: “All persons are created in God’s image and are made to glorify Him” [3].
  • So Preserving this shared way to teach virtues, and following the inherited duty to care for these children, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose taking away their existing team opportunities.
  • Note Permission for “males to train or practice” [1] does not restore playing in girls' games with the team.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO has not shown that keeping these particular girls' team places preserves the Christian practice of forming and caring for children.

  • Because The Baptist resolution it cites says to “affirm God’s good design that gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [3].
  • Because The U.S. bishops' education and marriage committee chairmen applied that teaching to school sports in 2021. They said students whose gender identity differs from their sex should have athletic opportunities “in co-educational activities or, where sexes are separated, in accord with their given sex.” [17]
  • Because They paired that rule with care for those children: “Harassment or unjust discrimination against them in this regard is unequivocally immoral.” [17]
  • So These teachings make sex-based eligibility part of Christian care in sport. Showing that sport and friendship help teach virtues does not show that preserving a placement contrary to that rule carries on the practice these teachings describe. This response does not address girls with intersex variations whose eligibility is uncertain.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill bars "a person whose sex is male" and does not name intersex variations. The letter warning about intersex girls gives no rule or example showing which variations would be classified as male. Sources: [1], [14].
original.retirement_reason: General virtue formation and care through school teams are not shown to continue an inherited Christian practice; the religious ministry example does not establish that link for the covered teams.

original.title: The bill takes a decision about children's upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill takes a decision about children's upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.

  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention teaches that “parents are the primary stewards of and decision-makers for their children, rather than teachers, doctors, or the state” [18].
  • Because Catholic teaching protects work that smaller groups can do themselves; it calls it an injustice to “assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.” [19]
  • Because Sports rules are already part of local responsibility: “Currently, schools, parents, and communities manage youth sports leagues and write rules about who can participate in different sports at different levels.” [14]
  • Because Existing individual reviews already weigh safety and fairness. The Congressional Research Service describes Illinois's 2024–25 rules as “requiring approval to participate based on consideration of individual circumstances” [6] and considering whether “allowing eligibility would be inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • Because H.R.28 would remove that choice at covered schools. As Representative Norcross explained, “It inflicts blanket bans without the ability of states, local governments, schools, and parents to make reasonable exceptions.” [20]
  • So Even when parents and a willing school approve a child's participation after individual review, the federal rule would bar girls' competition if it classifies that child as male. Preserving the family and local roles taught by [NAME]'s tradition gives a reason to oppose that loss of authority.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO has not shown that the particular sports exception removed belongs to the family and local duties its religious sources protect.

  • Because The cited Baptist resolution places parents' decisions “under the authority of God, recognizing that they will be held responsible for their choices” [18].
  • Because The Southern Baptist Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission explains: “The duty of parental authority is not the right to teach children whatever they desire. Rather, it is normed by what is good, true, and righteous.” [21]
  • Because That same body addressed this sports decision on January 13, 2025: “Schools that allow biological males to participate in female sports programs are discriminating against biological females.” [22]
  • So In this account, parental and school approval does not turn that eligibility exception into an exercise of Christian care or rightful parental teaching. The PRO cannot infer that religious authority protects the exception simply because parents and a school want it.
  • Because The Catholic principle of leaving work to smaller groups also serves duties beyond those groups. The PRO's source says, “To ensure the common good, the government of each country has the specific duty to harmonize the different sectoral interests with the requirements of justice” [19].
  • Because Illinois's 2024–25 policy made eligibility a decision for the statewide sports association: “IHSA will make final rulings on student participation.” [23] Its review considered whether eligibility would be “inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • So Showing that a lower body can run a review does not establish that its eligibility standard meets the religious account of justice. The PRO has not shown that allowing this exception is a duty the cited traditions reserve to families or local groups. Its claim of lost religious authority therefore lacks the needed link.

original.title: Sex-eligibility disputes can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Sex-eligibility disputes can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.

  • Because Schools would have to apply the bill's definition of sex, but it sets no method for checking disputed eligibility: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [24]
  • Because The women's sports organizations warn that resulting checks “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [14].
  • Because Intimate questioning has occurred under a comparable state ban. The National Women's Law Center reports that a Florida investigation included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25]
  • Because Catholic teaching connects children's privacy to moral upbringing: “Respect for privacy must be considered in close connection with decency and modesty” [26].
  • So Applying the rule in schools that now allow participation would require them to settle sex-eligibility disputes. The Florida account documents intimate questioning, and the organizations also warn of invasive checks. For [NAME], keeping the particular religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy supplies the Tradition connection; general safety and dignity are separate justifications.
original.con_html:
Response The floor manager identifies a records-based route, limiting the argument about bodily examinations.

  • Because The bill adds a violation of the federal education law, Title IX, for “a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] and defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1]. Its text sets no examination procedure.
  • Because The floor manager described a records-based way to apply the bill: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [14]
  • Because The Florida source reports a state investigation that included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25] That describes questioning, not a bodily examination.
  • So The floor manager’s records-based account bears on the proposed route from this rule to bodily examinations. It does not answer the documented risk of intimate questioning, or establish that the religious modesty concern disappears. This is a limited response to the examination branch only.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Education Department's civil-rights manual limits release of documents that would cause an unwarranted invasion of privacy. Illinois's association policy kept eligibility documents confidential unless the student or parents asked otherwise. The Utah board treated the public post as a breach of rules requiring members to respect student privacy. Sources: [27], [23], [28].

original.title: Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of wildlife water.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of wildlife water.

  • Because Interior reported that deploying border staff and equipment reduced damaging traffic: “By deploying personnel, equipment, and infrastructure, CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • Because The Forest Service identified crossing-related litter: “Perhaps one of the most well known of the impacts of illegal immigration is the litter left behind” [3].
  • Because That litter spoiled wildlife water: “Water sources near this contamination are often so fouled by pollution that wildlife can no longer use them.” [3]
  • So Section 201's staffing and section 103's surveillance funds support patrols of the kind Interior credits with these local reductions. Where added patrols cut crossings through wild areas, they can reduce this pollution. Protecting wildlife water serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
original.con_html:
Response The cited local gains do not establish that S.2's added patrols would reduce, rather than shift, the traffic that pollutes wildlife water.

  • Because Interior reported local reductions: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3]
  • So Enforcement can move traffic into remote wild areas as well as reduce it. Reductions “in a number of areas” do not show that S.2's added patrols would lower the litter reaching wildlife water overall. The PRO needs evidence that the added patrols would reduce such traffic near wild water sources rather than redirect it.

original.title: Better interception protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 Better interception protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.

  • Because Section 103 limits funding for southwest and northern border towers to systems tested and accepted by CBP “to deliver autonomous capabilities.” [1]
  • Because CBP reported faster interception with autonomous towers: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that “unauthorized trails and roads have been created on the Forest by illegal foot and vehicle traffic.” [3] Their spread “damages and destroys cactus and other sensitive vegetation; disrupts or prohibits revegetation; disturbs wildlife, their security and travel routes; causes soil compaction and erosion” [3].
  • Because Crossing-related damage left a fence protecting endangered habitat “ineffective in restricting livestock use” [3]. The result was habitat loss: “This fence damage has allowed the destruction of endangered species habitat to continue” [3].
  • So Funding staff and faster detection strengthens the ability to stop damaging traffic and fence damage. That protects plants, wildlife habitat, and soil from destruction, which [NAME] values.
original.con_html:
Response A shorter detection-to-capture time does not establish less damage to trails, plants, or fences.

  • Because The tower report describes a narrower result: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3]
  • So Response speed is not total travel through habitat or avoided fence damage, and enforcement can move traffic into wild areas. The PRO has not connected faster interception to less damaging traffic overall.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Surveillance baseline: CRS says P.L. 119-21 provides $6.17 billion for inspection and surveillance technology. Sources: [5].

original.title: Intercepting unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful introduced species.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 Intercepting unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful introduced species.

  • Because In March 2025, Interior described harm from unlawful border activity: “national parks, wildlife refuges and the species they protect are adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6].
  • Because Border operations have reduced the activity carrying these risks: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • So Added staffing and surveillance support interception of this traffic. Less unlawful travel through parks and refuges can reduce one route by which harmful species spread there. Reducing such introductions is a way to protect nature.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO treats immigration interception as invasive-species control without showing which introductions it would reduce.

  • Because Interior lists lands and species as “adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6], but does not identify the species or how they arrive.
  • Because Seeds can travel on people. The National Park Service explains: “Seeds can readily become lodged in our boots and stuck to our clothing.” [7]
  • So The missing step is keeping species from reaching habitat. Catching people after entry does not itself show that seeds have been kept out. Neither the list of harms nor the general report of reduced border activity shows that S.2 would reduce these introductions, or by which pathway.

original.title: Preventing damaging crossings also addresses a source of destructive wildfires.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 Preventing damaging crossings also addresses a source of destructive wildfires.

  • Because The Forest Service documented the link: “Large numbers of warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators have caused wildfires that have destroyed valuable natural and cultural resources.” [3]
  • Because S.2 supports an established way to reduce the underlying activity. Interior reported that border operations “have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • So Supporting interception before people travel and camp through natural areas strengthens prevention of these ignitions. Avoiding fires that destroy nature gives [NAME] another reason to favor S.2.
original.con_html:
Response The sources do not connect S.2's added interceptions to fewer abandoned campfires in the forests at issue.

  • Because The Forest Service identifies “warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators” [3] as a cause of wildfires.
  • Because The same testimony reports that enforcement beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3]
  • Because Section 201 funds CBP staff and operations “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • So The PRO relies on Interior's general report of reductions in some areas. The fire evidence comes from a forest where enforcement pushed traffic into the backcountry, so added patrols do not necessarily mean fewer people camping there. The PRO needs evidence that S.2's patrols would reduce crossings in fire-prone wildlands rather than shift them.

original.title: Funding Border Patrol's other duties supports early fire warnings and calls for firefighting help.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 Funding Border Patrol's other duties supports early fire warnings and calls for firefighting help.

  • Because Section 101 pays to “hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel to conduct functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1]
  • Because Those agents provide fire warnings. After agents spotted smoke near the border in April 2025, “They promptly contacted fire crews from the Forest Service and Mexico.” [8]
  • Because U.S. crews put out the resulting spot fires: “U.S. fire services swiftly put out spot fires caused by embers that blew across the border, while Mexican crews battled the main blaze to the south.” [8]
  • Because Agents also summoned help during a 2021 Jacumba Wilderness fire: “El Centro Station notified the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) of the situation.” [9] The resulting response succeeded: “The combined resources and firefighting efforts were able to control the fires.” [9]
  • So S.2 supports staff who detect fires and bring in the crews needed to control them. This strengthens protection of natural areas from spreading fire.

original.title: Joint patrols let land officers focus on protecting natural resources.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 Joint patrols let land officers focus on protecting natural resources.

  • Because The Forest Service reported that border enforcement took officers away from conservation: “The law enforcement efforts in response to cross-border violators and smugglers of controlled substances diverts our officers from other management and resource protection activities.” [3]
  • Because Interior documented “intelligence-supported joint patrols on Interior and USFS managed lands.” [2] It reported a division of duties: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” [2]
  • Because Alongside section 201's immigration staffing, section 103 funds “Enhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals, at the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1]
  • So S.2 supports the border-enforcement side of this division of work. Preserving land officers' time for protecting natural resources serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
original.con_html:
Response A division of duties within a joint patrol does not show that S.2's funding protects land officers' time for conservation.

  • Because Interior describes patrols that used officers from both agencies: “Border Patrol agents frequently conduct joint patrols with Interior law enforcement personnel on Interior-managed lands, including national parks, wildlife refuges, and public lands.” [2]
  • Because Its account of one operation says: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” [2]
  • So This shows assigned roles within joint operations that themselves draw on land officers. The Forest Service's 2006 complaint about diversion does not show that S.2's added CBP funding would reduce the enforcement work those officers now do. The PRO has not shown that the bill would free their time for conservation.

original.title: Patrol support helps land managers carry out planned burns that care for vegetation.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 Patrol support helps land managers carry out planned burns that care for vegetation.

  • Because The Forest Service uses fire for land care as well as fighting unwanted fires: “The Forest Service works to both fight wildland fires and to use prescribed fires as a tool to manage vegetative resources.” [3] Prescribed fires are planned burns.
  • Because Security is part of doing that work: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” [3] The same testimony states: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.” [3]
  • So Section 101's support for duties outside immigration and customs enforcement backs staff who help secure these work areas. Enabling people to carry out this care for vegetation supports the active defense of nature that [NAME] values.
original.con_html:
Response The testimony does not distinguish help with fire suppression from help with planned burns.

  • Because The testimony describes clearing fire areas and guarding firefighters: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” [3] It adds: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.” [3]
  • Because The discussion covers both kinds of fire work: “during prescribed fires or fire suppression operations” [3]. Prescribed fires are planned burns.
  • So Unspecified security help at fires does not establish that Border Patrol support enabled planned burns. Without that step, the claimed support for vegetation care rests on an assumption about which fire work agents helped with.

original.title: Better aircraft and boats support protection of marine life against illegal fishing.
original.pro_html:
Point 8 Better aircraft and boats support protection of marine life against illegal fishing.

  • Because Section 103 funds upgrades and new equipment for air and marine response, as quoted above.
  • Because CBP air and marine crews joined a 2024 operation that “located and stopped a total of 19 Mexican fishermen engaged in illegal fishing” [10].
  • Because The Coast Guard described the purpose as “safeguarding our valuable resources and protecting the delicate marine environment” [10].
  • So S.2 funds equipment used in this work. Strengthening the ability to stop illegal fishing protects marine life and serves [NAME]'s concern for nature.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The April 2026 law also covered “air and marine support; and the purchase or lease of various vehicles, vessels, aircraft, and unmanned aerial systems.” The 2024 fishing result came from a joint Coast Guard, CBP and Texas operation. Sources: [5], [10].

original.title: Better aircraft can add to the capacity CBP has occasionally lent to oil-spill cleanup.
original.pro_html:
Point 9 Better aircraft can add to the capacity CBP has occasionally lent to oil-spill cleanup.

  • Because Section 103 funds upgrades and new equipment for rapid air response, as quoted above.
  • Because During the 2010 Gulf spill, CBP reported that its crews were “providing airspace de-confliction and flight advisories to the numerous government agencies that are participating in the clean up and containment efforts.” [11] This means helping cleanup aircraft share the airspace safely.
  • So S.2's platform funds add to the fleet whose crews have been called on for this support. The use is occasional and depends on which aircraft are bought, but it can add to the capacity to coordinate pollution cleanup. Helping contain oil pollution serves [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The 2010 spill report describes the P-3 as a specialized surveillance and command aircraft. The reviewed record does not identify a §103 plan buying that capability. Sources: [11], [1].

original.title: It pays for flights that pollute the air and heat the planet.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It pays for flights that pollute the air and heat the planet.

  • Because Section 202 funds deportation transport: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Such transport includes flights: “ICE’s air transportation is being carried out through a network of chartered flights” [12].
  • Because These flights emit heat-trapping pollution: “US immigration enforcement flights are producing hundreds of thousands of metric tonnes of climate-damaging carbon emissions” [12].
  • Because They also pollute the air around airports: “planes frequently idling, taking off and landing in the same communities contributes to local air pollution” [12].
  • So Added transport funding supports flights with both kinds of pollution. [NAME]’s wish to protect the environment from pollution gives a reason to oppose that support.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: §202's $31.075 billion is a shared pool with no flight line. CRS reports a plan to use FY2025 reconciliation funds to offset $350 million in Transportation and Removal Operations in FY2027. The targeted search did not find a flight-program funding record separating added flights. Sources: [13], [1].

original.title: It funds detention operations that keep wildlife away from facility sites.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It funds detention operations that keep wildlife away from facility sites.

  • Because Section 202 pays to keep enforcement facilities in use: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1] It also funds “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1]
  • Because Dilley, Texas, is part of ICE’s detention network, and its operation depends on ICE funding. The site had been idled in 2024 “when funding for the contract with ICE was terminated and the facility was idled” [14]. In March 2025 its operator announced that “it has agreed under an amended intergovernmental services agreement (IGSA) between the City of Dilley, Texas, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to resume operations” [14].
  • Because ICE’s assessment found that the cleared site offered “limited natural habitat for native wildlife” but expected wildlife to avoid it during use: “migratory birds and other wildlife will likely avoid the proposed project area during construction activities and during operations.” [15]
  • So S.2 gives ICE more resources to run facilities with this effect. The disturbance at this already-cleared site is small, but protecting wildlife still gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added support.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: Dilley's assessment compares operation with never building. Operations resumed in March 2025 under an agreement running to March 2030. The targeted search did not find a record tying S.2 to Dilley's scale or duration. Sources: [15], [14], [13].

original.title: It supports air pollution from detention facilities and their vehicles.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It supports air pollution from detention facilities and their vehicles.

  • Because Section 202 funds “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” [1] and “Funding for fleet maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because ICE’s Dilley assessment identifies operating sources of air pollution: “vehicular use and emergency generators during the operation phase.” [15]
  • So Added money for these facilities and vehicle fleets supports activities that emit air pollution. [NAME]’s wish to prevent pollution gives a reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The Dilley assessment says extended generator use would occur during power disruptions, and its comparison assumes no facility. Sources: [15].

original.title: It supports detention operations that risk polluting land and water.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It supports detention operations that risk polluting land and water.

  • Because Section 202 funds the running of enforcement facilities through “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” [1].
  • Because Social Circle’s city government warns that operating ICE’s planned detention center would “risk sewage overflows into nearby land and water” [16].
  • Because Maryland’s assessment of the Williamsport warehouse proposal explains the same operating risk. Its agencies estimate sewage flow at “more than seven times the existing projected flow for the facility’s prior commercial use.” [17]
  • Because They explain the risk: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” [17].
  • Because The waterways at issue support wildlife: “A number of State-listed Endangered species, Species in Need of Conservation, and other Rare species rely on the waters in the vicinity of the Warehouse property.” [17]
  • So More operating money supports a detention network pursuing warehouse conversions with documented sewage risks, as Social Circle’s plans show. Protecting land, water, and the wildlife that depends on them gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that support.
original.con_html:
Response The sewage argument leaves out barriers to the conversions that existed before June 9, 2026.

  • Because Social Circle's city manager described a condition on water access: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity.” [18]
  • Because The April 15 preliminary court order barred Williamsport's detention conversion: “Defendants are enjoined during the pendency of this lawsuit from construction and renovation at the warehouse located at 16220 Wright Road, Williamsport, Maryland 21795 (the “Williamsport Warehouse”) for the purposes of operating the warehouse as a detention and processing facility;” [19]
  • Because Maryland's warning concerns exceeding existing sewer capacity: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” [17].
  • Because Its required response is to address that capacity: “Any necessary upgrades must comply with applicable State permitting requirements and be funded by DHS.” [17]
  • So S.2's operating money does not itself lift the water restriction, the court order, or the permit requirements. The warnings do not show that the bill makes operation beyond sewer limits more likely. That requires a link from the added funds to the unsafe operation despite those barriers.

original.title: It equips border patrols whose off-road driving damages desert wilderness.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It equips border patrols whose off-road driving damages desert wilderness.

  • Because Section 201 funds “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1] for immigration enforcement.
  • Because At Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, an interagency agreement allows emergency off-road patrols: “This agreement authorizes border enforcement agents to drive off-road in wilderness under exigent or emergency circumstances that involve threats to human health and safety.” [20]
  • Because In 2012, the National Park Service reported that, since the agreement took effect, “monitoring data have shown that off-road-vehicle impacts have increased” [20].
  • Because Its account of undesignated roads and trails explains the physical harm: “These incursions damage soils, vegetation, and wildlife habitat.” [21]
  • So Extra money for these patrols supports off-road driving that damages soil, plants, and habitat. Protecting wild places gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
original.con_html:
Response More border-patrol staffing does not by itself mean more damaging off-road driving at Organ Pipe.

  • Because Section 201 funds several uses of personnel: “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1].
  • Because The agreement behind the PRO's example allows agents to patrol “on foot or on horseback” [22].
  • Because The Park Service later documented staffing growth aimed at reducing vehicle use: “The U.S. Border Patrol Ajo Station has increased its Horse Patrol Unit (HPU) with the recent graduation of agents through the class. The Ajo Station HPU patrols at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in an effort to reduce mechanized equipment in the wilderness.” [23]
  • So Personnel funding and damaging vehicle use are separate steps. The PRO's 2012 damage trend does not show that S.2 increases such driving or keeps it going when it would otherwise stop. The same site's horse patrols show why staffing growth alone cannot establish that link.

original.title: It puts forest protection and restoration crews at risk of removal.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It puts forest protection and restoration crews at risk of removal.

  • Because Sections 201 and 202 pay immigration enforcement personnel “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Those activities reach forest workers. In 2025 Border Patrol arrested a firefighter whose work included “clearing fallen trees and other debris to prevent the Bear Gulch fire, a 9,000-acre blaze, from growing” [24]. He was later “quietly deported to Mexico” [24].
  • Because ICE has also removed tree-planting crews. After a 2007 raid on a contractor replanting burned land in Boise National Forest, “Ten of the workers were deported to Mexico and four others were released pending an immigration hearing” [25].
  • Because That work had a short planting window. The Forest Service spokesman explained: “You have to plant in cooler times, when the ground is moist” [25].
  • Because Delayed replanting threatens nature. In 2025 the Forest Resources Association warned that without timely reforestation, “these lands risk erosion, habitat loss” [26].
  • So More capacity to arrest and remove these workers puts time-sensitive forest care at risk. Protecting forests gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added capacity.
original.con_html:
Response The forestry examples do not show that S.2 raises the risk of leaving needed forest work without crews.

  • Because Follow-up reporting on the 2025 incident found continued crew assignments: “Both of the private crews have active agreements with the Forest Service and have been assigned to new fires.” [27]
  • Because The 2007 report describes an effort to replace arrested workers: “For now, Olson said his office is working with the company to get replacement workers as soon as possible.” [25]
  • Because The forestry association argues for more temporary work visas. Its proposed remedies include: “An exemption for forestry workers from the H-2B visa cap to address the reforestation backlog.” [26]
  • So Arrests alone do not establish the risk of forest work lacking crews; continued assignments and replacement efforts also matter. A warning about harm from delayed planting does not show that S.2 raises the chance of those delays. The PRO has not connected the added enforcement funds to a greater risk of unfilled planting or forest-protection work.

original.title: It strengthens surveillance tools that can deter people from defending nature.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It strengthens surveillance tools that can deter people from defending nature.

  • Because Section 103 funds CBP aircraft and related equipment: “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” [1]
  • Because That branch uses surveillance drones to help other law enforcement. A 2025 CBP statement reported that “MQ-9 Predators are supporting our federal law enforcement partners in the Greater Los Angeles area, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with aerial support of their operations.” [28]
  • Because CBP has used such tools at environmental protests: “Customs and Border Protection responded to the protests with its MQ-9 Reaper drone” [29]. The Standing Rock movement sought “to protect water, the climate, and Indigenous sovereignty” [29]. During a 2020 pipeline dispute, “CBP flew drones over its planned pipeline route and over the homes of anti-pipeline activists” [28].
  • Because Researcher Nathan Goodman identifies the barrier to participation: “Surveilling protesters is a concerning use of drones, as it may chill or repress speech, association and assembly protected by the First Amendment.” [28]
  • So S.2's platform money can enlarge or upgrade the aerial fleet whose drones have been lent for monitoring environmental defenders, although the bill does not specify drones. The added risk of deterring their participation gives [NAME], who values taking part in defending nature, a reason to oppose it.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: §103 states a 'rapid air and marine response' purpose and names no drones. No platform list or protest-mission frequency series was found. Sources: [1].

original.title: It helps find and rescue children suffering sexual abuse.
original.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps find and rescue children suffering sexual abuse.

  • Because Section 102 sets aside money for more investigators and analysts: “$108,500,000 shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” [1].
  • Because Their funded task is “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1]. The money also funds training for investigators and local police: “to train such personnel and State and local law enforcement regarding identifying victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1].
  • Because Representative Lee described the unmet need: “Today, more than 89,000 children depicted in child sex abuse material remain unidentified.” [2]. In fiscal year 2024, an international operation hosted by HSI's victim-identification lab led to the “identification and assistance of over 140 victims.” [3].
  • So More investigators, analysts and trained police strengthen the work of finding these children and helping them escape abuse. Protecting children who cannot secure their own safety serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and their chance of a safe childhood.

original.title: It supports teaching children and families how to prevent online sexual abuse.
original.pro_html:
Point 2 It supports teaching children and families how to prevent online sexual abuse.

  • Because Section 102 adds money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1] and for HSI's operations.
  • Because HSI's Project iGuardian teaches children, parents and community groups through “in-person presentations” [3]. Its wider campaign aims to “prevent and combat online child sexual exploitation and abuse” [3].
  • So S.2's general HSI funds can help sustain or expand this teaching, although the bill does not direct money to it. The teaching gives families tools to spot danger and seek help before abuse takes hold. Helping children protect themselves serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect general staffing funds for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) to more education for children and families.

  • Because Project iGuardian uses “special agents and subject matter experts” [3] to give presentations. More presentations therefore require their time, not just a larger agency budget.
  • Because November 2025 reporting described agents being reassigned to immigration work, “dramatically slowing investigations into child exploitation and sex trafficking” [4]. Agents' time was therefore under competing demands.
  • Because Section 102 funds agents and support staff for “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. Its specific child-protection training requirement concerns “such personnel and State and local law enforcement” [1], not presentations to families.
  • So The PRO identifies a teaching program that depends on agents' time, and training investigators to identify victims does not add that time. This leaves the step from general funds to more teaching uncertain. It does not show that general funds could not reach this work.

original.title: It strengthens protection and help for people forced into sex or labor.
original.pro_html:
Point 3 It strengthens protection and help for people forced into sex or labor.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI agents and “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because This work includes criminal investigations of coercion: “Homeland Security Investigations initiated 1,686 criminal investigations related to sex trafficking and forced labor, leading to 2,545 arrests.” [5]. These are fiscal year 2024 results.
  • Because An HSI-backed sex-trafficking case involving adults and children brought an abuser to justice: “the defendant was found guilty at a jury trial and sentenced to 380 months” [3] after using “violence, false imprisonment and the use of drugs.” [3].
  • Because HSI's victim program also ensures survivors “are informed of their rights” [3] and “receive necessary assistance” [3]. Earlier added funds enabled that program “to create 76 new full-time positions” [3].
  • So More resources for investigations and victim support strengthen both escape from coercion and help afterward. Freedom from forced sex and work, access to help, and justice against abusers serve [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and equal opportunities.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s examples do not show that S.2 would add trafficking investigations or survivor-support staff under the changed assignment policy.

  • Because November 2025 reporting described agents being reassigned to immigration work, “dramatically slowing investigations into child exploitation and sex trafficking” [4]. This directly challenges an unchanged link between HSI’s budget and its trafficking work.
  • Because The earlier expansion of the Victim Assistance Program came from targeted funding: “From FY 2020 to FY 2023, the VAP received congressional enhancement funds” [3]. That precedent shows what targeted money did, not what general HSI funding would do.
  • Because Its money must support “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]. That limits how these dollars may be spent; it does not say which other work they reach.
  • So The PRO has not shown that this funding would reach trafficking cases under those assignments, or add the survivor-support jobs its precedent describes. This weakens the step from HSI's budget to this work. It does not show that general funds could not help.

original.title: It strengthens the response to scams against older people and other victims.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It strengthens the response to scams against older people and other victims.

  • Because Section 102's staffing and operating funds support HSI's criminal work, including “wire fraud, identity theft, bank fraud” [3].
  • Because Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported that in fiscal year 2024, “HSI also conducted 258 elder fraud cases” [3], producing “121 indictments, 52 convictions, and $12.6 million seized.” [3]. HSI also investigated romance scams: “HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” [3] cases that year.
  • So More capacity to investigate these scams, secure convictions and seize criminals' proceeds strengthens protection against financial exploitation. [NAME] has a reason to protect victims' resources and seek justice for them, including strangers targeted because of age or trust.
original.con_html:
Response The fraud totals do not establish more protection against scams from S.2 under HSI’s changed priorities.

  • Because The fraud results are explicitly past results: “In FY 2024, HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” [3] cases and “258 elder fraud cases” [3]. They describe an earlier distribution of investigators’ work.
  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned en masse to immigration enforcement” [6]. Section 102 provides broad “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1], without reserving funds for elder or romance fraud.
  • So The PRO needs a reason to expect added investigators’ time to reach these scams under the priorities in place at the vote. The 2024 totals do not provide it.

original.title: It supports justice for victims of atrocities abroad.
original.pro_html:
Point 5 It supports justice for victims of atrocities abroad.

  • Because Section 102 adds resources for HSI staff and “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because HSI's human rights center helps prosecute people for “human rights violations and war crimes” [3] committed before they entered the United States. In fiscal year 2024, it “supported more than 180 investigations” [3] related to suspected war criminals.
  • So Resources for investigating and prosecuting these crimes strengthen efforts to hold abusers accountable. [NAME]'s concern for justice extends to victims abroad, including people [NAME] has never met.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The center's 180-plus investigations cover a mixed mission including removal and other agencies, and §102 excludes HSI's immigration-enforcement mission, so the count may include work §102 cannot fund. Sources: [3], [1].

original.title: It adds resources to intercept drugs that cause overdoses.
original.pro_html:
Point 6 It adds resources to intercept drugs that cause overdoses.

  • Because Section 103 adds $3.45 billion for inspection equipment, air and marine response, surveillance and related work: “$3,450,000,000 for the following” [1]. Its purposes include “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders” [1].
  • Because The funded work includes “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1], meaning ingredients used to make drugs. ICE describes the resulting danger as “the synthetic drugs that fuel overdose deaths” [3].
  • So Finding and intercepting these drugs keeps seized supplies from reaching people. More resources for that work strengthen protection for people at risk of overdose, whose lives matter to [NAME].
original.con_html:
Response Cheap replacement weakens the inference from a seized shipment to lower overall drug exposure.

  • Because Drug-policy researchers Jonathan Caulkins and Peter Reuter explain: “But traffickers can easily replace what is seized.” [7] Their stated mechanism is that fentanyl is cheap to make and easy to move: “It is absurdly cheap for high-level traffickers to replace seizures.” [7]
  • Because A 2026 systematic review (search through April 2025) treated some seizures as enforcement disruptions. The results it describes point in different directions: local or regional studies linked seizures to more overdoses nearby or the next year, while a Florida county study linked fewer seizures to more deaths. These are associations, not estimates for S.2's border resources. [8]
  • So The replacement mechanism challenges the PRO's step from seized shipments to lower net exposure and overdose risk. It does not deny that seized drugs themselves stay off the street, and neither the review nor cheap replacement proves that added interception has no benefit.

original.title: It strengthens the capacity to take convicted violent offenders into immigration custody.
original.pro_html:
Point 7 It strengthens the capacity to take convicted violent offenders into immigration custody.

  • Because Section 202 funds staff “to carry out immigration enforcement activities” [1] and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1].
  • Because This work includes taking custody of people convicted of attacks on children. ICE reported a January 2026 arrest of a man convicted of “first-degree rape of a child” [9]: “upon his release from prison Jan. 2, ICE took him into custody for removal to Mexico.” [9].
  • So Added staff and transport resources support taking convicted violent offenders into custody after prison release. Custody limits their access to potential victims in the community, giving [NAME] a reason to support protection against further attacks.
original.notes_html: Evidence note: The cited man was already in ICE custody in January 2026. §202(9) reserves at least $350 million for specified non-cooperating jurisdictions and covers more than violent convictions. The reviewed record does not identify the offense shares of arrests added by S.2. Sources: [9], [10], [1].

original.title: It strengthens criminal investigations of terrorist threats.
original.pro_html:
Point 8 It strengthens criminal investigations of terrorist threats.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI agents, support staff and “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because HSI's National Security Unit “supports counterterrorism investigations within HSI.” [3]. HSI's fiscal year 2024 results in this work included “70 criminal indictments” [3], and ICE credited HSI with helping produce “terrorism-related disruptions.” [3].
  • So Resources for investigating and disrupting terrorist threats strengthen protection for people exposed to violence. [NAME]'s concern includes potential victims who are strangers.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO’s earlier counterterrorism results do not show that new funds would restore or expand investigators’ work on threats.

  • Because The report places the “70 criminal indictments” [3] in fiscal year 2024. In January 2026, senators cited reporting that “a major joint FBI-HSI investigation into illicit Iranian oil shipments” [6] had “suffered from the redeployment” [6] of investigators.
  • Because Section 102 provides “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1] for eligible HSI work. It does not assign investigators back to these cases or reserve a counterterrorism staff increase.
  • So The PRO’s missing link is investigators’ time on threats under the assignment policy in place at the vote. An earlier criminal-case total does not show that added agency funds would supply it.

original.title: It supports protection of essential services from cyberattacks.
original.pro_html:
Point 9 It supports protection of essential services from cyberattacks.

  • Because Section 102 adds resources for HSI staff and “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. HSI's criminal work includes protecting computer systems.
  • Because HSI's Operation Cyber Centurion fights attacks on “major utilities, healthcare, public education” [3], financial systems and emergency services. In fiscal year 2024, it “disrupted 195” [3] computer break-ins and attacks.
  • So Resources to stop attacks on hospitals, utilities and emergency services protect people who depend on those services for safety and care. This serves [NAME]'s concern for people least able to protect themselves during an emergency.
original.con_html:
Response The cyberattack count does not establish more protection for essential services from S.2.

  • Because The report says, “In FY 2024, OCC disrupted 195” [3] intrusions and attacks. That measures the existing operation’s work, not the effect of additional funding under the later assignment policy.
  • Because The January 2026 letter reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned en masse to immigration enforcement” [6]. Section 102 funds broad “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1], without a separate allocation of cyber investigators or operating funds.
  • So The PRO cannot carry the earlier work pattern forward without showing how the new money would reach cyber investigations. The count supplies no such link to additional protection for hospitals or utilities.

original.title: It supports rescues of migrants in life-threatening danger.
original.pro_html:
Point 10 It supports rescues of migrants in life-threatening danger.

  • Because Section 103 funds “new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities” [1]. Section 101 funds Border Patrol personnel for “functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1].
  • Because These teams perform rescues. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) reported that an April 2024 aircrew located lost migrants, landed, and treated an unresponsive man who was “severely dehydrated and suffering from heat exhaustion.” [11]. A Border Patrol emergency medical technician then took over his care.
  • Because CBP explained the mechanism: “The ability of our agents to rapidly transition from a law enforcement role to conduct rescue operations where they can deliver immediate medical aid is crucial to saving lives.” [11].
